title: green beans
text:
Whole or broken pods of the common bean, stewed slow with a piece of pork until they give up their squeak and take on the meat's salt, and served in a cup or a compartment beside the barbecue. They are the plain vegetable on a Carolina barbecue plate — a house that keeps one vegetable and no buffet usually keeps these — and the Southern way with them is long cooking rather than short, so the pod goes soft and olive rather than staying bright.

The pod bean has been in Southern cookbooks as long as there have been Southern cookbooks, under the names the field gave it. Mary Randolph heads the receipt 'Ragout of French Beans, Snaps, String Beans' in 1824 and boils them fifteen minutes before finishing them in brown gravy — the short French method. Maria Massey Barringer, writing at Concord, North Carolina in 1867, gives an hour and a half in salt water and then butter and cream, and adds that the more common way is to boil them with a piece of thin middling, the side of the hog. That second sentence is the Southern one, and the one the barbecue plate inherited. On barbecue menus the bean is the mark of a short kitchen: when Beau Hammond opened Henry's Smokehouse in Greenville, South Carolina, the whole side list was coleslaw and simmered green beans.

The pods are snapped or cut into lengths and the strings pulled off, where there are any. They go into a pot with a piece of streak-of-lean, fatback, ham hock or bacon and enough water to cover, and simmer an hour or more until soft; new potatoes are often dropped in with them for the last stretch. Salt, black pepper, sometimes a little sugar or a splash of the pot's own vinegar. The pot liquor goes into the bowl with them. A shorter method — fifteen or twenty minutes, then butter and cream — is in the old books and is not what a pit serves.

On the plate at B's Barbecue in Greenville, North Carolina, where the sides are slaw, potatoes or green beans; the whole side list at Henry's Smokehouse in Greenville, South Carolina, with the coleslaw; on the buffets at McCabe's in Manning and Shealy's in Batesburg-Leesville; printed as string beans on the menu at Parker's in Wilson.

Root: green + bean; the older Southern names are string beans, for the fibre pulled off the pod before cooking, and snaps, for the sound the pod makes when broken.

green beans to B's Barbecue: one of the three sides: slaw, potatoes or green beans.

green beans to Henry's Smokehouse: half the original side list, with the coleslaw.

green beans to McCabe's Bar-B-Q: on the Manning buffet with the greens and the butter beans.

green beans to Shealy's Bar-B-Que: green and butter beans both, on the Batesburg-Leesville line.

green beans to Parker's Barbecue: printed as string beans on the Wilson menu.

green beans to boiled potatoes: the other plain eastern vegetable, often cooked in the same pot.

green beans to collards: the other pork-cooked green; a buffet with room keeps both.

green beans to baked beans: the sweet bean on the same board, which is why a menu distinguishes them.

green beans to barbecue tray: the vegetable compartment, where a house keeps one.

green beans to fixins: one of the fixins on an eastern plate.

Not to be confused with baked-beans: Green beans are the pod, cooked with pork and served in their own liquor; baked beans are dried white beans in a sweet brown sauce.

Beans String, and break them in halves; boil in salt and water, and throw in a piece of soda the size of a pea, if they are old, or you wish them a fine color. Boil them for an hour and a half; pour off the water, and dress with butter and cream, and sprinkle over some pepper. But a more common way is to boil them with a piece of thin middling.

Ragout of French Beans, Snaps, String Beans Let them be young and fresh gathered, string them, and cut them in long thin slices; throw them in boiling water for fifteen minutes; have ready some well seasoned brown gravy, drain the water from the beans, put them in the gravy, stew them a few minutes, and serve them garnished with forcemeat balls; there must not be gravy enough to float the beans.

Lima Beans Let them boil about an hour, and when the water is poured off, season with salt, pepper, and butter. Send to table hot. Dried Lima beans must be soaked over night, and boiled two hours, or until they are soft, and should have some cream added to the dressing.

title: hash and rice
text:
A thick stew, or gravy, of pork cooked down with onions until it can be eaten with a spoon, ladled over white rice beside the barbecue. It is South Carolina's side the way Brunswick stew is Georgia's, Virginia's and North Carolina's, and it is barely known outside the state. The old hash was made from what the whole hog left after the barbecue — the head, the liver and the lights (the lungs) — simmered for a day in an iron pot; most restaurants now use shoulder or ham. Three loose regions: mustard in the Midlands, vinegar and liver in the Lowcountry, beef and onions in the Upstate.

Hash was on the table before the Civil War in the counties along the Savannah River. Robert Moss found it in the Abbeville Press and Banner — 'rich hash' at a barbecue at Matthews' Spring in 1854, 'smoking hash' at Robinson's Spring in 1858 — and at an 1861 barbecue for the Edgefield Riflemen, and Estella Jones, who had been enslaved on plantations near Augusta, remembered the men cooking hash and rice there. The cooks were Black, the pots were iron, the fire was wood and the cooking took a day; what went in was the head, the liver and the lights that the whole hog left behind, which Moss reads in the name itself, haslet, the old word for the viscera. Howard Conyers, who grew up with it in the Black churches of the Midlands, calls it liver-and-lights hash and says it is now nearly impossible to get unless you kill your own hog, because federal rules keep lungs out of commercial processing. Hash houses stood across the Upstate, some set up by textile-mill owners to draw farmers to town. The Post and Courier reported in 2020 that hash was fading from the state's restaurants; Moss answered in Southern Living that new places were adding it to their menus. *Tradition holds —* the pot is stirred all night, and some say it must be cooked by the light of the moon; Lake High of the South Carolina Barbeque Association calls the finished thing 'liquid sausage'.

The meat — shoulder, ham, or the head and liver where a pit still uses them — is boiled until it falls from the bone, picked, then ground through a hand-crank grinder or chopped, and returned to the pot with onions and its own stock to simmer until it thickens to gravy. The seasoning marks the region: mustard in the Midlands and the Dutch Fork, vinegar and ketchup in the Lowcountry, beef with onions and butter and no dominant base in the Upstate (called white hash), a red hash around Sumter. Potatoes go in at some pits and never at others. Served by the ladle over white rice, beside the pork, on a buffet plate or in a styrofoam bowl.

Hash is on the buffet at Dukes in Orangeburg and Walterboro, at Sweatman's in Holly Hill, at Midway in Buffalo and at True BBQ in West Columbia; Big T in Gadsden and Brown's in Kingstree still put hog's head and liver in the pot (Moss, 2020). A survey found it most common around Columbia. Fire departments and civic clubs cook it in big pots for fundraisers.

Root: French hacher 'to chop up' (from Old French hache 'axe') → English hash, verb, 1650s, 'to hack, chop into small pieces' → hash, noun, 1660s, 'a stew of meat cut into small pieces'.

hash and rice to South Carolina mustard barbecue: the style whose plate it sits on, over rice, beside mustard-sauced pork; in the Midlands the mustard is in the hash too.

hash and rice to Pee Dee whole-hog barbecue: where liver hash holds on, around Florence, Latta and Hemingway.

hash and rice to whole hog: the hog whose head and organs made the first hash.

hash and rice to hog killing: the source of the head, liver and lights, and of the wash pot it was cooked in.

hash and rice to Brunswick stew: the stew that holds hash's place in Georgia, Virginia and North Carolina: tomato, corn and beans, and no rice under it.

hash and rice to chicken bog: the other rice pot of South Carolina, cooked for the tobacco crew where hash is cooked for the barbecue.

hash and rice to Carolina Gold: the word for both the Lowcountry rice the dish sits on and the mustard sauce beside it.

hash and rice to mustard-based barbecue sauce: in the Midlands pot as well as on the meat.

hash and rice to Dutch Fork: the German-settled fork of the rivers where mustard goes into the hash.

hash and rice to Dukes Bar-B-Que: where hash and rice has been on the buffet since Earl Dukes opened in Orangeburg in 1955.

hash and rice to Sweatman's Bar-B-Que: where hash sits beside whole hog and mustard sauce in Holly Hill.

hash and rice to Midway BBQ: the Upstate's hash, in Buffalo.

hash and rice to Brown's Bar-B-Que: one of the pits that still cooks hash from hog's head and liver.

hash and rice to Lake High: who calls it liquid sausage.

hash and rice to Robert F. Moss: who found it in the 1854 newspapers and traced the name to haslet.

hash and rice to South Carolina Barbeque Association: Lake High's association, which judges hash with the barbecue.

hash and rice to pig pickin': in South Carolina the pickin's side is hash or pilau over rice.

hash and rice to fundraiser barbecue: the fire-department and club hash pots.

Not to be confused with brunswick-stew: Brunswick stew is red with tomato and full of corn and butter beans; hash is brown or mustard-yellow, smooth enough to spoon, and comes over rice.

Not to be confused with chicken-bog: In bog the rice is cooked in the pot with the chicken; hash is a gravy ladled over rice cooked apart.

To Hash Pig's Head Ingredients: Black pepper, salt, a little sage.; 2 onions chopped fine.; A little red pepper.; 1 teaspoonful mace.; 1 teaspoonful cloves. Take head, feet, and haslet of pig; boil them until done, then cut them up fine, taking out the bones.

Put it back in the same vessel with liquor and cook till done, then thicken with a little flour. Add two hard-boiled eggs and one cup walnut catsup. — Mrs. Dr. G.

Southern Hash Ingredients: 4 raw potatoes,; ½ cup of water,; 2 green peppers,; 1½ cups cold chopped beef,; 2 tomatoes,; Salt and pepper,; 1 onion,; Toast points. Put vegetables through the meat chopper, using coarse cutter; cook in the stock, covered, until tender; add beef, salt, and pepper, and when hot turn on a platter and garnish with toast points. If corned beef and stock are used, use salt with care.

To Make Hash (receipt 123) Meats that have been once done, only require to be warmed over. To cook them again renders them tough and insipid. Cut up the vegetables to be used for seasoning — onions, potatoes, tomatoes, etc., as may be preferred. Put the butter, flour, salt, pepper, and vegetables (or spices if preferred as seasoning) into the stew-pan with all the cold gravy that may have been saved; essence of ham answers a good purpose; a few inches of portable soup is very good if there should not be sufficiency of gravy; a teacup of boiling water for a pound of meat; very little water should be used. Cover the stew-pan and let this stew gently a quarter of an hour, shaking the stew-pan frequently. Have the meat minced fine, removing all bones and gristle, add to the gravy, stirring it in well. Let it remain until the meat is thoroughly hot, and serve. Use catsup upon the plate for extempore dressing. Very little cooking is necessary and very little gravy. When there is stuffing, a small quantity may be used.

title: hushpuppies
text:
Balls or fingers of cornmeal batter — meal, a little flour, egg, buttermilk or water, salt, soda, often onion — dropped by the spoonful into hot oil and fried until the outside is crisp and dark gold and the inside soft and steaming. In the Carolinas they are the bread of the fish fry and, since the 1940s, of the barbecue tray: Lexington pits serve them with the shoulder and red slaw in place of rolls, and most eastern pits give them with whole hog, though a third of the pits in the Wilson–Greenville counties give corn sticks instead. Sweeter and lighter than a corn stick, and fried, not baked.

The first of them had a fish in the name. Romeo Govan, born into slavery in the 1840s, settled after Emancipation near Cannon's Bridge on the Edisto River, five miles from Bamberg, South Carolina, and by the early 1900s ran a club house where the state's political and civic clubs came for his fish fries; the Augusta Chronicle wrote in 1903 of his never-to-be-forgotten 'red horse bread' — cornmeal, water, salt and egg dropped by spoonfuls into the lard the fish had fried in, named for the red horse, a river fish. Govan died in 1915; red horse bread lived on at fish fries in Bamberg, Orangeburg and Dorchester counties through the 1920s. Across the Savannah the same fritter was picking up another name: the Macon Telegraph in 1927 has a church fish-fry chairman cooking 'the hushpuppies', in quotation marks, a word still strange, and by 1940 a Chronicle fishing columnist could write that red horse cornbread is often called hush puppies on the Georgia side. Florida fishing camps fed them to Northern visitors and the name won. In North Carolina the hushpuppy walked from the fish camps of the Piedmont rivers into the barbecue houses in the 1940s: Kennedy's in Greensboro advertised barbecue, Brunswick stew, slaw and hushpuppies in 1949, and Warner Stamey — whose son Keith says he picked the idea up from a friend's fish camp, the Friendly Road Inn in Greensboro — made them the bread of Lexington-style barbecue.

Self-rising cornmeal, or meal with soda and a little flour, salt, an egg, buttermilk or water, and chopped onion for the savoury kind; some pits sweeten the batter and some add beer or jalapeño. The batter rests thick enough to hold a spoon, is dropped into oil at frying heat — in the old way, the oil the fish came out of — and fried until it floats and browns. Lexington houses fry them to order and shape them round, oblong or as fingers, dense or light, house by house. Served hot in the tray or in a paper bag as a side.

Lexington Barbecue: hushpuppies small $3.10, large $3.90 cash (September 2026); the Barbecue Center gives a choice of hushpuppies or a potato bun with every plate. House-Autry Mills of Four Oaks still sells the Original Recipe Hushpuppy Mix descended from Walter Thompson's post-war Swansboro business.

Root: hush + puppy. 'Hush puppy' was slang for something that keeps a thing quiet — hush money in a 1738 British account of smuggling, and from 1879 the gravy or pot liquor that kept the hounds from growling, meaning a growling stomach — and was applied to deep-fried cornmeal by 1899; current in Georgia by 1927 (Moss).

hushpuppies to Lexington-style barbecue: the style that made them barbecue bread, from the 1940s, in place of rolls.

hushpuppies to Eastern North Carolina barbecue: the bread at two eastern pits in three; the third gives corn sticks.

hushpuppies to cornbread: the baked or stick-shaped bread it displaced across most of the state.

hushpuppies to barbecue tray: the handful in the corner of the tray.

hushpuppies to red slaw: its partner in a Lexington tray.

hushpuppies to Brunswick stew: on Kennedy's 1949 Greensboro plate together.

hushpuppies to Warner Stamey: who carried them from a Greensboro fish camp to the barbecue tray.

hushpuppies to Stamey's Barbecue: which calls hushpuppies with barbecue a Stamey's invention.

hushpuppies to Lexington Barbecue: sells them by the small or large order.

hushpuppies to Bar-B-Q Center: hushpuppies or a potato bun with every plate.

hushpuppies to pig pickin': eaten at the pickin with slaw and beans.

hushpuppies to fixins: the tray's fixins, in the eastern word: hushpuppies, slaw, potatoes.

Not to be confused with cornbread: A hushpuppy is fried, round or finger-shaped and light inside; a corn stick is a dense eight-inch baton; Skylight's cornbread is a flat baked cake. If it came out of a fryer and is not a stick, it is a hushpuppy.

Hush Puppies Ingredients: Vegetable oil for frying; 1½ cups yellow corn meal; 1 cup all-purpose flour; 1 teaspoon baking powder; ½ teaspoon baking soda; 1¾ teaspoons salt; 3 eggs, lightly beaten; ⅛ teaspoon cayenne pepper; ¼ cup chopped green onions; 1 cup milk; ¼ cup vegetable oil 1. Pour oil 3–4 inches (7.5 cm to 10 cm) deep in a pan and preheat to 370°F (~190°C).
2. In bowl mix cornmeal, flour, baking powder, baking soda, salt, and cayenne.
3. Mix in eggs, green onions, milk, and ¼ cup vegetable oil.
4. Spoon 6–7 tablespoons of the batter into preheated oil.
5. Fry, stirring constantly for overall browning, until golden brown.
6. Remove from heat and drain on paper towels.

Corn Fritters Having removed the shucks and silks from a dozen young tender ears of corn, grate or scrape the grains fine from the cobs, mix with it the beaten yolks of four eggs, two spoonfuls of flour, a salt-spoonful of salt, and a teaspoonful of pepper; mix the whole together, stirring it till it is well intermingled; then drop it by spoonfuls into a pan of boiling butter or lard, making them all as nearly the same shape and size as possible; turn them over once, and when both sides are of a light brown, serve them up. It is a breakfast dish, and is quite an agreeable relish.

Virginia Corn Fritters Ingredients: 1 can corn,; ½ cup milk,; ½ cup dried and sifted crumbs,; 1 teaspoon salt,; 1 teaspoon baking powder,; 1 egg well beaten,; 1 tablespoon flour. Chop the corn, and add other ingredients in order given. Drop from a tablespoon into hot, deep fat and fry until brown.

title: mac and cheese
text:
Macaroni in a cheese sauce, most often cheddar, baked in a dish until the top browns. On a Carolina barbecue buffet it sits with the vegetables and is taken as one, cut in squares from a hotel pan rather than spooned; a stovetop version bound with a white sauce is the other common form. In the Lowcountry and in Black Southern kitchens the baked, custard-set kind is often called macaroni pie.

The dish reaches the South through the first cookbook written here. Elizabeth Raffald printed a baked macaroni with cream, butter and Parmesan in England in 1769; one account has James Hemings, enslaved by Thomas Jefferson and trained as a cook in France, bringing the method to the United States, and Jefferson served 'a pie called macaroni' at a state dinner in 1802. Mary Randolph's The Virginia House-Wife of 1824 carries a recipe under the name macaroni and cheese: three things, macaroni, cheese and butter, layered and baked in a hot oven. Mrs. A. P. Hill's Southern cookbook of 1867 gives the same layering and then a custard version with three beaten eggs poured over. Factory macaroni and factory cheese put it within reach of every household, and by then it had stopped being a rich person's dish. On a Carolina barbecue menu it is a late arrival and a well-established one: at Luella's in Asheville it is on the board because the daughter the restaurant is half named for likes it.

Macaroni is boiled in salted water until just tender and drained. For the baked kind it is layered in a dish with grated cheddar, salt and pieces of butter, covered with milk or cream, and baked until the top browns; for the custard kind beaten eggs and evaporated or whole milk are poured over the layers so the dish sets and can be cut. A stovetop version makes a Mornay — a white sauce with cheese melted into it — and stirs the macaroni through. At a pit it is baked in a hotel pan in the morning and held warm on the line.

On the buffet at Dukes Bar-B-Que in Orangeburg, at Shealy's in Batesburg-Leesville, at Brown's in Kingstree, and at Jackie Hite's in Leesville while it ran. Among the sides at Lewis Barbecue in Charleston. At Luella's in Asheville it is the daughter's recipe. Barack Obama ate it at 12 Bones in Asheville on April 23, 2010, with ribs, corn pudding and sweet tea.

mac and cheese to Dukes Bar-B-Que: on the buffet line with the collards and the fried okra.

mac and cheese to Shealy's Bar-B-Que: one of the vegetables on the Batesburg-Leesville line.

mac and cheese to Brown's Bar-B-Que: 'macaroni' on the Kingstree buffet, between the liver hash and the sweet potatoes.

mac and cheese to Jackie Hite's Bar-B-Q: on the buffet beside the hash and rice.

mac and cheese to Lewis Barbecue: among the Charleston sides.

mac and cheese to Luella's Bar-B-Que: the daughter's recipe, and half the reason her name is on the sign.

mac and cheese to 12 Bones Smokehouse: what Barack Obama ate there on April 23, 2010, with ribs and corn pudding.

mac and cheese to hash and rice: the other starch on a South Carolina buffet; a plate often takes both.

mac and cheese to barbecue tray: a square of it in the tray, counted as a vegetable.

mac and cheese to fixins: one of the fixins on a Dukes buffet.

Macaroni Boil as much macaroni as will fill your dish, in milk and water, till quite tender; drain it on a sieve, sprinkle a little salt over it, put a layer in your dish, then cheese and butter as in the polenta, and bake it in the same manner.

[The polenta receipt it points back to, from the page before:] …slices of cheese and butter, put the dish in a quick oven; twenty or thirty minutes will bake it.

Macaroni (receipt 564) Wash half a pound of macaroni; boil it in plenty of water until tender; lay in a shallow earthen dish a layer of the macaroni (the pieces should be broken the same size), one of grated cheese, and salt to taste. Lay over slices of butter; cover with sweet milk or cream. Bake in a moderate oven, ten or fifteen minutes. Serve hot. Another way is, to arrange alternate layers of boiled macaroni and grated cheese. Pour over a custard made of three well beaten eggs, two tablespoonfuls of stale grated bread, one tablespoonful of butter, and half a teacup of cream or sweet milk. Bake half an hour, or until the custard is set. If boiled too long, it will lose its shape; if baked too much, it will be dry and tough.

Aunt Katy's Macaroni Ingredients: One-half small sized package of macaroni,; One-third pound cheese.; One cup of milk.; Butter the size of a walnut.; One-half cup of bread crumbs. Put macaroni on to boil in water with a little salt. When tender drain off water. Put in a baking dish first a layer of macaroni, then cheese, crumbs and butter. Pour milk over it and bake.

Macaroni and Cheese I Ingredients: ½ cup (8 tbsp / 1 stick / 125 g / 4.4 oz) butter; ½ cup (70 g / 2.5 oz) flour; 4 cups (1 L / 1.1 quart) milk, heated; 1 cup (125 g / 4.4 oz) cheddar cheese; 1 cup (125 g / 4.4 oz) Parmesan or Monterey Jack cheese; ½ tsp cayenne pepper, or to taste; 1 pound (450 g) macaroni noodles, boiled and drained 1. Make a roux using the butter and flour.
2. Add the heated milk, and whisk until smooth to complete the white sauce.
3. Mix in the cheese and cayenne pepper.
4. Mix the cheese sauce into the cooked macaroni noodles until well-coated.

Macaroni and Cheese (Baked) Ingredients: [Base] ½ lb (227 g) dry elbow macaroni; [Base] 3 Tbsp butter; [Base] 3 Tbsp flour; [Base] 1 Tbsp powdered mustard; [Base] 3 cups milk; [Base] 1 red onion, finely chopped; [Base] 2 tsp Tabasco pepper sauce; [Base] 1 bay leaf; [Base] ½ tsp paprika; [Base] 1 standard egg; [Base] 12 oz (340 g) sharp cheddar, shredded; [Base] 1 tsp salt; [Base] Fresh black pepper; [Topping] 3 Tbsp butter; [Topping] 1 cup panko bread crumbs 1. Preheat oven to 350 °F.
2. In a large pot of boiling, salted water, cook the pasta until it is al dente.
3. While the pasta is cooking, melt the butter in a separate pot.
4. Whisk in the flour and mustard and keep it moving for about five minutes. Make sure it is free of lumps.
5. Stir in the milk, onion, bay leaf, and paprika. Simmer for ten minutes and remove the bay leaf.
6. Temper in the egg.
7. Stir in ¾ of the cheese.
8. Season with salt and pepper.
9. Fold the macaroni into the mix and pour into a 2-quart casserole dish.
10. Top with remaining cheese.
11. Melt the butter in a sauté pan, add breadcrumbs, and toss to coat.
12. Top the macaroni with the bread crumbs.
13. Bake for 30 minutes.
14. Remove from oven and rest for 10 minutes before serving.

title: outside brown
text:
The dark crust from the outside of a pork shoulder — the bark, where ten hours of smoke and dip have cooked into the surface — ordered by name at Lexington pits. Regulars ask for extra outside brown on a tray or sandwich; ordered 'brown', the meat comes chopped from that crust rather than from the pale inside. The word marks the Piedmont. Eastern pits chop the whole hog together, skin and all, and have no order for it, though NCpedia notes that some North Carolinians follow South Carolina in separating skin, the dry 'outside meat' and the juicier 'inside meat'.

Bob Garner, writing about Lexington Barbecue in 2012, watched the shoulders roast ten hours over oak coals, hickory when it could be had, the attendants shovelling fresh coals from the fireboxes under the dripping meat every half hour; when the shoulders came off, that outside 'brown', as it is called, was lifted off the meat and saved for special orders. A regular quoted by Carolina Country in 2018 counted 'chopped brown' among the ten ways to order. When Southern Living's readers named Lexington Barbecue the best in the state in 2026, the News & Observer explained the house words to newcomers: regulars ask for extra outside brown, the caramelized, heavily smoked end bits, and the pork comes dressed in a thin vinegar-and-ketchup dip. Barbecue Bros, in 2019, corrected a New York pitmaster who had called it an off-menu item: it is the bark from the shoulders, which locals know to ask for. *Tradition holds —* the crust is prized because it carries the most smoke and dip, and because a shoulder yields little of it; one shoulder feeds many trays and the brown runs out first. *Inference —* the word does for the Piedmont what the chopped skin does for the east: it puts the pit's crust, not only its meat, into the order.

Order the tray or sandwich and add the word: 'brown', 'outside brown' or 'extra brown'. The counter takes the crust set aside from the morning's shoulders and chops it in, or chops the whole order from it. It is darker and drier than the inside meat and has taken more of the dip. Coarse chopped shows it best; fine chopping hides it. *Tradition holds —* the supply is finite and late in the day the answer is often no.

Lexington Barbecue's menu (September 2026) lists chopped, sliced and coarse chop trays and sandwiches and no brown; the order is spoken at the counter. The News & Observer's 2026 guide to the house treats it as the thing regulars ask for.

outside brown to Lexington-style barbecue: the style whose word this is; nowhere else in the Carolinas is the crust ordered by name.

outside brown to pork shoulder: the cut whose outside it is.

outside brown to Lexington dip: cooked into the crust over the fire and added again on the block.

outside brown to hickory and oak: the coals whose smoke makes the crust; Lexington Barbecue burns mostly oak, hickory when it can get it.

outside brown to barbecue tray: the order it modifies.

outside brown to barbecue sandwich: the other order it modifies.

outside brown to Lexington Barbecue: where the brown is lifted off the shoulders and saved for special orders.

outside brown to Bar-B-Q Center: the other Lexington counter where the word is understood.

outside brown to Wayne Monk: whose pit Garner described, shoulders and coals and the brown set aside.

outside brown to pork skins: the eastern crust: chopped hog skin, where the Piedmont has bark.

outside brown to chopped: the cut it is usually served in; 'chopped brown' is one of the ten ways to order.

outside brown to Bob Garner: who wrote down how the brown is set aside at Lexington Barbecue.

Not to be confused with pork-skins: Outside brown is meat, the dark outer layer of a shoulder; pork skins are the pig's hide, blistered or fried. Brown is a Lexington order; skins are an eastern chop or a side.

Eastern North Carolina Barbecued Pig Ingredients: 80 pound pig (butchered with head removed); Salt; 40 pounds charcoal (for charcoal cooking option); Your favorite vinegar-based Eastern NC sauce 1. Salt hams, ribs/midsection and shoulders liberally and place skin side up on either a gas or charcoal grill or a BBQ pit.
2. Keep lid closed, and aim for a heat of approximately 275–350°F.
3. Allow 1 hour per 10 pounds cooking time (gas or charcoal).
4. 2 hours before being done, place pig with the skin side down. As soon as it is flipped, pour BBQ sauce on meat side.
5. Close lid and allow skin to crisp.
6. The pig will be done to perfection when the ham bone can be twisted freely.
7. Lift lid and allow guests to pick/pull meat, or the chef can remove meat and chop to their liking on a chopping block.

To Barbecue Any Kind of Fresh Meat (receipt 200) Gash the meat. Broil slowly over a solid fire. Baste constantly with a sauce composed of butter, mustard, red and black pepper, vinegar. Mix these in a pan, and set it where the sauce will keep warm, not hot. Have a swab made by tying a piece of clean, soft cloth upon a stick about a foot long; dip this in the sauce and baste with it. Where a large carcass is barbecued, it is usual to dig a pit in the ground outdoors, and lay narrow bars of wood across. Very early in the morning fill the pit with wood; set it burning, and in this way heat it very hot. When the wood has burned to coals, lay the meat over. Should the fire need replenishing, keep a fire outside burning, from which draw coals, and scatter evenly in the pit under the meat. Should there be any sauce left pour it over the meat. For barbecuing a joint, a large gridiron answers well; it needs constant attention; should be cooked slowly and steadily.

To Barbecue Shoat Take either a hind or fore quarter, rub it well with salt, pepper, and a small portion of molasses, and if practicable, let it lie for a few hours; then rinse it clean, and wipe it dry with a cloth, and place it on a large gridiron, over a bed of clear coals. Do not barbecue it hastily, but let it cook slowly for several hours, turning it over occasionally, and basting it with nothing but a little salt-water and pepper, merely to season and moisten it a little. When it is well done, serve it without a garnish, and having the skin taken off, which should be done before it is put down to roast, squeeze over it a little lemon juice, and accompany it with melted butter and wine, bread sauce, raw sallad, slaugh, or cucumbers, and stewed fruit. Beef may be barbecued in the same manner.

title: peach cobbler
text:
Sliced peaches sweetened and thickened in a deep dish and covered with a crust — pastry, biscuit dough or a batter — then baked until the top browns and the fruit bubbles at the edge. It is a barbecue dessert of the same family as banana pudding, ordered by the cup or the square after the tray, and served warm, often with ice cream. The Southern kind is frequently closer to a deep-dish pie, with a bottom crust as well as a top.

Cobbler is what English settlers made when they could not make a suet pudding: with Dutch ovens, they covered a stewed filling with a layer of pastry, and later with plain biscuits, scone batter or dumplings fitted together. The first recorded recipe may be in The Kentucky Housewife, Lettice Bryan's book of 1839, where it is 'A Peach Pot-Pie' and the text says cobler is what it is often termed. Abby Fisher, born into slavery in South Carolina and dictating her book in San Francisco in 1881, gives it with two layers of pastry, peaches cut to the size of a plum, and cinnamon. The name's origin is not settled — it may come from the archaic cobeler, a wooden bowl, or from the cobbled look of the crust. North Carolina has its own deep-dish version under its own name, the sonker, made in and around Surry County. At Allen & Son outside Chapel Hill, Keith Allen rolled the cobbler crusts from his grandmother's recipe and the desserts were the second reason people came.

Peaches are peeled and sliced, tossed with sugar and a thickener — cornstarch or flour — and sometimes lemon juice and cinnamon, and either put straight into a buttered baking dish or brought to a boil in a pan first so the syrup thickens. The topping is rolled pastry, spoonfuls of biscuit dough, or a batter poured over; a Southern deep-dish version lines the bottom of the dish as well, cuts air-holes in the top and bakes it brown. Forty to fifty minutes in a hot oven. Served warm, with cold sweet milk in the old books and with vanilla ice cream now.

On the dessert board at Lexington Barbecue, whose list is pies and cobbler with no pudding on it; at Allen & Son in Chapel Hill it was made in the house from a family recipe, with ice cream churned daily.

peach cobbler to Lexington Barbecue: on a dessert list of pies and cobbler, with no banana pudding.

peach cobbler to Allen & Son Barbeque: rolled from Keith Allen's grandmother's recipe, with ice cream made daily.

peach cobbler to banana pudding: the other barbecue dessert; a house tends to lead with one or the other.

peach cobbler to pig pickin' cake: the third of the desserts a Carolina pit is likely to have.

peach cobbler to barbecue tray: what comes after it, not with it.

peach cobbler to sweet tea: what it is eaten with.

Not to be confused with banana-pudding: Cobbler is baked, hot, and has a crust; banana pudding is cold, built in layers, and has no oven in it after the custard.

A Peach Pot-Pie A peach pot-pie, or cobler, as it is often termed, should be made of clingstone peaches, that are very ripe, and then pared and sliced from the stones. Prepare a pot or oven with paste, as directed for the apple pot-pie, put in the prepared peaches, sprinkle on a large handful of brown sugar, pour in plenty of water to cook the peaches without burning them, though there should be but very little liquor or syrup when the pie is done. Put a paste over the top, and bake it with moderate heat, raising the lid occasionally, to see how it is baking. When the crust is brown, and the peaches very soft, invert the crust on a large dish, put the peaches evenly on, and grate loaf sugar thickly over it. Eat it warm or cold. Although it is not a fashionable pie for company, it is very excellent for family use, with cold sweet milk.

[An Apple Pot-Pie, pages 267–268, for the paste it refers to:] Rub the bottom and sides of a porridge-pot, or small oven, with butter, and then with dry flour. Roll out some pieces of plain or standing paste about half an inch thick, line the sides of the pot or oven with the pieces of paste, letting them nearly touch in the bottom.

Peach Cobbler (recipe 143) Peel the peaches (freestones) and make a pastry the same way as for pie, and roll out the dough as thin as for pie crust. Put one layer at the bottom of the dish, and cut the peaches into pieces the size of a plum and fill the dish with them, sprinkling them freely with fine sugar. Cover them over with another layer of pastry, cut with a knife two or three air-holes on the top and put to bake. Let it bake brown. It makes a delicious luncheon or dessert. Season the peaches with powdered cinnamon to taste. See recipe for all kinds of pastry.

Sweet Peach Cobbler Ingredients: [Filling] ½ cup (about 120 ml) granulated sugar; [Filling] 1 tablespoon (15 ml) cornstarch; [Filling] 4 cups (950 ml) sliced peeled peaches; [Filling] ¼ teaspoon ground cinnamon; [Filling] 1 teaspoon (5 ml) lemon juice; [Topping] 1 cup (about 240 ml) all-purpose flour; [Topping] 1 tablespoon sugar; [Topping] 1½ teaspoons baking powder; [Topping] ½ teaspoon salt; [Topping] 3 tablespoons shortening; [Topping] ½ cup (about 120 ml) milk 1. [Filling] Preheat oven to 400°F.
2. [Filling] Combine granulated sugar and cornstarch in a mixing bowl.
3. [Filling] Stir in peaches and lemon juice to make a sugary-brown syrup.
4. [Filling] Bring the peach mixture to a boil in a saucepan, and simmer until it thickens. Transfer to a 2-quart casserole dish, and put into the oven.
5. [Topping] Combine the flour, sugar, baking powder, and salt in a mixing bowl. Stir, until well mixed.
6. [Topping] Add shortening, and cut with a pastry blender until well mixed.
7. [Topping] Mix in milk to make a ball of dough.
8. [Assembly] Remove casserole dish from the oven. Add dough in spoon-sized dollops on top of fruit.
9. [Assembly] Return to 400°F oven. Bake for 25–30 minutes, until topping turns brown.
10. [Assembly] Serve.

Easy Peach Cobbler Ingredients: 1 stick margarine; 1 teaspoon baking powder; ¾ cup all-purpose flour; 1 cup white granulated sugar; ¾ cup milk; 5 fresh peaches, sliced 1. Preheat oven to 375°F.
2. Melt margarine in quart size baking pan or dish. Set aside.
3. Mix baking powder, flour, sugar, and milk. Pour this batter over the melted margarine, and do not stir.
4. Arrange peaches over the batter.
5. Bake 20–30 minutes.

Basic Cobbler Ingredients: ½ cup (1 stick) butter; Salt (optional; add only if butter is unsalted); 1 tsp baking powder; 1 cup self-raising flour; 1 cup milk; 1 cup white granulated sugar; 1 cup fresh fruit (e.g. peaches, blackberries, cherries, etc.) 1. Preheat oven to 350°F (175°C).
2. Place the butter in a deep 9½ x 12-inch baking dish. Put dish in oven to melt butter while preparing other ingredients. If butter is unsalted, add a touch of salt to the pan as well.
3. Add flour and sugar to a bowl and sift together lightly. Create a well in the center of the mixture, and pour the milk into the well. Mix together with a wire whisk until smooth.
4. Remove pan from oven. Pour batter into dish on top of melted butter. Do not stir. Spoon the fresh fruit out evenly across the top, but again, do not stir.
5. Place cobbler in oven and bake uncovered until golden brown.

title: pickles
text:
Cucumbers held in brine or vinegar until they sour, sliced into rounds or spears and put on the plate beside the meat, with the sandwich, or loose in a dish on the table. Sweet pickle — cucumbers in a vinegar-and-sugar syrup with spices — is the common Carolina one; chow-chow, a chopped relish of cabbage, green tomato, onion and pepper, does the same job in a spoonful. The point of them on a barbecue plate is acid and salt against fat.

The pickled cucumber is old and worldwide, and the sweet Southern one is a strand of it: cucumbers marinated in vinegar, sugar and spices rather than left to sour in salt. The bread-and-butter pickle — sweeter than most, spiced with coriander — is credited to Omar and Cora Fanning, Illinois cucumber farmers who trademarked the name in 1923 after bartering pickles made from their undersized cucumbers with their grocer for staples. North Carolina's pickle industry started the same way, out of a surplus. In the mid-1920s Shikrey Baddour, a Lebanese immigrant from Goldsboro, saw farmers around Mount Olive wasting cucumber crops and began buying them, brining them in tanks and offering the brine stock to pickle firms; nobody bought it. In 1926 the Mount Olive business leader I. F. Witherington relaunched the idea as a company that would pack and sell the pickles itself, and thirty-seven shareholders put in $19,500 — a community proposition, they called it. The plant stands where the board bought an acre from the farmer J. A. Westbrook for $1,000, at the corner of Cucumber Boulevard and Vine Street. Mt. Olive now sells more than 230 million jars a year and employs more than 1,200 people in North Carolina. In 1999 the Farm Labor Organizing Committee called a boycott over the pay and conditions of cucumber pickers; it ended in 2004 when the company agreed to raise what it paid for cucumbers and growers pledged higher wages.

For a sweet pickle the cucumbers are cut, soaked, and cooked or steeped in vinegar with sugar, turmeric, celery seed, mustard seed and whole spices, then sealed in jars; for a sour or dill pickle they are packed in a crock or barrel with garlic, dill heads, mustard seed, leaves and salt, covered with cooled boiled water, weighted under the brine and left to ferment for weeks. Chow-chow is chopped cabbage, green tomato, onion and pepper salted overnight, drained, then simmered in vinegar with sugar, mustard seed and celery seed. On the plate they are cut in rounds or spears; on a chopped sandwich they go under the slaw or on top of it, by the house's habit.

Pickles are part of the standing list of fixins in both states, and the South Carolina plate — pork, rice, hash, coleslaw, sweet pickles, white bread, iced tea — carries them by default. Mt. Olive, in Wayne County, was the top-selling pickle brand in the South in an analysis of 2024 nationwide consumption by the delivery service Instacart.

pickles to barbecue tray: the sour thing on the tray, against the fat of the meat.

pickles to barbecue sandwich: laid on the meat or eaten alongside, by the house's habit.

pickles to white slaw: on the same South Carolina plate: pork, rice, hash, slaw, sweet pickles, white bread.

pickles to hash and rice: what the pickle cuts through on a South Carolina plate.

pickles to South Carolina mustard barbecue: part of the Midlands plate as it is usually set out.

pickles to fixins: named in the list of fixins on both states' plates.

Not to be confused with red-slaw: Both are chopped, sour and red-flecked in a dish on the table. Chow-chow is a preserve put up in jars, mostly green tomato and cabbage; red slaw is made fresh from cabbage and dressed with the pit's dip.

Cucumber Pickle Take enough cucumbers to fill a two-gallon jar. Cut into lengthwise pieces and soak until fresh. Cover with equal parts of water and vinegar, and boil an hour and ten minutes. Then take them out and boil one and one-half hours in one gallon of fresh vinegar, two pounds of sugar, one tablespoonful of celery seed, one tablespoonful of tumeric, one teaspoonful each of cloves, mace and ginger, one tablespoonful of black pepper, and one of horse radish. When cold add one-half teaspoonful of cayenne pepper.

Tar Heel Chow Chow Chop one head of cabbage, one gallon of green tomatoes, and one quart of onions. Add one-half cup of salt, put in a bag and let it drain for twenty-four hours.

Then put in kettle and add about two pounds of brown sugar, one cup of white mustard seed, and one-half cup of celery seed. Cover with good apple vinegar and cook until done, about three or four hours. To the above add one or two pods of chopped red pepper.

Aunt Caroline's Own Pickle Chop fine one-half gallon of green tomatoes, one pint of onions, one pint of green and red peppers with seeds taken out, and one gallon of cabbage. Mix well and sprinkle two tablespoonsful of salt over it and let stand all night. Add three quarts of vinegar, two pounds of sugar, three teaspoonsful of celery seed, three of mustard seed two of spice, and one of cloves. Let simmer two hours.

To Pickle Cucumbers Gather them full grown, but quite young — take off the green rind, and slice them tolerably thick; put a layer in a deep dish, strew over it some chopped onion and salt; do this until they are all in; sprinkle salt on the top, let them stand six hours, put them in a colander — when all the liquor has run off, put them in a pot, strew a little cayenne pepper over each layer, and cover them with strong cold vinegar; when the pot is full, pour on some sweet oil, and tie it up close; at the end of a fortnight, pour off the first vinegar, and put on fresh.

Cucumbers Make a strong salt and water, and let the cucumbers lie in it for two weeks. Then soak all night in fresh water. The next day put them into a bright brass kettle, with a little alum, and water enough to cover them. Put grape-leaves on top, and a plate to keep in the steam. Simmer gently for a half a day. Let them get entirely cold, and then put them into fresh alum water, over the fire, and continue doing this, until they are quite fresh. Then, if they are a fine green, put them into a jar, and boil some vinegar and spices in a porcelain kettle, and pour over them. Have plenty of vinegar to cover the pickles, and cork them up tightly.

title: pig pickin' cake
text:
A layer cake of convenience-food parts: yellow or butter-golden cake mix beaten with eggs, oil and a can of mandarin oranges, juice and all, baked in three eight-inch pans and frosted with a can of crushed pineapple folded into instant vanilla pudding and whipped topping, sometimes with pecans or coconut on top, and served cold. It is North Carolina's barbecue dessert by name — the pig pickin' being the whole-hog party where guests pick the meat off the pig — and it is carried to those parties; Hysmith places it at barbecue restaurants too, though it is a home cake first. Our State calls it an essential companion to any good barbecue, noun not verb.

The cake has no founding story that anyone has documented, and two writers have looked. KC Hysmith, tracing it in 2024, found the oldest recipe she could name in the Raleigh News & Observer in 1975 and a reference in the Boca Raton News in 1980; every ingredient but the eggs comes from a can or a box, which reads like a brand's test kitchen, but she could not find which brand, and the 'Nancy Ware's cake' some sources credit stays a mystery. She reads it as a variation of the Pineapple Dream Cake of the convenience-food years. John Shelton Reed told her North Carolinians did not say 'pig-picking' until the 1970s, so the name is a child of that decade; *Inference —* the cake is older than its name, renamed for the party it was carried to. Liz Biro, in Coastal Review in 2017, gives the folk reason the state claims it — the name, and the way orange and pineapple cool the mouth after tangy pork — and notes that when Google sorted Thanksgiving searches by state in 2014, the New York Times reported pig pickin' cake as North Carolina's first. Our State printed Mavis Brannon of Mooresville's version the same year, sent in by her daughter, who remembered her yeast rolls as well. Chowhound records pea pickin' cake and sunshine cake as other names; Biro calls the first a mistake.

One box of yellow or butter-golden cake mix, four eggs, a quarter to three-quarters cup of oil and an 11-ounce can of mandarin oranges, chopped and undrained, beaten together and divided among three greased and floured 8-inch pans; 350 degrees for 15 to 20 minutes, then cooled through. The frosting is a 16- or 20-ounce can of crushed pineapple, drained, stirred into a small box of instant vanilla pudding, with two 8-ounce tubs of whipped topping folded in and, in Biro's version, a cup of chopped pecans. The layers are stacked and covered, top and sides, and the cake goes into the refrigerator; it is served cold and keeps there, loosely covered, a few hours by Our State's count. Some cooks bake it as a single layer or as cupcakes and finish it with orange segments, coconut or toasted pecans.

A home cake, carried to pig pickins and Thanksgiving tables: the dish North Carolinians searched for most in November 2014, by Google's count as the New York Times reported it. Recipes in Our State (2017) and Coastal Review (2017); Hysmith (2024) and Chowhound (2025) on the name. The barbecue-house menus read for this record — Lexington Barbecue, the Barbecue Center, Sam Jones, Parker's — do not list it.

Root: pig pickin' (the whole-hog party, named for picking the meat off the cooked pig) + cake.

pig pickin' cake to pig pickin': the party it is named for and carried to; the name is no older than the 1970s, when the party got its name.

pig pickin' cake to Eastern North Carolina barbecue: whole hog is what a pickin cooks, and vinegar pork is what the orange and pineapple are said to cool.

pig pickin' cake to whole hog: the pig that gets picked before the cake is cut.

pig pickin' cake to banana pudding: the other barbecue dessert; the pudding is on the restaurant menu, the cake on the picnic table.

pig pickin' cake to sweet tea: poured with it at the pickin.

pig pickin' cake to John Shelton Reed: who dates the expression 'pig-picking' to the 1970s, and with it the cake's name.

Not to be confused with banana-pudding: The cake is sliced; the pudding is spooned. Orange and pineapple in a frosted layer cake, against bananas and wafers in custard.

Pig pickin' cake Ingredients: 1 box yellow or butter-golden cake mix; 4 eggs; ¼–¾ cup vegetable oil; 1 can (11 oz) mandarin oranges, chopped and undrained; 1 can (16–20 oz) crushed pineapple, drained; 1 small box instant vanilla pudding mix; 2 tubs (8 oz each) whipped topping; chopped pecans or coconut, to finish (optional)

title: pork skins
text:
The pig's hide, cooked until it blisters and cracks. On an eastern whole hog the skin faces up through the night and is turned to the coals at the end to crisp; at Skylight Inn it is chopped into the meat, where the crunch and the salt are part of what 'barbecue' means. Sold on their own, skins are a side or a snack: fresh fried squares with pimento cheese at Sam Jones BBQ, a pork skin sandwich with slaw at Lexington Barbecue. In the Pee Dee the hog is sometimes skinned before cooking and the skin fried on its own. A crackling keeps a little fat and meat under the skin; a rind is skin alone.

The skin is the pit's own by-product. At a hog killing the fat is rendered for lard and the cracklings are what is left in the pot, and *tradition holds —* crackling bread, cornbread with cracklings baked in, was the winter bread of the farm. On the eastern pit the same crust comes off the barbecue: the small hogs of the Carolinas are cooked hot enough for the skin to crisp, and the skin takes up more of the smoke than the meat does, so the chopped skin carries the flavor of the fire into every bite. At a pig pickin some cooks wipe the ash from the skin with paper towels or a whisk broom before the hog is turned, to keep the cracklings clean. Tennessee cooks larger hogs at lower heat and the skin never crisps — one of the marks that separate the Carolina hog from the Memphis one. At Skylight Inn the chop takes in tenderloin, inner meat and crisped skin together, which NCpedia records as the eastern habit: in some areas bits of skin are integral to the finished product. South of the line the Pee Dee sometimes strips the hide before the pig goes on and fries it apart, and NCpedia notes North Carolinians who follow that lead, sorting skin from outside meat from inside meat.

On the pit: the hog cooks skin-up, is turned skin-down at the end, and the blistered skin is chopped with cleavers into the meat, or lifted, salted and broken into pieces. Fried: the skin is cut into squares, rendered slowly, then fried hot so it puffs. Commercial rinds are dried pellets rehydrated and fried in pork fat at 200–210 °C, which swells them to five times their size; the pink or purple spot on a bagged rind is a USDA inspection stamp. Eaten with the fingers, salted, with hot sauce, or with pimento cheese.

Sam Jones BBQ lists fresh fried pork skins with housemade pimento cheese (September 2026). Lexington Barbecue sells a pork skin sandwich with slaw at $4.50 cash, $4.65 card (September 2026). Bagged rinds from the gas station are the same thing at a distance.

pork skins to Eastern North Carolina barbecue: the style that chops the skin into the meat instead of setting it aside.

pork skins to whole hog: the hog they come off; in the Carolinas the skin is crisped on purpose.

pork skins to Skylight Inn BBQ: where the crisped skin goes through the chop with the tenderloin and inner meat.

pork skins to Sam Jones BBQ: where fresh fried skins come with pimento cheese.

pork skins to Lexington Barbecue: where skins are sold as a sandwich with slaw.

pork skins to Pee Dee whole-hog barbecue: where the hog is sometimes skinned before cooking and the skin fried separately.

pork skins to outside brown: the Piedmont's crust: bark from a shoulder, where the east has skin.

pork skins to hog killing: where cracklings began, as the residue of the lard pot.

pork skins to cornbread: crackling bread is cornbread with these baked in.

pork skins to pig pickin': where the skin is wiped clean of ash before the hog is turned, for the cracklings.

pork skins to chopping block: where the skin goes into the meat under the cleavers.

pork skins to hog: the animal whose hide this is.

Not to be confused with outside-brown: Skin is glassy and blistered and shatters; outside brown is dark meat from the outside of a shoulder and chews. If it came off a whole hog in the east it is skin.

To Try the Fat (receipt 215) The lard for cooking is made from the leaf fat, the fat from the chine, head and trimmings of the joints, etc. Wash it well, and soak twelve hours; if put to soak in the evening let it remain until next morning; wash it in tepid water, changing it twice; cut it in small pieces; pour a little water in the bottom of the kettle to prevent the fat from scorching (very little water is necessary); boil briskly until the oil from the meat is nearly extracted, and the process almost completed; then reduce the fire; stir frequently, turning the meat up from the bottom; when done, the cracklings will be a good brown, and float to the top and break crisp. Great care must be taken after the oil begins to look clear, to prevent its burning (the least taste of that kind will injure its quality); at the same time the cracklings must be thoroughly done, the water entirely evaporated, or the lard will turn sour. Strain first through a colander, pressing the oil out; then place a muslin or other thin cloth over the mouth of the jar, and strain again.

To whiten Lard To twelve gallons of lard add a pint of lye. Put the lye in when the lard is first put on. When the cracklings are a light-brown the lard is done. Strain through a thin cloth put inside of a colander.

Eastern North Carolina Barbecued Pig Ingredients: 80 pound pig (butchered with head removed); Salt; 40 pounds charcoal (for charcoal cooking option); Your favorite vinegar-based Eastern NC sauce 1. Salt hams, ribs/midsection and shoulders liberally and place skin side up on either a gas or charcoal grill or a BBQ pit.
2. Keep lid closed, and aim for a heat of approximately 275–350°F.
3. Allow 1 hour per 10 pounds cooking time (gas or charcoal).
4. 2 hours before being done, place pig with the skin side down. As soon as it is flipped, pour BBQ sauce on meat side.
5. Close lid and allow skin to crisp.
6. The pig will be done to perfection when the ham bone can be twisted freely.
7. Lift lid and allow guests to pick/pull meat, or the chef can remove meat and chop to their liking on a chopping block.

title: potato salad
text:
Boiled potatoes cut up cold and dressed with mayonnaise, with hard-boiled egg, onion, celery, sweet pickle or relish and often a spoon of yellow mustard that colours the whole bowl. It is served cold beside the barbecue, and in the Carolinas it is the mayonnaise side that answers to the vinegar of the meat. Mustard in the dressing is common enough in South Carolina that a bowl of it can read as the same yellow as the sauce.

American potato salad came in with German immigrants in the nineteenth century, and the earliest American recipes are the German kind: cooked potatoes dressed with oil, vinegar and herbs, served warm. The north German version — cold, with mayonnaise, hard-boiled egg and sweet or sour pickle — is the one the American bowl most resembles. Mayonnaise made the change possible on this scale, and in the Carolinas that means Eugenia Duke, who began bottling hers in Greenville, South Carolina around 1923. Aunt Caroline's Dixieland Recipes, printed in Chicago in 1922, already gives the Southern shape of it: five cold boiled Irish potatoes diced, three hard-boiled eggs, parsley, celery, salt and both peppers, bound with an oil dressing made at home. *Inference —* the sweet pickle and the mustard that distinguish a Carolina bowl from a German one are the same two things that distinguish the region's slaw and its sauce.

Potatoes are boiled in their skins, peeled and diced while still warm so they take the dressing, then cooled. Hard-boiled eggs are chopped in, with onion, celery and sweet pickle relish; the dressing is mayonnaise, sometimes cut with a little of the pickle liquor, and yellow mustard to taste. Salt, black pepper and paprika finish it. It is made in the morning and kept cold, and at a pit it is dished with an ice-cream scoop.

On the plate at Grady's in Dudley, where the day's vegetables are peeled and chopped by hand that morning; on the buffet at Brown's in Kingstree; among the sides at Lewis Barbecue in Charleston, which lists it as creamy potato salad; on the Dukes buffets in the Orangeburg family of houses.

potato salad to Grady's Barbecue: one of the day's vegetables, peeled and chopped by hand that morning.

potato salad to Brown's Bar-B-Que: on the buffet with the macaroni and the farm's vegetables.

potato salad to Lewis Barbecue: listed as creamy potato salad among the Charleston sides.

potato salad to Dukes Bar-B-Que: on the buffet line with the collards and the mac and cheese.

potato salad to Duke's mayonnaise: the mayonnaise most Carolina kitchens bind it with.

potato salad to boiled potatoes: the same potato, hot and undressed, on the eastern plate.

potato salad to white slaw: the other cold mayonnaise side; a plate often carries both.

potato salad to barbecue tray: a scoop in the tray, cold against the hot meat.

potato salad to fixins: one of the fixins on a South Carolina buffet.

Not to be confused with boiled-potatoes: Boiled potatoes come hot, whole or halved, with no dressing but butter or the pork's sauce. Potato salad is cold, cut small and bound with mayonnaise.

Potato Salad Five medium sized, cold, boiled Irish potatoes, diced; three hard boiled eggs and a few pieces of parsley chopped fine, and one cup of diced celery. Season with salt, black and red pepper and mix well with oil dressing.

[Wesson Oil Dressing, the dressing it calls for, printed with it:] Yolks of three eggs, one-half teaspoon of salt, one-fourth teaspoon of mustard, one-fourth teaspoon of red pepper, juice of one lemon, pint of Wesson Oil. Beat yolks until thick; then add salt, pepper, mustard and part of lemon juice. Lastly add the oil one drop at a time at first, then slowly until dressing is thick, and then the remainder of the lemon juice.

Potato Salad Ingredients: 2 pounds (~1 kg) potatoes; 6 slices of bacon; ½ cup (120 g) finely-chopped yellow onion; 2 tablespoons white granulated sugar; ½ teaspoon celery seed; 2 hard boiled eggs; ¼ cup (60 g) flour; ½ cup (120 ml) vinegar; 1 cup (240 ml) water; 1 tablespoon fresh parsley; 1 ½ teaspoon salt; Pepper; Paprika 1. Cook bacon strips, cut into small pieces, and set aside for later.
2. Boil potatoes for 5–10 minutes or until softened; cut into small chunks or thick slices.
3. Place potatoes in a large bowl and let them come to room temperature.
4. In a bowl combine flour, celery seed, parsley, chopped onion, salt, and pepper.
5. Pour the water and vinegar into a pot, stir in sugar and bring to a boil. Add the dry mixture and stir until thickened.
6. In the original bowl place potatoes and bacon, pour on thickened mixture.
7. Break apart eggs and stir lightly into the bowl to combine.
8. Place in large serving bowl and sprinkle with paprika.
9. Serve

American Potato Salad I Ingredients: 2 pounds (3–4 ea.) medium russet potatoes; 1 tablespoon plus ½ teaspoon salt; 2 tablespoons distilled white vinegar; 1 medium rib of celery; ¾ teaspoon celery seed; ¾ cup mayonnaise; ¾ teaspoon powdered mustard; 2 tablespoons minced onion; 2 tablespoons minced fresh parsley leaves; ¼ teaspoon ground black pepper; 3 tablespoons sweet pickle relish 1. Peel and cut potatoes into ¾ inch cubes.
2. Cover potatoes with an inch of water in a large saucepan and bring to a boil.
3. Add 1 tablespoon salt to boiling water and reduce heat to medium.
4. Simmer about 8 minutes, stirring gently once or twice, until potatoes are tender. Taste a piece—don't overcook.
5. Drain potatoes and place in a large bowl.
6. Toss potatoes gently with vinegar using a rubber spatula.
7. Cool potatoes. They must be no more than barely warm to mix.
8. Chop celery fine.
9. Stir together celery, celery seeds, mayonnaise, dry mustard, onion, parsley, pepper, and ½ teaspoon salt.
10. Gently fold together dressing mix and potatoes.
11. Cover and refrigerate at least an hour, until thoroughly chilled.

American Potato Salad II Ingredients: 3 pounds small white potatoes (use waxy or red potatoes); Salt; Ground pepper; 5 large hard boiled eggs, chopped; 1 medium red onion, chopped finely; 2 tbsp chopped sweet basil leaves; 1 cup corn; ½ cup freshly-squeezed lemon juice (from 2–3 lemons); ½ cup extra-virgin olive oil; 2 tbsp pasta seasoning 1. Place potatoes and 2 tablespoons of salt in a large pot of water. Bring the water to a boil, and cook for 15–20 minutes, until the potatoes are tender when pierced with a knife. Drain the potatoes in a colander.
2. Place the chopped eggs in a large bowl.
3. Sauté the onions until light golden brown and add to the bowl with the eggs.
4. When the potatoes are cool enough to handle, cut them in quarters, or smaller, depending on their size. Place the potatoes in the bowl with the eggs. Add the corn along with some salt, pepper and pasta seasoning to the potato and egg mixture. Set aside.
5. In a small bowl add the lemon juice while whisking in olive oil slowly. Add to the potatoes, mix all ingredients. Chill for 30 minutes before eating.

title: red slaw
text:
Finely chopped green cabbage dressed with vinegar, ketchup, sugar, salt and black pepper — or with the pit's own dip — and no mayonnaise. It is the slaw of Lexington and the Piedmont, red-pink in the boat beside the chopped shoulder, on the sandwich under the meat, and on hot dogs as a relish; it is what the counter means by 'slaw' from Lexington to Shelby. Because it carries no mayonnaise it keeps without refrigeration, which suits an outdoor pit. Across the rest of the state the pale mayonnaise slaw is the default and this one is called barbecue slaw.

The dressing is the dip. In Lexington the thin sauce of vinegar, ketchup, water, salt and pepper that dresses the shoulder also goes into the cabbage, so the slaw is coloured by the same bottle as the meat; NCpedia records it as red coleslaw, 'barbecue slaw', coloured with ketchup or dip. The Lexington sandwich is defined by it — the town's own account calls red slaw the sandwich's most distinguishing feature — and it goes on hot dogs as a relish, where the Carolina hot dog's chili, slaw and onions are the same three things in a bun. *Tradition holds —* the slaw went red because the first pits were tents and curb stands without ice, and a vinegar dressing holds where mayonnaise will not; it was also the dressing a pit already had on the block. In the late 1990s Wendy's put red slaw on a 'Carolina Classic' burger with chili, onions and American cheese and trademarked the name, which is as far as the slaw has travelled under its own. At Keaton's in Rowan County the house slaw is the same idea run hot: cabbage in vinegar, tomato, cayenne and celery seed.

Green cabbage chopped fine — finer than a Northern slaw, close to minced — and dressed with vinegar, ketchup, sugar, salt and black pepper, or with a ladle of the house dip; some pits add hot sauce, mustard seed or onion. It is made ahead and kept cold, and the vinegar keeps it. Served in the second half of the tray, on the sandwich under the meat, and on a hot dog with chili and onions; the Barbecue Center and Lexington Barbecue both put it on the sandwich unless you ask for none.

Every Lexington pit serves it and most keep a mayonnaise white slaw for the asking. It rides in the boat with a chopped tray at $8.00 cash at Lexington Barbecue and on the $5.70 chopped sandwich (September 2026). Outside the Piedmont, red slaw on the tray is the sign of a pit cooking in the Lexington manner.

Root: Dutch koolsla 'cabbage salad' (kool 'cabbage', from Latin caulis, + sla 'salad') → American English coleslaw, 1794 → slaw, the American clipping; 'red' is the Lexington marker for the ketchup or dip in the dressing, against 'white' for mayonnaise.

red slaw to Lexington-style barbecue: the style it marks: the slaw is red because the pit's dip is in it.

red slaw to Lexington dip: its dressing, or the model for it: vinegar, ketchup, salt, pepper, sugar.

red slaw to white slaw: the other slaw, mayonnaise-dressed and pale, which the east and South Carolina eat.

red slaw to Eastern North Carolina barbecue: the style that dresses its slaw white; the two slaws divide the state with the two sauces.

red slaw to barbecue sandwich: goes on it, under the meat, and defines the Lexington sandwich.

red slaw to barbecue tray: fills the other half of the boat.

red slaw to slaw: the word, Dutch koolsla clipped to one syllable.

red slaw to Lexington Barbecue: where it is on every sandwich and in every tray.

red slaw to Bar-B-Q Center: the other Lexington counter that puts it on the sandwich by default.

red slaw to Keaton's Barbecue: whose hot vinegar slaw is red slaw with cayenne.

red slaw to barbecue chicken: at Keaton's the hot slaw sits beside dipped chicken.

Not to be confused with white-slaw: Colour. Red slaw is pink to red from ketchup or dip and tastes of vinegar; white slaw is pale, creamy and sweet with mayonnaise. Red means Piedmont.

Cold Slaw Take vinegar and water in equal proportions (unless the vinegar is very strong); add butter, the size of an egg, and a little flour. Pour into a saucepan over the fire, and stir until it is thick; then pour in the beaten yolks of two eggs, and some salt. When it has been on the fire ten minutes more, stir in the cabbage, nicely shreded with a cabbage-cutter. The cabbage must be taken up, as soon as it is hot.

You may add a saltspoonful of mustard to the sauce, if you like it. Salt the cabbage.

Cold and Hot Slaws To make cold-slaw, take a nice, fresh cabbage, wash and strain it (after submitting it to the insect-destroying process); cut off the stalk, shave down the head into very small strips with a cabbage-cutter or very sharp knife. It must be done evenly. Put it into a deep china-dish and prepare for it the following dressing: Melt in a sauce-pan a quarter of a pound of butter, with half pint of water, a large tablespoonful of vinegar, a saltspoonful of salt and a little cayenne. Give this a boil, and pour it hot on the cabbage. Send to the table cold.

To prepare warm-slaw, cut the cabbage as for cold-slaw (red cabbage is best); put it in a deep dish, cover closely, and set it on the top of the stove for half an hour or till warm all through; do not let it boil. Then make a dripping as for cold-slaw. Boil this mixture in a sauce-pan, and pour it hot over the warm cabbage; send to table immediately.

Cold Slaw (receipt 366) Cut a head of hard white cabbage into very fine shavings. It is seldom shaved fine enough. For a quart of the cabbage take the yolks of three eggs, beat them well; stir into a tumbler and a half of vinegar two teaspoonfuls of loaf sugar, a tablespoonful of olive oil, one of thick, sweet cream, or a piece of butter as large as a walnut, a heaped teaspoonful of mustard, salt and pepper to taste; mix with the egg, and put this sauce into a stew-pan; when hot add the cabbage; stew until thoroughly hot, which will only require four or five minutes. Toss it up from the bottom with a silver or wooden fork. Take it up and set where it will become perfectly cold, on ice is best. The quantity of vinegar will depend upon its strength.

Red slaw, as described Ingredients: green cabbage; vinegar; water; ketchup; spices and seasoning, varying by house

title: sweet tea
text:
Black tea brewed strong, sweetened with sugar while hot — so it dissolves, rather than being stirred into a cold glass — and poured over ice. It is the drink of the Carolina barbecue house in both states and every sauce region: sold by the glass, the quart and the gallon, brewed on the stove at Grady's in Dudley, named by Dukes in Orangeburg among the five things people come for, and served, Wikipedia says, wherever whole hog is. Some cooks temper it with a pinch of baking soda against bitterness; lemon is the usual addition. Its presence on a menu is one sign used to tell whether a place counts as the South.

Sweet tea began as a luxury of three shipped-in things — tea, sugar and ice, the ice the dearest — and became cheap when all three did. The oldest known recipe for it is in Housekeeping in Old Virginia, a community cookbook compiled by Marion Cabell Tyree (copyright 1878, and dated 1879 by the historian Robert Moss): ice, sugar, hot green tea, lemon. Green tea was the tea of the 19th-century South; the Second World War cut off its sources and black tea from British India took its place, and by the war's end black tea was the American tea. Moss, checking Summerville, South Carolina's 2013 claim to be 'The Birthplace of Sweet Tea' — a trademarked tagline, a Sweet Tea Trail and billboards on I-26 and I-95, resting on Dr. Charles Shepard's Pinehurst Tea Plantation of 1888–1915, the first successful tea farm in the country — found the Boston Journal recommending iced tea in July 1868, twenty years before Shepard planted, and Fannie Farmer's 1896 Boston Cooking-School Cook Book telling readers to pour tea over cracked ice and sweeten to taste. Summerville answered with a jar: 'Mason', fifteen feet tall, filled on National Tea Day 2016 with 2,524 gallons of sweet tea, the world's largest, a record traded since 2010 among Chick-fil-A, Summerville and Lipton. In 2003 a Georgia House bill, apparently an April Fool's joke, would have made selling iced tea without offering sweet tea a misdemeanor; it never came to a vote.

Tea bags or loose black tea steep in a pot of boiling water — some cooks add a pinch of baking soda — and the sugar goes in while the tea is hot; cold water and ice bring it down. At Grady's, Gerri Grady brews it on the stovetop for the day's service; at Allen & Son Keith Allen brewed it himself and sold it by the litre. It is served in a tall glass over ice, with lemon if you want it. Pits sell it to go by the pint, quart, half gallon and gallon — Parker's in Wilson lists all four — and the Barbecue Center in Lexington prices it from a 10-ounce cup to the gallon jug. The sugar can run to 22 degrees Brix, twice a Coca-Cola.

Lexington Barbecue: 'Iced Tea (Unsweet on Request)', $2.90 cash, $3.00 card (September 2026). The Barbecue Center: 10 oz $2.50, 16 oz $2.90, 32 oz $3.75, half gallon $6.00, gallon $8.50. Summerville holds a Sweet Tea Festival each September and keeps the record jar.

sweet tea to Lexington-style barbecue: 'Iced Tea (Unsweet on Request)' at Lexington Barbecue: sweet is the default.

sweet tea to South Carolina mustard barbecue: one of the five things Dukes in Orangeburg says people come for.

sweet tea to Lexington Barbecue: $2.90 cash in September 2026, unsweet on request.

sweet tea to Bar-B-Q Center: priced from the 10-ounce cup to the gallon jug.

sweet tea to Grady's Barbecue: brewed on the stovetop by Gerri Grady.

sweet tea to Dukes Bar-B-Que: named by Tony Kittrell with the barbecue, hash and rice, the sauce and the sliced bread.

sweet tea to Parker's Barbecue: sold by the pint, quart, half gallon and gallon.

sweet tea to Allen & Son Barbeque: by the litre, brewed by Keith Allen himself.

Iced Tea Use one scant teaspoonful of tea to one cup of boiling water. Pour boiling water over tea leaves and let stand until milk warm. Then strain and sweeten to taste while tea is still warm, as it requires less sugar. Serve with crushed ice, green mint leaves, and sliced lemon and orange.

Tea — Southern Style Take one-half teaspoonful of tea to one cup of boiling water. Put the tea in the pot, pour the boiling water upon it and let stand where it will keep hot for five minutes. Then serve. Tea should never be boiled for it makes it bitter.

Iced Tea Ingredients: 3 tea bags; 1 teaspoon stevia; 2 teaspoons citric acid crystals (or malic / tartaric / citric blends); 4 teaspoons sugar 1. Fill a drip coffee maker with cold water and place the tea bags in the basket.
2. Place the stevia, acid, and sugar in the pot, and place the pot in the machine.
3. Let it run through its cycle, then chill the product. This is a concentrate and will make several litres of iced tea.
4. Place some ice in a tall glass and fill 80–90% with cold water. Pour in some iced tea nectar. You may reduce the water and add some fruit juice if desired.

title: white slaw
text:
Finely chopped cabbage in a dressing of mayonnaise or whipped salad dressing, sweet and pale: the slaw of eastern North Carolina and of most of South Carolina. It goes on the tray beside the chopped whole hog and on the bun of the sandwich, where its sweetness sets off the vinegar and pepper of the meat. Eastern pits use mayonnaise almost universally; NCpedia lists white or yellow coleslaw among the eastern sides, the yellow taking mustard. The name exists only where the red slaw does. Everywhere else in the state this is coleslaw, from the Dutch koolsla, cabbage salad.

Coleslaw came to the colonies with the Dutch — the 1667 cookbook De Verstandige Kock gives a landlady's recipe of cabbage strips in melted butter, vinegar and oil — and the word is Dutch too, koolsla, cabbage salad, in American English by 1794 and spelled 'cold slaw' by ear until the 1860s. The mayonnaise version is younger than the word, since mayonnaise itself dates from the mid-eighteenth century, and it is the version the South took up, with buttermilk slaw a Southern variant. In North Carolina the coleslaw is fine-chopped and vinegary and served with barbecue; in the east it is dressed with mayonnaise or whipped salad dressing almost without exception and put on the bun of the sandwich, the way Memphis puts slaw on its pork sandwich. The South Carolina plate — pork, rice, hash, coleslaw, sweet pickles, white bread, iced tea — carries the same slaw beside mustard-sauced pork. *Tradition holds —* the sweetness is the point: against a whole hog dressed with vinegar and pepper, the slaw is the sweet thing on the tray.

Cabbage chopped fine, often with a little carrot or onion, dressed with mayonnaise or whipped salad dressing, sugar, vinegar, salt and pepper, and chilled until it weeps a little. Eastern pits chop it nearly as fine as the meat so the two mix on the bun. A yellow slaw takes mustard in the dressing. Served cold beside the hot pork on the tray, spooned on the sandwich, and on hot dogs across the Coastal Plain.

Sam Jones BBQ lists a sweet slaw (2026); Skylight Inn serves its tray with slaw and cornbread; the Lexington pits keep a white slaw for those who ask. South Carolina buffets put it beside hash and rice.

white slaw to Eastern North Carolina barbecue: the style whose slaw this is, mayonnaise-dressed against the vinegar of the meat.

white slaw to South Carolina mustard barbecue: on the South Carolina plate beside hash, rice, pickles and white bread.

white slaw to red slaw: the Piedmont's slaw, dressed with dip instead of mayonnaise; the word 'white' exists to tell them apart.

white slaw to barbecue sandwich: goes on the bun over the meat in the east.

white slaw to barbecue tray: fills the other side of an eastern tray.

white slaw to Skylight Inn BBQ: on the tray with barbecue and cornbread.

white slaw to Sam Jones BBQ: listed as sweet slaw.

white slaw to slaw: the word, Dutch koolsla clipped.

white slaw to vinegar-and-pepper sauce: the sharpness the slaw's sweetness answers on the same tray.

white slaw to hash and rice: its neighbour on a South Carolina buffet plate.

Not to be confused with red-slaw: White slaw is pale and creamy with mayonnaise; red slaw is pink with ketchup or dip and has none. White is the east and South Carolina; red is Lexington.

Coleslaw I Ingredients: 4 tablespoons mayonnaise or 2 dL olive oil; ¼–½ cup (about 50–100ml) cider vinegar (optional); 1 head white cabbage; 1 medium red onion, thinly sliced 1. If adding cider vinegar, add it to the mayonnaise and mix together well.
2. Slice or shred the cabbage, as coarsely or finely as desired.
3. In a large bowl, mix cabbage and onion together with mayonnaise.
4. Set aside to allow the flavours to merge at least 20 minutes but preferably for a couple of hours.

Coleslaw II Ingredients: ¼ head napa cabbage, shredded; ¼ head red cabbage, shredded; ½ cup mayonnaise; ¼ cup apple cider vinegar; ½ tsp freshly-ground celery seed; ¼ tsp freshly-ground cumin; 1 tsp freshly-ground coriander; 1 tbsp dry mustard powder; Salt 1. Toss cabbage with a few big handfuls of kosher salt. Place in a colander in a bowl and let sit at room temperature 2 hours.
2. Drain cabbage. Rinse with clean water and let them go for a spin in your salad spinner until relatively dry.
3. Combine vinegar and spices. Microwave on high until mixture comes to a boil.
4. Fold in mayonnaise and cabbage. Chill until cold.

Salad for Slaw Ingredients: 3 eggs well beaten.; Nearly a cup of sugar.; 1 tablespoonful butter.; 1 tablespoonful mustard.; Pepper and salt to your taste.; Tumbler of milk.; Tumbler of vinegar. Stir well over the fire until as thick as custard. Let it cool and pour over cabbage. — Mrs. R. A.

Dressing for Cold Slaw Ingredients: 1 cup of vinegar.; 2 eggs well beaten.; 1 teaspoonful salt.; 1 teaspoonful mustard.; 1 tablespoonful sugar.; 1 tablespoonful butter.; A little black pepper. Mix together the butter, salt, pepper, sugar, mustard; add the eggs last.

Have the vinegar boiling and pour it on, stirring all the time. Then pour it back in the saucepan and boil a few minutes. Pour on the slaw when cold. — Miss W.

Cold Slaw Take vinegar and water in equal proportions (unless the vinegar is very strong); add butter, the size of an egg, and a little flour. Pour into a saucepan over the fire, and stir until it is thick; then pour in the beaten yolks of two eggs, and some salt. When it has been on the fire ten minutes more, stir in the cabbage, nicely shreded with a cabbage-cutter. The cabbage must be taken up, as soon as it is hot.

You may add a saltspoonful of mustard to the sauce, if you like it. Salt the cabbage.
