title: block pit
text:
An open pit built above ground of cinder blocks — concrete blocks — wide and shallow, a little longer than a split hog, with a rack across the top on which the pig lies and a bed of charcoal below; brick or steel are the alternatives, and the charcoal is made in a fireplace or a burn barrel beside it. It is the whole-hog pit of the Carolinas, the one a farm, a fire department or a family can lay in an afternoon. *Tradition holds —* the blocks go up dry, without mortar, two or three courses high, a gap is left for the shovel, and a sheet of tin or plywood closes the top.

The trench came first. *Tradition holds —* the farm barbecue of the Carolinas was cooked over a pit dug in the ground, and Mallard Creek Presbyterian Church in Charlotte cooked its 1929 barbecue that way, hickory coals shoved under whole hogs in ditches; by the 1980s metal cookers had replaced the church's dirt pits, with some meat still cooked on open pits inside a screened building. NCpedia records that few commercial pits today are dug in the ground. The cinder block — cheap, fireproof, stackable — is what the open pit became when it climbed out of the ditch. It is the pit of the pig pickin' and the cook-off, and the pit the whole-hog restaurants of the east grew from: the Skylight Inn's hogs cook over charcoal made in fireplaces beside the pits, and Rodney Scott's over hardwood charcoal shoveled from a burn barrel. The Cuban roasting box, by contrast, is a closed box of concrete blocks and steel mesh with the coals on top.

Blocks are laid in a rectangle a little longer and wider than the split hog; a rack spans the top, the hog goes on skin-side up, and a lid holds the heat. Coals from the burn barrel are shoveled in and spread beneath the carcass on a regular round through the night — *Tradition holds —* heavier under the hams and shoulders, thinner under the loin. The fat that drips hisses on the coals, and a flare-up is the danger the cook watches for; an uncontrolled pit fire can take the pit and the building. After eight to twenty-four hours the hog is flipped once, skin down, to crisp.

The block pit is the pit of the yard, the church lot, the fire station and the competition; restaurants that cook whole hog mostly cook in masonry or steel pits under a roof, and the form — a bed of coals, a rack, a hog, a lid — is the same.

block pit to whole hog: the cut it is sized to: a split carcass on a rack over coals.

block pit to burn barrel: the coal-maker beside it.

block pit to direct heat: coals spread directly beneath the carcass.

block pit to hickory and oak: the wood burned down for its coals.

block pit to brick pit: the closed, chimneyed Piedmont pit for shoulders; the block pit is open and for hogs.

block pit to pig cooker: the steel, wheeled version on gas or charcoal.

block pit to pig pickin': the party cooked on it.

block pit to fundraiser barbecue: the fire department's Saturday pig is cooked on one, or on a cooker.

block pit to Mallard Creek Barbecue: began in dirt ditches in 1929 and moved to metal cookers in the 1980s.

block pit to Skylight Inn BBQ: its hogs cook over charcoal made in fireplaces beside the pits.

Not to be confused with brick-pit: A block pit is open, unmortared and sized to a whole hog; a brick pit is a closed chamber with a door and a chimney, built for shoulders.

Not to be confused with pig-cooker: A block pit is stacked masonry on the ground; a pig cooker is a steel box on a trailer.

title: brick pit
text:
The masonry pit of the Piedmont: a closed brick chamber with a rack for the shoulders and a chimney through the roof to carry off the smoke. Coals made from oak and hickory go in through the door and are spread on the floor under the meat; the door shuts and the shoulders cook nine to twelve hours at about 200 to 225 degrees. The Barbecue Center in Lexington describes its pit as a brick oven with three chambers, 'comparable to an oversized smoker', and Lexington Barbecue's roof carries a row of smoking stacks. The line of chimneys on a Lexington roof is how you know a wood pit from the road.

The closed pit is the restaurant's answer to the trench. *Tradition holds —* the Lexington style began under tents on the courthouse square in the 1910s and moved indoors as its cooks built permanent pits, and the pits they built were brick because brick holds heat and a chimney takes the smoke out of a dining room. NCpedia's entry records that few commercial pits today are dug in the ground, and that economy, fastidiousness and health rules keep most Piedmont pits from basting with the ketchup-and-vinegar sauce, which flares; it goes on at the table instead, hence its name, dip. The Barbecue Center has cooked in its pit since 1955 under the Conrad family, and Lexington Barbecue, founded in 1962, cooks 'with wood, not gas' over oak and hickory coals only; a new pit hand there trains for a year before working the pits alone, and the heat from the fires, one visitor wrote, is overwhelming as the coals are turned. The North Carolina Historic Barbecue Trail admits only pits that cook on grates over wood or charcoal, so its Piedmont stops — Stamey's in Greensboro, Short Sugar's in Reidsville, the Bar-B-Q Center, Red Bridges in Shelby — are brick pits by definition.

Oak and hickory logs burn to coals in a fireplace or burner at the end of the pit house; a crew member shovels the coals through the pit door and spreads them evenly under the shoulders — the round Lexington calls 'firing the pits' — then shuts the door. The shoulders sit on the rack, salted but not basted or marinated, for nine to twelve hours at 200 to 225 degrees; the Barbecue Center puts three hundred a week through its three chambers. The smoke leaves by the chimney. Finished shoulders come off to the block to be chopped, coarse chopped or sliced.

The brick pit is still the plant of the Lexington restaurants — Lexington Barbecue, the Barbecue Center — and of the Piedmont stops on the Historic Barbecue Trail. Lexington Barbecue's site says it cooks with wood, not gas.

brick pit to Lexington-style barbecue: the style cooked in it: shoulders only, over hickory and oak coals, under a chimney.

brick pit to pork shoulder: the cut sized to its rack.

brick pit to hickory and oak: the coals on its floor.

brick pit to burn barrel: the fireplace or burner beside it does the barrel's job.

brick pit to direct heat: coals on the floor directly beneath the rack.

brick pit to block pit: the open, unmortared whole-hog pit of the east; the brick pit is closed and chimneyed.

brick pit to gas and electric cookers: what replaced the brick pit at many restaurants.

brick pit to Lexington dip: not basted in a closed pit because it flares; served at the table instead, which is why it is called dip.

brick pit to Lexington Barbecue: cooks over oak and hickory coals under a roof of smoking stacks; a new hand trains a year.

brick pit to Bar-B-Q Center: a three-chamber brick oven cooking three hundred shoulders a week since 1955.

brick pit to Stamey's Barbecue: the Greensboro pit house on the Historic Barbecue Trail.

brick pit to Wayne Monk: founded Lexington Barbecue in 1962; his sons Rick and Wayne run it.

brick pit to pit: the word, which in the Piedmont means this brick chamber.

brick pit to North Carolina Barbecue Society: its Trail's rule — wood or charcoal on grates — makes the Piedmont stops brick pits.

Not to be confused with block-pit: A brick pit is closed, with a door and a chimney, and cooks shoulders; a block pit is open, stacked from cinder blocks, and is sized to a split whole hog. Both are called 'the pit'.

Not to be confused with pig-cooker: A brick pit is masonry and stays put; a pig cooker is steel on wheels.

title: burn barrel
text:
A repurposed steel drum — or, at Scott's in Hemingway, two 55-gallon drums welded together — in which logs are burned down to coals: the wood goes in at the top, the coals are pulled out from below and carried by shovel to the pit. It is the coal-maker of the wood pit, the reason a whole hog can sit over a steady bed of coals for twelve hours with no flame under it. Older pit houses use a fireplace for the same job — the Skylight Inn burns its oak and hickory in fireplaces beside the pits — and the barrel is the version anyone can weld.

The barrel is the modern form of an older arrangement. *Tradition holds —* the trench pit of the farm barbecue had a fire burning at one end and coals raked down its length under the meat; when the pit climbed above ground into blocks and brick, the fire moved into a fireplace or a drum beside it. Mallard Creek Presbyterian Church in Charlotte cooked its first barbecues, from 1929, in ditches with hickory coals shoved underneath the whole hogs. At Scott's Bar-B-Que in Hemingway, Rodney Scott feeds hunks of hickory, oak and pecan through the top of the welded drums and pulls hot coals from below to stoke the pit. In November 2013 the family's wooden cookhouse caught fire — 'shooting like a torch', the fire department told him — and Scott took his hogs on the road to raise at least $100,000, part to rebuild and part for a fund to preserve the region's food traditions.

Split logs go in at the top and burn with the draft from the bottom; as they collapse into coals the cook rakes them out with a flat shovel and spreads them in the pit under the meat. *Tradition holds —* the bed goes heavier under the hams and shoulders and thinner under the loin, and a hog cooked through a night takes a fresh shovelful on a regular round, so the barrel is kept fed the whole time. Lexington crews call the same round, in a brick pit, 'firing the pits'.

Every wood-fired whole-hog pit keeps a barrel, a fireplace or a burner going through the night; the drum is the standard beside a block pit and at Scott's. Gas and electric cookers do without it, and the labor it stands for is the reason owners give for switching.

burn barrel to hickory and oak: the wood it turns into coals.

burn barrel to direct heat: its coals go straight under the meat.

burn barrel to block pit: the open pit it feeds, a shovel's walk away.

burn barrel to brick pit: the closed Piedmont pit fed the same way, from a fireplace or burner at the end of the pit house.

burn barrel to whole hog: what its coals cook through the night.

burn barrel to Scott's Bar-B-Que: two 55-gallon drums welded together, fed with hickory, oak and pecan.

burn barrel to Rodney Scott: the pitmaster whose barrel and pit fire NPR described in 2014.

burn barrel to Skylight Inn BBQ: uses fireplaces beside the pits instead of a drum.

burn barrel to Mallard Creek Barbecue: began in 1929 with hickory coals shoved under hogs in ditches.

burn barrel to gas and electric cookers: the cookers that need no barrel and no one to tend it.

burn barrel to pitmaster: the person who tends it through the night.

Not to be confused with pig-cooker: A burn barrel makes coals; nothing is cooked in it. A pig cooker holds the pig.

title: chopping block
text:
A thick wooden block and a pair of cleavers, on which cooked pork is turned into barbecue. The whole hog is pulled from the bones onto the block and chopped, skin and all, until the meat is fine enough to hold a thin vinegar sauce; the salt and the sauce go on at the block — at the Skylight Inn, vinegar, salt, pepper and Texas Pete. A Lexington shoulder is chopped fine, chopped coarse into small chunks, or sliced, and at Lexington Barbecue never pulled. Jane and Michael Stern called the sound of cleavers on the block one of the most alluring aspects of whole hog barbecue in the Carolinas.

The chop is the Carolinas' answer to a question other regions answer with a knife or a fork. *Tradition holds —* the eastern chop comes from the whole hog itself: light meat, dark meat, fat and skin from one animal are one dish only once they are chopped together, and the chop is what lets the crisp skin be eaten in every bite. Eastern-style meat is chopped after it is pulled from the bone, for a finer texture and so that it holds the thin vinegar sauce; Lexington-style is served pulled or lightly chopped, with larger strands of muscle, and the Lexington restaurants add the sliced tray. NCpedia records a South Carolina habit that has crossed the state line: separating the skin, the dry 'outside meat' and the juicier 'inside meat', so the customer chooses; some whole-hog restaurants let the customer choose white meat, dark meat or both, and prize the 'middlin' from the belly and the 'catfish' from under the tenderloin. The three cuts of the Piedmont are a price list. At Lexington Barbecue in September 2026 a chopped tray was $8.00 cash, a sliced tray $8.20 and a coarse-chop tray $8.60, with slaw and rolls or hush puppies; at the Barbecue Center a chopped tray was $9 small and $12 large, sliced or coarse chopped $10 and $13, dip on the meat, slaw included, hush puppies or a potato bun.

The cooked meat is pulled from the bones by hand and heaped on the block; the cook works the cleavers across the heap, folding the pile back on itself, adding the crisp skin in pieces once the meat is broken down, and seasoning on the block. For a Lexington shoulder the meat is chopped fine, chopped coarse for 'chunks', or sliced, and the dip goes on before it is trayed. A sandwich takes the chop and slaw on a soft bun.

The block and cleavers are in use at the Skylight Inn and in most whole-hog kitchens; Lexington menus carry the three cuts, and 'chopped' is the ordinary order on both sides of the state.

chopping block to whole hog: the carcass that becomes one dish on the block.

chopping block to pork shoulder: chopped fine, chopped coarse or sliced on the same block.

chopping block to pork skins: the crisp skin chopped through the eastern barbecue.

chopping block to vinegar-and-pepper sauce: goes on at the block, with salt.

chopping block to Texas Pete: part of the Skylight Inn's seasoning at the block.

chopping block to Lexington dip: goes on the chopped shoulder before it is trayed.

chopping block to barbecue tray: what the chop is served as, with slaw.

chopping block to barbecue sandwich: the chop and slaw on a soft bun.

chopping block to pulled pork: the preparation that skips the block; Lexington Barbecue never pulls.

chopping block to outside brown: the Piedmont's word for the shoulder's dry outer meat, which the Carolinas separate from the inside meat.

chopping block to Skylight Inn BBQ: chops tenderloin, inner meat and crisped skin together at the block.

chopping block to Lexington Barbecue: chopped, coarse chop or sliced; never pulled.

chopping block to Bar-B-Q Center: chopped, sliced or coarse chopped 'chunks', dip on the meat.

Not to be confused with chopped: The block is the tool and the place; 'chopped' is the word for the result and the order.

title: direct heat
text:
The Carolina way of putting fire to meat: a bed of hardwood coals directly beneath the hog or the shoulders, with no flame and no separate firebox. The coals are made elsewhere — in a burn barrel or a fireplace — and shoveled in, so the meat sits over glowing charcoal and its own dripping fat rather than in a stream of smoke. The contrast is the offset smoker of Central Texas: a cylinder with a smaller firebox attached at one end, whose burning post-oak fire sends heat and smoke sideways through the chamber past the meat — indirect heat. The whole-hog article, the Mallard Creek church and the Barbecue Center all describe the coals going under the meat.

The word carries the method. The Wikipedia article on barbecue draws its line between the indirect barbecues of the United States — meat roasted or smoked over wood or charcoal at low temperature for hours — and the direct grilling of most of the world, done over hot coals for minutes; in a typical American home barbecue the coals are dispersed to the sides. The Carolina pit sits across that line: the coals are directly under the meat, as on a grill, but far enough below and slow enough that the cook is barbecuing, not grilling. True 'Cue quotes a federal meat-labeling rule that defines barbecued meat as 'cooked by the direct action of dry heat resulting from the burning of hard wood'. Texas divides the same way: Central Texas cooks with indirect heat from a pecan, post-oak or mesquite fire, and West Texas over direct mesquite heat 'in a method very similar to grilling'. *Inference —* in geometry the Carolina pit is closer to the West Texas cowboy fire than to the Austin smoker, and the reason both Carolina styles burn their wood to coals first is that flame under a fat hog is a fire. Ed Mitchell in Wilson cooks 'hot and fast' with a bank of coals surrounding the hog, starting at 500 degrees and letting it fall to 250; Rodney Scott shovels coals under a hog lying belly-down for eight to twelve hours; the Barbecue Center in Lexington 'fires the pits' by distributing coals evenly beneath the shoulders.

Coals go in under the meat in a thin, even bed and are renewed from the burn barrel through the cook; the meat is never over flame. *Tradition holds —* the bed goes heavier under the hams and shoulders of a whole hog and thinner under the loin. Fat drips onto the coals and vaporizes — *Inference —* the source of much of what the Carolinas call wood flavor — and a flare-up from that fat is the whole-hog cook's constant danger. The pit is closed with a lid or a door to hold the heat, and a hog is flipped once near the end.

Every pit on the North Carolina Historic Barbecue Trail and every True 'Cue certificate cooks this way by definition — on grates over pits with wood or charcoal. *Tradition holds —* the offset smoker has arrived too: Lewis Barbecue in Charleston cooks Central Texas brisket in offset smokers, and is described here the same way as a wood pit.

direct heat to burn barrel: makes the coals that go under the meat.

direct heat to hickory and oak: the wood burned down for the bed.

direct heat to block pit: the open pit built for it.

direct heat to brick pit: the closed pit built for it: coals on the floor, rack above, chimney over.

direct heat to whole hog: the cut cooked over a bed of coals for a night.

direct heat to pork shoulder: the Piedmont's cut, over the same coals in a brick pit.

direct heat to pig cooker: on charcoal it works the same way; on gas the burner stands in for the coals.

direct heat to gas and electric cookers: heat from a burner or an element, smoke from a chip box: neither coals nor firebox.

direct heat to Ed Mitchell: cooks hot and fast with a bank of coals around the hog, 500 degrees falling to 250.

direct heat to Rodney Scott: shovels burn-barrel coals under a belly-down hog for eight to twelve hours.

direct heat to Campaign for Real Barbecue: quotes the federal definition — direct dry heat from burning hardwood — on its wood page.

direct heat to pit: the word for the hole, then the box, that holds the coals under the meat.

direct heat to Lewis Barbecue: the Charleston restaurant that, tradition holds, cooks Texas brisket the other way, in offset smokers.

Not to be confused with hickory-and-oak: Direct heat is where the fuel sits; hickory and oak are the fuel. A Texas firebox burns the same woods beside the meat instead of beneath it.

title: gas and electric cookers
text:
The cookers most Carolina barbecue is cooked in: steel ovens fired by propane, natural gas or an electric element, with a thermostat and racks, and often a box for wood chips or a log to put smoke on the meat. A gas smoker lights a burner directly under a box of wood or charcoal; an electric one runs a heating element that holds any temperature from a cold smoke to about 275 degrees. New barbecue restaurants mostly open on them and many older ones switched. They cook overnight unattended, hold a set temperature, make no soot and need no one to shovel coals at three in the morning, and they are the machine behind a great deal of what both states call barbecue, sauce and slaw included.

The argument has two sides and each states its reasons. The cooks who switched say it plainly: gas and electricity are cheaper and easier and the product is more consistent — John Shelton Reed grants all three — and a wood pit needs someone awake through the night, produces soot, and burns more fuel and labor for the same meat. Many owners also say the health department made them do it. Reed and the True 'Cue campaign he co-founded put a Challenge in the Raleigh News & Observer on April 23, 2014, offering a prize to anyone who could name the regulation; two years on no one had, and Daniel Vaughn in Texas and Robert Moss in South Carolina had reported the same from their states. Reed writes that one state official mentioned environmental concerns and that the actual motives remain unclear. On the other side stands the billboard at the Skylight Inn, whose four tenets include that barbecue must be cooked with wood, and the True 'Cue Pledge for those who hold that if it is not cooked with wood it is not barbecue; the campaign's wood page calls smoke 'the umami of barbecue', quotes Pete Jones, Rodney Scott and Wilber Shirley among its witnesses, and Alton Brown's joke that with gas 'you can control the heat. But you're going to go to hell.' Reed draws the line with care: the campaign has 'no beef' with cooks who use gas or electricity for ignition and temperature control so long as wood smoke reaches the meat, and reserves 'faux 'cue' for meat cooked with no smoke at all. The pig pickin' article records the same split at the backyard: propane for a steady temperature, charcoal 'touted as producing better-tasting meat'. Jim Early, searching a hundred counties for pits still cooking over wood coals, found fewer than thirty.

Shoulders or a split hog go on the racks in the evening with the smoke box loaded, the thermostat holds the temperature overnight, and in the morning the meat comes off to the block. There is no burn barrel, no shoveling round and no chimney; the cook's labor is loading, unloading and chopping. The sauce, the slaw and the chop are the same as at a wood pit, which is why the customer often cannot tell and the campaigns exist to tell them.

Wood pits are a counted minority: about seventy North Carolina restaurants held True 'Cue certificates in January 2018, and the Historic Barbecue Trail listed about two dozen. *Inference —* the rest of the barbecue sold in both states comes off gas or electricity.

title: hickory and oak
text:
The hardwoods of the Carolina pit. Hickory and oak are the woods a Carolina cook burns, usually together and usually burned down to coals before they go under the meat: Lexington pits cook over oak and hickory coals, the Skylight Inn burns oak and hickory logs in fireplaces beside its pits, and Scott's in Hemingway feeds hickory, oak and pecan through the top of a burn barrel. South Carolina's barbecue is smoked over hickory or oak; Lexington's over a hardwood fire, usually hickory. Both are dense, slow-burning and abundant in the eastern forest, and both give the strong smoke that pork carries. Pecan is itself a hickory — Carya illinoinensis — with a sweeter, milder smoke.

Wood smoke flavors the meat, so the woods a region has decide how its barbecue tastes; hickory, oak and mesquite give a strong smoke, and pecan, maple, alder and the fruit woods a milder, sweeter one, which is why the strong woods go with pork and beef. Pecan, a hickory native to the south-central United States, is sold as a smoking wood for a 'sweet and nutty flavor stronger than many fruit woods'; Rodney Scott burns it with hickory and oak. Skin takes up more of the smoke than meat does, which is one reason the eastern chop keeps its skin. Ed Mitchell in Wilson burns oak and hickory logs and adds charcoal briquettes. *Inference —* in a Carolina pit the wood is burned to coals before it reaches the meat, so most of the flame's smoke is spent; what the meat then breathes is largely its own fat and juices vaporizing on the coals, and that is the flavor Carolina cooks call 'wood' rather than 'smoke' — the same log gives a different result in a Texas offset smoker, where the meat sits in the smoke of a burning fire. True 'Cue, the campaign that certifies wood-cooked pits, calls wood smoke 'the umami of barbecue' and 'barbecue's soul'.

Logs burn down to coals in a fireplace or a burn barrel; the coals are shoveled into the pit under the meat, and Lexington crews 'fire the pits' by spreading them evenly beneath the shoulders. At a pig pickin' the fuel is often bagged charcoal with chunks of blackjack oak or hickory added for flavor, or a separate stove of hardwood whose coals are shoveled under the grate; Ed Mitchell adds charcoal briquettes to his oak and hickory.

Hickory is the sign-painter's word across both states and oak the workhorse beside it; every pit on the North Carolina Historic Barbecue Trail and every True 'Cue certificate is a wood fire of one or both. Scott's in Hemingway burns pecan with the other two.

hickory and oak to whole hog: the cut whose skin takes the most smoke.

hickory and oak to Eastern North Carolina barbecue: the Skylight Inn's oak and hickory fireplaces are the east's version.

hickory and oak to Skylight Inn BBQ: burns oak and hickory logs in fireplaces beside its pits.

title: hog killing
text:
The winter slaughter of the farm's hogs, done on the first cold day of autumn or winter, when the meat would keep. In rural North Carolina neighbors gathered before dawn; water was heated with fire-hot stones dropped into barrels; the penned and fattened hogs were killed with knives, bled, scalded, hung on a gambrel — a spreader bar through the hind legs — and scraped clean of hair; the carcasses cooled overnight and were cut up the next day, the hams, sides, shoulders, jowls and heads salted down in the smokehouse. Lard was rendered, the fat cooked down to cracklings, the trim ground for sausage. It is the farm year's pork day, and the social form the pit barbecue grew up beside.

William S. Powell's entry in the Encyclopedia of North Carolina (2006) describes the day as farms kept it: as many as a hundred hogs penned and fattened on peas, potatoes, corn gleaned from the harvested fields or mast from the woods; workers from the neighborhood gathered well before dawn; stones heated in an open fire and dropped into barrels to heat the scalding water; the hogs killed with large knives, bled, scalded, hung and scraped; cooled overnight, cut up and salted the next day on a tilted platform in the smokehouse, the dripping brine caught in troughs and boiled down to save the salt for the stock. The weeks after were spare ribs, liver and sausage; the hams came a month or two later. Carolina Country followed the Jackson family of Hopkins through a January hog killing in 2019: Terry Jackson directing, his son in training, neighbors and friends at the scalding vat; sausage seasoned with salt, red pepper and sage and a patty fried over the wood fire for approval; lard rendered and cracklings saved; hams and shoulders carried to the salt room; chitterlings, feet and bones for broth; a pot of homemade soup at midday for everyone who came. The pit's relation to the day is old: George Washington raised pigs for slaughter in November at Mount Vernon and, once the enslaved people had cured the hams and bacon, whole pigs were pit-roasted over coals 'as a treat'. John Shelton Reed writes that barbecue was never home cooking, and until the early twentieth century was reserved for harvests, fundraisers and political rallies. *Tradition holds —* the hog killing and the pit shared a season and a crowd, and a pig set aside from the killing was the cheapest way to feed the neighbors who came to help.

Cold weather first. The hog is stuck and bled, scalded in a vat or barrel of water just under the boil and scraped clean of hair, then hung head-down from a gambrel, gutted, and left overnight to cool and firm. Next day it is cut into hams, shoulders, sides for bacon, loins and ribs; the trim is ground and seasoned for sausage, the fat rendered in a kettle for lard with the crisp bits kept as cracklings, the intestines cleaned for chitterlings, and the feet and bones boiled for broth. Hams and shoulders are salted or smoked to keep.

The community hog killing survives on some farms — Carolina Country followed one in 2019 — and the pig for a pit comes from a processor: the Skylight Inn buys most of its hogs from meat processors in Ayden. *Tradition holds —* the word survives in the weather: a hard frost is hog-killing weather.

hog killing to whole hog: the pig that, tradition holds, came off the killing and onto the pit.

hog killing to pig pickin': the feast; the killing is the work. One is winter labor, the other a party.

hog killing to pork skins: cracklings, the fat's crisp remainder, are the killing's snack; pork skins are the pit's.

hog killing to hash and rice: the head and liver South Carolina stewed into hash came from a day like this.

hog killing to block pit: the open pit that, tradition holds, was dug beside the killing.

hog killing to hog: the animal, penned and fattened for this day.

hog killing to political barbecue: the other occasion for a whole pig before the twentieth century, per Reed.

hog killing to Skylight Inn BBQ: buys its hogs from processors in Ayden; nobody kills them on the farm any more.

Not to be confused with pig-pickin: A hog killing is butchering for the year's meat; a pig pickin' is cooking one pig for one crowd.

title: pig cooker
text:
A steel box on a trailer chassis, long enough for a split hog, with a hinged lid, a grate, and either a row of propane burners underneath or a bed for charcoal: the cooker of the pig pickin', towed to the church lot, the tailgate or the fire station and home again. Carolina Cooker of Micro, North Carolina, builds one of 12-gauge steel with four propane burners on a leaf-spring trailer, listed at $2,599.99 in September 2026; BQ Grills of Elm City builds towable charcoal-and-wood cookers of eighth-inch steel in five- and six-foot lengths at $7,200 to $9,800. The article on the pig pickin' calls the grills 'as varied as the methods of producing them', some homemade, some custom-made.

The pig pickin' moved the whole hog off the farm pit and onto wheels. *Tradition holds —* welded cookers appeared in eastern North Carolina after the Second World War, when propane and a cutting torch put a pit within reach of anyone with a trailer hitch, and the rental cooker followed. What the article on the pig pickin' records is the argument the cooker started: propane 'is said to maintain a consistent temperature, whereas charcoal or charwood are often touted as producing better-tasting meat', and the cooks who run charcoal add chunks of blackjack oak or hickory for the smoke, or keep a separate stove of hardwood to make coals and shovel them under the grate. The cooking is communal and 'usually directed by an authority figure' — the host, helped by friends and family — and the pig goes on meat-side down for four to eight hours and is flipped once when it stops dripping fat. Ed Mitchell learned on a family cooker in Wilson: at fourteen or fifteen he tended the fire after the men, having passed the moonshine, fell asleep, and his grandfather woke to a cooked pig and poured him his first glass.

The split hog goes on the grate meat-side down; on gas the burners run low, on charcoal the coals are lit in the bed or shoveled in from a hardwood stove; the lid comes down for four to eight hours until the dripping slows, and the hog is flipped once, skin down, to crisp. Some cooks wipe the ash from the skin with paper towels or a whisk broom before the flip so the cracklings come out clean. Off the cooker the meat is chopped, pulled, or picked straight off the bones by the guests.

Cookers are built and sold across the Coastal Plain — Micro and Elm City among the makers — and every pig pickin', tailgate and fire-department plate sale runs on one. Gas is the ordinary choice and charcoal the argued-for one.

pig cooker to pig pickin': the party it exists for.

pig cooker to whole hog: the cut it is built around: a split carcass on a six-foot grate.

pig cooker to gas and electric cookers: its restaurant-size relatives, fixed and thermostated.

pig cooker to block pit: the masonry pit it replaced on wheels.

pig cooker to burn barrel: the hardwood stove some cooks keep beside a charcoal cooker.

pig cooker to direct heat: on charcoal it works the Carolina way, coals under the meat; on gas the burner stands in for the coals.

pig cooker to hickory and oak: the chunks added to the charcoal for smoke.

pig cooker to fundraiser barbecue: the Saturday plate sale is cooked on one.

pig cooker to political barbecue: the cooker behind the candidate's free plate.

pig cooker to barbecue chicken: the other meat on the same grate at a fire-department plate sale.

pig cooker to Ed Mitchell: cooked his first pig, unbidden, on the family cooker in Wilson.

Not to be confused with gas-and-electric-cookers: A pig cooker is the wheeled steel box of the yard and the plate sale; the gas or electric cooker of a restaurant is fixed, thermostated and indoors.

Not to be confused with burn-barrel: A pig cooker holds the pig; a burn barrel only makes the coals.

title: pork shoulder
text:
The front leg and shoulder of the pig, sold as one primal — a primal being one of the large first divisions of a carcass — or split in two: the butt, the upper half with the blade bone, and the picnic, the lower arm half, which cured on the bone is a 'picnic ham'. The butt's name is a barrel, not an anatomy. In the North Carolina Piedmont, shoulder is the only cut that counts as barbecue: Lexington pits salt it, lay it over oak and hickory coals for nine to twelve hours, and serve it chopped, coarse chopped or sliced under a red dip. It is darker meat than the loin and stays moist through a long cook, and it is what packers ship when they will not ship a carcass.

New England butchers of the colonial and Revolutionary era stored and shipped pork in barrels called butts, and the shoulder cut they packed that way took the name of the port; a 1912 University of Illinois bulletin notes the barrels still going to Germany and Denmark, and 'Boston butt' first appears in print in 1915. In the Carolinas the cut's rise is the whole hog's decline. The Piedmont settled on shoulders early — *Tradition holds —* because a shoulder fit a small brick pit and a lunch counter's day in a way a carcass did not. By the 1980s the corporate farms replacing independent hog farms shipped butchered shoulders and hams rather than whole pigs, which pushed restaurants elsewhere the same way. Mallard Creek Presbyterian Church in Charlotte, which began in 1929 by cooking three or four pigs and a goat, told Our State in 2016: 'Now we just use the butt.' South Carolina hash, once made from heads and liver, is now mostly made from leftover shoulder.

Lexington pits cook shoulders only, salted but not basted or marinated, on racks over oak and hickory coals for nine to twelve hours at about 200 to 225 degrees; the Barbecue Center puts three hundred a week through its pit. Elsewhere a butt is rubbed, smoked until it reaches 195 to 205 degrees inside, and shredded. Off the pit the Piedmont serves it three ways — chopped fine, coarse chopped in small chunks, or sliced; never pulled, at Lexington Barbecue — and dresses it with dip. *Tradition holds —* the crusted outer meat is sold apart as outside brown.

Shoulder is the cut of the Piedmont's pits — Lexington Barbecue, the Barbecue Center, Stamey's, Red Bridges, Short Sugar's — and of most new restaurants in both states, because it arrives boxed from the packer; a pulled-pork menu anywhere in the country means this cut. At Lexington Barbecue a chopped tray was $8.00 cash and $8.25 by card in September 2026.

Root: Boston + butt, a barrel: in colonial and Revolutionary-era New England butchers stored and shipped this shoulder cut in barrels called butts, and the Boston-area method of cutting it gave the cut its name. Picnic (the lower shoulder): cured on the bone it is a 'picnic ham'; no origin for the name is cited here..

pork shoulder to Lexington-style barbecue: the style that uses only this cut, darker and moister than the loin, under a red dip.

pork shoulder to whole hog: the older cut it displaced wherever packers stopped shipping carcasses.

pork shoulder to chopping block: where it is chopped fine, chopped coarse or sliced.

pork shoulder to brick pit: the closed Piedmont pit a rack of shoulders fits.

pork shoulder to pulled pork: the national name for this cut smoked and shredded; Lexington chops or slices it and does not pull.

pork shoulder to Lexington dip: the thin vinegar-and-ketchup sauce the Piedmont puts on the chopped shoulder.

pork shoulder to hash and rice: modern South Carolina hash is mostly made from leftover shoulder.

pork shoulder to Mallard Creek Barbecue: cooked whole pigs in 1929 and pork butts by 2016.

pork shoulder to Lexington Barbecue: cooks shoulders over oak and hickory coals and serves them chopped, coarse chopped or sliced, never pulled.

pork shoulder to Bar-B-Q Center: cooks three hundred shoulders a week in a three-chamber brick pit.

pork shoulder to Wayne Monk: founded Lexington Barbecue in 1962 on this cut.

pork shoulder to Stamey's Barbecue: a Greensboro shoulder pit interviewed for the Southern Foodways Alliance's North Carolina project.

pork shoulder to Red Bridges Barbecue Lodge: a Shelby shoulder pit on the Historic Barbecue Trail.

pork shoulder to Short Sugar's Pit Bar-B-Q: a Reidsville shoulder pit on the Historic Barbecue Trail.

Not to be confused with pulled-pork: 'Pulled pork' names a preparation of this cut; on a Lexington menu the same shoulder is 'barbecue', and it comes chopped or sliced.

Not to be confused with whole-hog: Shoulder meat is all dark and has no crisp skin; a whole-hog chop mixes light meat, dark meat and skin.

title: whole hog
text:
The entire dressed pig — dressed meaning gutted and scraped of hair, the head sometimes left on — split open along the backbone, laid flat over coals and cooked as one piece, then pulled from the bones and chopped together: ham, shoulder, loin, belly and, in the Carolinas, the crisped skin. It is the oldest form of open-pit barbecue in the United States and the cut that defines eastern North Carolina and the Pee Dee of South Carolina. A hog of 80 to 120 pounds dressed weight is the usual size for a pig pickin'; restaurants choose small hogs and cook them hot so the skin crisps, and a whole animal can run to 300 pounds.

Robert Moss finds the ritual barbecue of whole hogs established in the British colonies by the eighteenth century; the communal feast of whole pigs or sheep spread from Virginia into the Carolinas in the mid-1700s and fed fundraisers, church gatherings and political rallies. The Oxford Encyclopedia of Food and Drink in America calls whole hog the oldest style of open-pit barbecue in the country. The first sit-down restaurant built on it was Bob Melton's, opened at Rocky Mount in 1924; for most of the twentieth century such places had white owners and Black cooks, and new pits were founded by cooks trained at older ones. In Hemingway, South Carolina, the Scott family's variety store cooked one hog a week when Rodney Scott started at eleven and grew to seven or eight a day. The hazards are in the method: fat renders and pools in the cavity, so the meat cooks in its own fat, and a lean 'bacon hog' such as the American Yorkshire is chosen because a fat one feeds the fire. Pit fires are the common disaster; Scott's wooden cookhouse burned in November 2013 — 'shooting like a torch', the fire department told him — and the family took its hogs on the road to raise at least $100,000 to rebuild. In 2017 Daniel Vaughn of Texas Monthly counted the whole-hog restaurants of the country and found them falling: packers ship shoulders and hams, not carcasses; a whole hog costs more labor, fuel and soot than a shoulder; and much of its weight is bone and fat that cannot be sold.

The carcass is split so it lies flat; the backbone may be cracked and the head split. It goes on the rack skin-side up — meat-side down, in the east's phrase — over a bed of coals and cooks for eight to twenty-four hours, most of that time unturned, before one flip to crisp the skin; at Scott's the flip comes at the eight-to-twelve-hour mark and a full-size mop bathes the meat in the family's vinegar-and-pepper sauce. The meat is not basted before the flip, though some cooks season it with a dry rub. Turning a heavy carcass takes several hands. Off the pit the meat is picked from the bones and chopped fine or pulled into threads; the eastern chop takes the crisp skin in, and the Pee Dee sometimes skins the pig first and fries the skin separately.

Whole hog is the restaurant cut of the Coastal Plain and the Pee Dee — the Skylight Inn, B's, Grady's, Parker's and Wilber's in North Carolina; Scott's in Hemingway and Rodney Scott's in Charleston in South Carolina — and the cooking of most pig pickin's. Vaughn's 2017 count found fewer whole-hog restaurants each year; cooks who keep it say their customers come for the ritual.

whole hog to Eastern North Carolina barbecue: the style whose name it is: the east cooks the entire pig and chops it, skin and all.

whole hog to Pee Dee whole-hog barbecue: the South Carolina region that keeps the whole hog under a vinegar-pepper sauce; the pig is sometimes skinned first and the skin fried.

whole hog to pig pickin': the gathering built on it: a whole hog cooked for a crowd and picked off the bones by hand.

whole hog to block pit: the open cinder-block pit sized to a split carcass.

whole hog to burn barrel: where the coals come from on a wood pit: logs burned down in a barrel or fireplace and shoveled under the hog.

whole hog to pig cooker: the trailer cooker that takes a whole hog on gas or charcoal at a pig pickin'.

whole hog to direct heat: the heat under it: coals directly beneath the carcass, not smoke drawn from a firebox.

whole hog to chopping block: where the whole hog becomes barbecue: cleavers on a block, skin chopped through the meat.

whole hog to pork skins: the crisp skin the eastern chop is judged on, chopped into the meat.

whole hog to hash and rice: what South Carolina made of the head, liver and trimmings left after the chop.

whole hog to pork shoulder: the cut that replaced it in the Piedmont and at most new restaurants, because packers ship shoulders, not carcasses.

whole hog to hog killing: the winter slaughter that, tradition holds, once supplied the pig for the pit.

whole hog to hog: the animal, and the east's word for the carcass on the pit.

whole hog to Skylight Inn BBQ: cooks its hogs heads-on over oak and hickory coals in Ayden.

whole hog to Scott's Bar-B-Que: the Hemingway store that went from one hog a week to seven or eight a day.

whole hog to Rodney Scott: the Pee Dee pitmaster whose whole hog won a James Beard chef award in 2018.

whole hog to Ed Mitchell: the Wilson pitmaster who cooks whole hog because, he says, a sandwich needs shoulder, ham and belly together.

whole hog to Bob Melton: opened the first sit-down whole-hog restaurant, at Rocky Mount in 1924.

Not to be confused with pork-shoulder: A chop with crisp skin and both light and dark meat through it is whole hog; a uniformly dark, moist chop with no skin is shoulder.

Not to be confused with pig-pickin: Whole hog is the cut and the method; a pig pickin' is the party at which it is eaten off the bones.

title: 12 Bones Smokehouse
text:
A mountain barbecue house now trading from Hendersonville Road in Arden, south of Asheville, after Hurricane Helene took its River Arts District room in September 2024. Tom Montgomery and Sabra Kelley opened the first one in 2005 in a cinder-block shack on an Asheville floodplain; Bryan and Angela King have owned it since about 2012. Ribs are the signature — blueberry-chipotle and other glazes that are not Carolina orthodoxy — with pulled pork alongside. Barack Obama ate here in April 2010, which is the thing most often said about it.

The first 12 Bones was a cinder-block shack in a floodplain in the River Arts District, opened in 2005 by Tom Montgomery and Sabra Kelley. Bryan and Angela King bought it — 2012 by two 2024 accounts, 2011 by a 2017 one — and Explore Asheville's profile puts the ownership plainly in Bryan King's own words, that he owns 12 Bones with his wife Angela. On April 23, 2010 Barack Obama came in and ate ribs, mac and cheese, corn pudding and sweet tea; accounts differ on whether he visited twice or three times. In January 2017 the original Riverside Drive building was closed and demolished for a road project and a roundabout, and the business moved to Foundy Street beside Wedge Brewing. Then on September 27, 2024 Helene put the floodplain under water. Bryan King described going inside to find mud in the attic and the building almost completely submerged, and called it a very long recovery. By April 2025 the business had told Blue Ridge Public Radio it would not rebuild on Foundy Street. Arden is what is left, open seven days now rather than the weekday lunches the Asheville room kept.

Ribs are the thing: a dry rub and a run of glazes, the blueberry-chipotle the one people name, which is not how a Piedmont or a Coastal Plain pit finishes pork. Pulled pork, sides and a brewing operation fill the rest. An Explore Asheville listing says the meats are smoked long and slow over oak and cherry; that reads as the restaurant's own copy and could not be confirmed on the company's site, which is why the fuel here is left unknown.

Open seven days, 11 a.m. to 8 p.m., at 2350 Hendersonville Road, Arden — the only location the company lists. The Foundy Street room in Asheville's River Arts District closed with Helene in September 2024 and will not be rebuilt.

12 Bones Smokehouse to pork shoulder: the cut behind its pulled pork, beside the ribs it is better known for.

12 Bones Smokehouse to barbecue tray: the plate in the mountains, where the glazed rib rather than the chopped shoulder is the order.

12 Bones Smokehouse to Buxton Hall Barbecue: the other Asheville barbecue name of the same decade; Buxton Hall closed in 2023, 12 Bones lost its river room to Helene in 2024.

title: Allen & Son Barbeque
text:
The hickory-fired pork-shoulder restaurant on Millhouse Road at N.C. 86 north of Chapel Hill that Keith Allen opened in 1971 at nineteen and closed in the first week of December 2018, quietly, to avoid a long goodbye. Allen split the hickory himself, fired the pit every half hour for nine hours, and dressed the chopped shoulder with the hot vinegar sauce he had from his father — an eastern sauce on Piedmont meat. His wife Tammy waited tables for thirty years and made the ice cream; the pies, cobblers and banana pudding were the second reason to come. A separate Allen & Son in Pittsboro, under a licensing agreement, stayed open.

Keith Allen's father James ran an Allen & Son in Chatham County, and Keith was cooking at twelve or thirteen after his father bought the business; his father died at 51 or 52. In 1971 Keith opened the Chapel Hill restaurant with $3,000, Our State reported in 2017. He started work at 2:30 in the morning five days a week, split hickory logs by hand for the heat and the flavor — 'I keep cooking with wood because I'm chasing that flavor' — and cooked sixteen-pound shoulders down to nine or eleven over nine hours. 'Nobody's hands but mine touch my barbecue, until the customer's do.' The authors of Holy Smoke interviewed him at length; the Southern Foodways Alliance gave him its Guardian of the Tradition award in 2007. He had no son to take it on; his daughter went to graduate school in geospatial science. In early December 2018 he closed without notice, and Chapelboro reported on December 6 that the Pittsboro Allen & Son on U.S. 15-501 would continue under a separate licensing agreement. UNC Press published a closing interview with him two weeks later.

Sixteen-pound shoulders over hickory Allen split himself, the pit fired every thirty minutes for nine hours, the meat chopped and dressed with a vinegar sauce he called hot and spicy. Chicken, catfish and cheeseburgers filled out the menu, and the desserts — ice cream made daily, cobblers from his grandmother's recipe, coconut chess and peanut butter pies, pecan pie, banana pudding — were made in the house, with sweet tea.

Closed since December 2018. The building at 6203 Millhouse Road, Chapel Hill, is not the Pittsboro Allen & Son, which continued separately; this record is the Chapel Hill restaurant only.

Allen & Son Barbeque to Lexington-style barbecue: the cut and the wood are the Piedmont's: shoulders over hickory.

Allen & Son Barbeque to Eastern North Carolina barbecue: the sauce was the east's, hot vinegar from his father, on Piedmont meat.

Allen & Son Barbeque to pork shoulder: sixteen pounds going in, nine to eleven coming out.

Allen & Son Barbeque to hickory and oak: hickory, split by hand by the owner for the heat and the flavor.

Allen & Son Barbeque to vinegar-and-pepper sauce: his sauce, inherited, hot and spicy.

Allen & Son Barbeque to banana pudding: on the dessert board with the pies and cobblers.

Allen & Son Barbeque to sweet tea: on every table.

Allen & Son Barbeque to John Shelton Reed: interviewed Allen at length for Holy Smoke.

title: Alston Bridges Barbecue
text:
The Shelby pork-shoulder house of the other Bridges family, on East Grover Street in Cleveland County, where Alston Bridges and his wife Mabel bought the property in 1955. Alston learned the trade from his brother-in-law Warner Stamey, managing Stamey's Log Cabin Barbecue in Lexington for two and a half years first. About fifty shoulders a day go through the kitchen; the tray is chopped or coarse-chopped pork with red slaw and hushpuppies. What is under the meat is disputed: three accounts describe electric cookers or gas, one promotional listing says wood-smoked.

Two Bridges families cook barbecue in Shelby and they are not related — a shared ancestor somewhere in the 1700s is as close as the local history will put them. Warner Stamey trained both Red Bridges and Alston Bridges in the 1940s, and Alston's apprenticeship is the documented one: he and Mabel moved to Lexington, he managed Stamey's Log Cabin Barbecue for two and a half years, and then they came to Shelby and bought 620 East Grover Street. The county history gives the year as 1955 and a visiting writer gives 1956. Alston died in 1970; his son Kent and Kent's wife Linda took it on, and the county history says Kent and Linda's children operate the business now. Our State found Alston's grandson Reid Bridges behind the counter in 2013, explaining the difference between chopped and coarse-chopped. The fuel is where the sources part. Our State wrote in 2013 that he starts the pork on electric cookers and finishes it in a pit. A visiting writer in March 2024 found the smoke missing and put it down to a move from pit to gas some years earlier. The NC Pork Council's listing calls it wood-smoked. Neither the Historic Barbecue Trail nor the Campaign for Real Barbecue lists the house, and both exclude gas and electric.

About fifty pork shoulders a day, from a short-shank cut the kitchen buys through a Gastonia distributor. Our State's account of the method has the pork starting on electric cookers and finishing in a pit. The meat is chopped or coarse-chopped to order and served with red slaw, the cabbage cut fine and dressed with the Piedmont dip, and hushpuppies. The menus read: Pigs are Beautiful.

Open at 620 East Grover Street, Shelby. Hours differ across three listings, and the restaurant's own site was posting a Labor Day closing and a September 8 return when read on September 16, 2026. Check before driving.

Alston Bridges Barbecue to Lexington-style barbecue: the style of its tray, cooked forty miles west of Lexington itself.

Alston Bridges Barbecue to pork shoulder: the cut — about fifty short-shank shoulders a day.

Alston Bridges Barbecue to Warner Stamey: his brother-in-law and teacher; Alston managed Stamey's Log Cabin Barbecue before opening here.

Alston Bridges Barbecue to red slaw: the slaw on its tray, dressed with the dip.

Alston Bridges Barbecue to Red Bridges Barbecue Lodge: the other Bridges barbecue in Shelby, from another family Stamey also trained.

Not to be confused with red-bridges-barbecue-lodge: Two Bridges, one town, no relation closer than a possible common ancestor in the 1700s. Red Bridges Barbecue Lodge is on US 74 and burns hickory and oak; Alston Bridges is on East Grover Street and its fuel is disputed in the sources. Warner Stamey taught both men in the 1940s.

title: Backyard BBQ Pit
text:
A Black-owned barbecue restaurant on N.C. 55, the Apex Highway, in southeast Durham, opened in April 2007 by Fabianne and Melvin Simmons, who bought a struggling restaurant and made it a neighborhood institution: chopped barbecue and sandwiches, ribs, smoked chicken and oxtails, cooked over wood coals and made from scratch. Its later years were hard — a $50,000 GoFundMe in 2023, a change of owners, eight months dark for renovations before a March 2024 reopening, and in April 2026 a report that it was weeks from closing unless a buyer came. Its status in September 2026 is not confirmed on this disk.

Melvin Simmons ran the pit for more than sixteen years, Fabianne with him, from the April 2007 opening through recessions and the pandemic. In 2023 the family asked the public for $50,000 to keep the doors open. The reports on disk then part: Spectacular Magazine wrote in April 2026 that Angela McLean had taken the restaurant over in 2023, while CBS 17 reported in March 2024 that Damien Holloway, as new owner, had redone 'every single thing in the building' — equipment, floors, walls, ceilings, bathrooms — over eight closed months and was set to reopen, the grand opening slipping for weather. The Assembly, surveying the state's Black-owned pits in February 2026, found the restaurant exploring a sale, its future uncertain. By April 2026 McLean told Spectacular that customers were choosing between a meal and gas for the car, and that without a buyer the restaurant could close by the end of the month.

Barbecue chopped and sandwiched, ribs, smoked chicken and oxtails, cooked over wood coals and made from scratch, by the owners' accounts to the Durham press. Which cut, which sauce and which sides are not described in the sources on this disk, and no price is recorded.

Status unknown as of September 2026: the last reports on this disk, from February and April 2026, had it for sale and near closing. The address is 5122 N.C. Highway 55 (Apex Highway), Durham.

Backyard BBQ Pit to chopped: chopped barbecue was the first line of its menu.

Backyard BBQ Pit to barbecue sandwich: the sandwich, with ribs and oxtails beside it.

Backyard BBQ Pit to Grady's Barbecue: the other Black-owned pit The Assembly surveyed in 2026, cooking whole hog in Wayne County.

Backyard BBQ Pit to Adrian Miller: whose Black Smoke is the frame the press used for it: a Black-owned pit and what it takes to keep one.

title: Bar-B-Q Center
text:
A pork-shoulder pit and ice-cream counter on North Main Street in Lexington, Davidson County, that began in 1955 as a dairy bar, put a shoulder on a pit one slow winter, and has been the Conrad family's since: Sonny Conrad (1938–2013), who started on curb service there as a teenager in 1955 and became owner in 1969, his wife Nancy, and their sons Michael and Cecil. Shoulders cook over hickory; the barbecue comes chopped, sliced or 'brown' — the smoky outside of the shoulder — with the dip and red slaw. The ice cream never left: about 200 gallons a week, much of it in a banana split of three and a half pounds.

The dairy bar of 1955 sold ice cream on Main Street, and in the 1960s the strip was a cruising street for hot rods; Sonny Conrad later put up metal railings to keep the place a family one, Our State wrote in 2014. Ice cream sales dip in winter, so one winter a pork shoulder went on a pit, and the restaurant's own history says it moved to its present building at 900 North Main in the late 1950s. Conrad had begun as a curb-service boy in 1955; in 1969 he married Nancy, a waitress there, and became the owner. He told the Southern Foodways Alliance in November 2011 that the kitchen made a hundred gallons a week each of dip and red slaw, that four customers in ten still ate in their cars, and that 'red slaw. That's a good vegetable.' He died in 2013; Nancy still worked, and the sons ran the day to day. Southern Living and Good Morning America have both come for the banana split. New airtight pits went in around 2013, glowing orange with coals; the dining room seats about a hundred at booths and a counter.

Pork shoulders cook over hickory coals with the family's spice blend; the meat is chopped or sliced, or served brown from the smoky outside, with the Lexington dip — thin, vinegar-based, reddened with ketchup — and red slaw, hushpuppies, baked beans and cornbread. Curb service brings the tray to the car. The banana split weighs three and a half pounds and is built for a table.

Open Monday to Saturday 11 to 9, at 900 North Main Street, Lexington, per OpenStreetMap (2026), which tags the address to Thomasville in error; the 27292 postcode and the restaurant's own site say Lexington. Dine-in and curb service.

Bar-B-Q Center to Lexington-style barbecue: the style, with the town's largest curb-service trade and a dairy bar's dessert.

Bar-B-Q Center to pork shoulder: the cut, over hickory.

Bar-B-Q Center to outside brown: 'brown' here is the smoky outside of the shoulder, ordered by name.

Bar-B-Q Center to Lexington dip: a hundred gallons a week of it, by Sonny Conrad's count in 2011.

Bar-B-Q Center to red slaw: a hundred gallons a week; 'that's a good vegetable.'

Bar-B-Q Center to hushpuppies: on the plate with baked beans and cornbread.

Bar-B-Q Center to hickory and oak: hickory, in airtight pits installed around 2013.

Bar-B-Q Center to Lexington Barbecue: the Monk family's pit across town, the other name visitors come with.

Bar-B-Q Center to Cook's Barbecue: the small brick-pit house south of town, closed since 2022.

title: Bessinger's Bar-B-Q
text:
A Bessinger family barbecue house at 1602 Savannah Highway in Charleston's West Ashley. Thomas Bessinger came from Holly Hill to Charleston with his brother Melvin in 1955, opened his own restaurant in 1960, and in 1961 the brothers opened Piggy Park Drive-In on the highway; renamed Bessinger's in 1971, it is run by Thomas's sons Tommy and Michael. It serves chopped pork in the family's mustard sauce, ribs, hash and rice, and a buffet on weekend evenings, and the South Carolina Barbeque Association lists it as 100-Mile Barbecue — a house worth a hundred-mile drive. It is the Charleston branch of the family whose Columbia branch is Maurice's Piggie Park.

Joseph Jacob 'Big Joe' Bessinger traded the family cow, a mule and fifty dollars for the Holly Hill Café in 1939 and served mustard-sauced barbecue there. After the war his son Melvin put his Army pay into a second Holly Hill restaurant, Eat At Joe's, in 1946, and the younger Thomas — born in Orangeburg in 1931 — started cooking there at fourteen. Thomas joined the Army after school and cooked two years overseas for soldiers. In 1955 Melvin closed Eat At Joe's and moved to Charleston, bringing Thomas; Thomas opened his own restaurant there in 1960, and in 1961 the brothers opened Piggy Park Drive-In on Savannah Highway together. After ten years they renamed it Bessinger's — The Barbecue Family. In 1982 Melvin crossed the Cooper River to open Melvin's in Mount Pleasant, and the brothers went their own ways. When their brother Maurice raised Confederate flags over his Columbia restaurants in July 2000, the press described the Charleston brothers' businesses as independent concerns, 'sans the politics'; grocery chains that dropped Maurice's sauce stocked Melvin's, and Maurice stopped speaking to him. Thomas Bessinger Sr. died on November 10, 2023, at ninety-two, with the restaurant in his sons' hands.

Chopped pork dressed in the family's yellow mustard sauce, from a pit behind the building; ribs, St. Louis cut, wet with the same sauce; hash over rice that the Barbeque Association's listing rates 'very, very good'; and onion rings the size of a doughnut. The buffet runs Friday and Saturday evenings and Sunday midday.

Open seven days, 10:30 a.m. to 9:30 p.m., with the buffet Friday and Saturday 5:30 to 8:30 p.m. and Sunday noon to 8, per the Barbeque Association's listing; OpenStreetMap recorded 11 to 9 in November 2023. 1602 Savannah Highway, Charleston. Checked September 15, 2026.

Bessinger's Bar-B-Q to mustard-based barbecue sauce: the sauce Big Joe worked out in Holly Hill, served here since the drive-in years.

Bessinger's Bar-B-Q to Joe Bessinger: the father, whose Holly Hill Café of 1939 is where the sons learned.

Bessinger's Bar-B-Q to Maurice Bessinger: Thomas's brother; his flags of 2000 were his own, and the Charleston houses were reported as separate concerns.

Bessinger's Bar-B-Q to Maurice's Piggie Park BBQ: the West Columbia chain of the same family and sauce; a separate business.

Bessinger's Bar-B-Q to Sweatman's Bar-B-Que: the Holly Hill family that worked on the mustard sauce with Big Joe.

Bessinger's Bar-B-Q to hash and rice: on the menu and the buffet; the Association's reviewer rated it 'very, very good'.

Bessinger's Bar-B-Q to Home Team BBQ: the newer West Ashley barbecue, opened in 2006 about a mile away on Ashley River Road.

Bessinger's Bar-B-Q to South Carolina Barbeque Association: lists it as 100-Mile Barbecue.

Not to be confused with maurices-piggie-park: Bessinger's is the Charleston house, Thomas's since 1960; Maurice's Piggie Park is the West Columbia chain since 1953. Same father, same sauce, separate businesses — and Maurice's is the one with the court case and the flags.

title: Big T Bar-B-Q
text:
A Black-owned wood-burning pit on Congaree Road at Gadsden, in lower Richland County below Columbia, run by Larry Brown, known as Teddy and as Big T, who has sold barbecue to the Columbia area for more than thirty years. Logs burn down in a warped burn box behind the smokehouse and the coals are shovelled into low metal pits under pork shoulders. Hash goes over rice, made with pork and offal in the Midlands way. A second house on Garners Ferry Road in Columbia serves the same barbecue from a buffet.

Neither the founding year nor a founding date is on this disk; what the listings agree on is that Larry Brown has been at it in this part of Richland County for over thirty years. He is not a Sweatman, and Big T has no connection to Sweatman's Bar-B-Que at Holly Hill, though the two names travel together in loose accounts of South Carolina barbecue. The evidence that the business is Black-owned is the directory kind rather than the profile kind: EatOkra, which indexes Black-owned restaurants, carries it, and the chef Todd Richards put it in his guide to Black-owned barbecue. A 2019 newspaper profile that would have said it in a reporter's words could not be fetched for this record. The South Carolina Barbeque Association's own page files Big T under Worth the Trip and describes the method — slow over coals and wood at the Gadsden operation — while saying the hash there is a little mild for the writer's taste, which is the sort of judgement a project like this one records rather than adopts. Brown's son Travis works the pits. The Gadsden house closes Sunday, Monday and Tuesday; the Columbia house runs a buffet.

Logs burn down to coals in a large warped burn box behind the smokehouse, and the coals are shovelled into low metal pits under pork shoulders — not whole hogs. The hash is the Midlands kind, pork and offal cooked down and ladled over white rice. Cards and cash are both taken. The Garners Ferry Road house in Columbia serves from a buffet; Gadsden does not.

Open at 2520 Congaree Road, Gadsden, closed Sunday, Monday and Tuesday, with a second house at 7535 Garners Ferry Road, Columbia. The map point is the Congaree Road centreline rather than the building: the geocoder returned the road, not the house number.

Big T Bar-B-Q to pork shoulder: the cut: shoulders over shovelled coals, not whole hogs.

Big T Bar-B-Q to burn barrel: the principle of its fire, here a warped burn box behind the smokehouse.

Big T Bar-B-Q to hash and rice: the Midlands plate it serves — pork and offal cooked down, over white rice.

Big T Bar-B-Q to Campaign for Real Barbecue: certified both its houses as cooking on wood or charcoal alone.

Big T Bar-B-Q to South Carolina Barbeque Association: files it under Worth the Trip and describes the coals-and-wood method at Gadsden.

Big T Bar-B-Q to Adrian Miller: wrote the history of African American barbecue that the Black-owned directories sit downstream of.

Not to be confused with sweatmans-bar-b-que: No relation. Sweatman's is Harold 'Bub' Sweatman's whole-hog house at Holly Hill in Orangeburg County, opened 1977 and sold twice since. Big T is Larry Brown's shoulder pit at Gadsden in Richland County. Loose accounts sometimes attach a Sweatman surname to Big T; no source read here does.

title: Bobbee O's BBQ
text:
A Black-owned barbecue counter on Statesville Road in north Charlotte, opened in 2008 by Bob Steven Roberts after four years working on his sauce. The board runs to pulled pork, ribs, brisket and wings rather than whole hog, and the room is counter service with online ordering. Roberts's niece Chloria Chandler is his business partner. It is one of the few barbecue businesses in Mecklenburg County that the Black-owned business directories carry, and the only one in this project's Charlotte records.

Bob Steven Roberts spent four years on the sauce before he opened. He had lived in California and New Jersey before coming to North Carolina more than thirty years ago, cooked in Fayetteville and Raleigh, and landed in Charlotte. His niece Chloria Chandler works with him as his business partner; she told QCity Metro in November 2021 that her favourite is the ribs, because she had been eating them since she was in her mother's stomach. The Black-owned business directories carry him: EatOkra lists the restaurant, NBA.com put it first in a list of ten Black-owned Charlotte restaurants in February 2023, and the chef Todd Richards included it in his guide to Black-owned barbecue, updated May 2025, with a note that this is the place for a sampler plate. What is under the meat is not settled. A 2024 lifestyle listing says hickory; a barbecue blog reported second-hand in 2016 that the kitchen ran a cabinet smoker and was not trying for wood smoke, and its own 2012 visit found no smoker in sight. The restaurant's site says nothing about fuel, so no wood tag is set here. *Inference —* the sauce, not the fire, is what every account of this kitchen is actually about.

Counter service and online ordering: pulled pork, ribs, brisket and wings by the plate or the pound, with the house sauce that took four years to settle. There is no whole hog on the board in any source read, and no hash. Cards are taken. The room keeps long hours by barbecue standards, into the evening six nights and to eight on Sunday.

Open, on the listings read, at 9401 Statesville Road, Suite C, Charlotte; an earlier address on Old Statesville Road appears in accounts from 2012. No closure notice was found and no news-grade source confirms trading in 2026, so treat the status as reported rather than checked.

Bobbee O's BBQ to pork shoulder: the cut behind its pulled pork; there is no whole hog on the board.

Bobbee O's BBQ to barbecue sandwich: the plate most of its accounts describe, with the sauce that took four years.

Bobbee O's BBQ to Adrian Miller: wrote the book on African American barbecue that frames why a directory of Black-owned pits exists at all.

title: Bobby's BBQ
text:
A Texas-leaning smokehouse on North Main Street in Fountain Inn, Greenville County, owned by Octavius Nelson, called Tay, and his wife Sarah. Brisket, pulled pork, ribs, turkey and house-made sausage come off the pits; there is no hash and no buffet, which sets it apart from most South Carolina barbecue houses. The name is for Tay's father Bobby Nelson Sr. and his brother Bobby Jr., both dead before the business began. A seasoning line came first, in 2010; the restaurant followed.

Tay Nelson started working with his father in a Greenville restaurant at twelve. Bobby Nelson Sr. died in 2008 and Bobby Jr. in 2009, and what Tay built next was assembled out of what they left him: he blended a seasoning from the spices his father had used, sold it from 2010, and taught himself to smoke from tutorials on the internet. The restaurant opened in 2018, though the business's own page dates the barbecue side to 2014 and the seasoning to 2010, so the anniversary depends on which thread is counted. The ownership line is unusually plain, in the business's own words: Bobby's BBQ is owned by Tay Nelson and his wife Sarah. That is the sentence the woman-owned tag here rests on. What the record does not carry is a Black-owned tag. Nothing on the business's own pages uses the phrase, EatOkra does not list it, and a Post and Courier piece that might have settled it returned an error on two attempts. The press the business does have is broad and national — ABC News in 2020, Tamron Hall in 2021, a Forbes gift guide, a Google economic impact report — rather than the barbecue-world kind.

Brisket, pulled pork, ribs, turkey and house-made sausage, in the Central Texas manner rather than the Midlands one: no hash on the menu, no mustard tradition, no buffet. The seasoning blend that started the business in 2010 is still sold. Cards and cash are both taken. The kitchen runs four days, Thursday to Saturday, and the smoke is wood, on the strength of the certification rather than any published description of the fire.

Open Thursday to Saturday, 11 a.m. to 8 p.m., closed Sunday to Wednesday, at 1301 North Main Street, Fountain Inn. Both the restaurant's own site and the OpenStreetMap harvest agree on the address.

Bobby's BBQ to pork shoulder: the cut behind its pulled pork, beside a Texas board of brisket and sausage.

title: Brown's Bar-B-Que
text:
A farm family's buffet house on the Williamsburg County Highway north of Kingstree, in the Pee Dee, opened in 1981 as a take-out window by Thomas M. Brown Jr., a row-crop farmer, with a dining room added about ten years on. Whole hogs are cooked and chopped, mopped on the pit with a vinegar-and-hot-pepper sauce the family calls barbecue gravy, and set on a long buffet with ribs, smoked ham, barbecued and fried chicken, barbecued and baked turkey, perloo, liver hash and rice, and vegetables the Browns grow themselves — corn, squash, okra, butter beans, collards, cabbage. The Barbeque Association names it among the state's top barbecue houses.

Thomas Brown learned to cook as a teenager laid up after a motorcycle accident broke his leg, working a hot plate within reach of the bed. He farmed — soy, wheat, hay and oats for market — and in 1981 opened a take-out window on the highway; the dining room came a decade later. The farm feeds the buffet: corn, squash, zucchini, broccoli, okra, butter beans, collards and cabbage in season. When the Southern Foodways Alliance came through the Pee Dee in June 2012, Rien Fertel recorded the Browns, and Angela Brown told him, 'We always take barbecue everywhere we go.' Kingstree is a whole-hog town — its Pig Pickin' festival each fall draws cooking teams, seventy of them in 2010, to compete on the county's vinegar-based barbecue — and Brown's is its standing barbecue house, more than forty years on. In April 2024 a visiting writer paid $14.95 for the buffet and ate liver hash over rice with salt, pepper and Texas Pete.

Whole hogs on the pit, mopped as they cook with the barbecue gravy — vinegar and hot pepper — then chopped. The buffet runs the length of the room: chopped barbecue, ribs, smoked ham, barbecued and fried chicken, barbecued and baked turkey, perloo (rice cooked with chicken), white rice, liver hash — hash with the liver in it, as the name says — macaroni, sweet potatoes, coleslaw, potato salad, the farm's vegetables, a salad bar and pecan pie. Buffet $14.95 in April 2024; a whole-hog plate with bread, baked beans and slaw is the take-out order.

Open Wednesday to Saturday 11 a.m. to 9 p.m. and Sunday 11 to 3, closed Monday and Tuesday, per Destination BBQ; 809 North Williamsburg County Highway (US 52), Kingstree. Checked September 15, 2026.

title: B's Barbecue
text:
A whole-hog and chicken pit on the edge of Greenville, Pitt County, in a converted country store on a road the county named for it. Bill McLawhorn, the B, opened it in 1978 with his wife Peggy; their daughters Judy Drach, Tammy Godley and Donna McLawhorn have run it since his death in 2007. There is no telephone, no take-out menu and no closing time: the doors open at nine in the morning and shut when the day's barbecue and chicken are gone, usually early afternoon. Cash or check only. The line forms before opening.

Bill McLawhorn gave up farming in 1978 and bought a convenience store just inside Greenville's city limits; he and Peggy worked out the sauce together and cooked out back, selling up front. He refused a telephone — 'If you need me, come get me' — and the refusal outlasted him. Bob Garner wrote it up for Our State in 2012 as a place of red picnic tables and cafeteria-style counter service with no promise the food would still be there at noon. Judy Drach told the Southern Foodways Alliance in 2009 that the family could have built something bigger with more staff and a day off, 'but when you start doing all that, then it's like any other restaurant and that's not what we wanted it to be.' Bill died in 2007 and the sisters took it on. The pits were once wood-fired brick; after fires the family went over to charcoal, and the pigs go on around nine at night to be ready by nine in the morning. The county renamed the road B's Barbecue Road.

Whole hogs and chickens cook overnight over charcoal, the hogs going on about 9 p.m. The pork is chopped by hand, never ground, and dressed with the McLawhorns' vinegar sauce; the chicken is sold by the half or the whole bird. In 2016 Our State printed the board: barbecue dinner $7.75, sandwich $3.75, a pound $8.50, half a chicken $7, a whole one $11.50. The customer orders at the counter and eats at a picnic table or in the car.

Open Tuesday to Saturday from 9 a.m. until sold out, at 751 B's Barbecue Road, Greenville. No phone. Cash or check. Hours pattern from Our State (2012 and 2016); check before driving.

title: Bum's Restaurant
text:
A wood-fired whole-hog restaurant in downtown Ayden, Pitt County, opened in 1963 by Latham 'Bum' Dennis, of the family that counts Skilton Dennis's 1830 wagon as the start of barbecue for sale here, and run by his son Larry, who cuts the wood, burns the coals and starts around four in the morning. Unlike most eastern pits it keeps a buffet of vegetables cooked that day — collards from the family garden, cabbage pastry, stewed rutabaga, black-eyed peas, boiled potatoes — beside the chopped barbecue. The sign is modest; the smell does the advertising.

Latham Dennis opened Bum's in 1963. The family's claim runs back to Skilton Dennis, who *tradition holds —* sold smoked hog meat commercially from 1830, a date the Southern Foodways Alliance recorded from the Dennises themselves, and to Otter Dennis, whom the family connects to the founding of Ayden; the Skylight Inn's Joneses paint the same 1830 on their billboard. Bum told the Alliance's Rien Fertel in December 2011, with Larry beside him, that in this kind of restaurant 'what you got to do you got to love it and it's a way of life.' Our State in April 2014 found Larry cutting oak and pecan and burning it down to embers before dawn, and Shirley Dennis, the family's matriarch, decorating the overflow dining room with Gone with the Wind memorabilia, a parking space reserved for her outside. Bum Dennis died in December 2022; Larry runs the restaurant. The vegetable buffet is what the writers single out: collards grown by the family, cabbage pastry, rutabaga, black-eyed peas, boiled potatoes, a table few other eastern pits keep.

Whole hogs cook over embers burned down from oak and pecan; the pork is chopped and dressed eastern-style, with vinegar and pepper. The barbecue is one station of a cafeteria line: the rest is the day's vegetables — collards from the family garden, cabbage pastry (cabbage stewed with strips of flat dumpling dough), rutabaga, black-eyed peas, boiled potatoes — and the plate is built by pointing.

Open, at 566 East Third Street, Ayden; Larry Dennis runs it. Hours are not recorded on this disk, and the last press confirmation read is from 2022; check before driving.

title: Buxton Hall Barbecue
text:
A whole-hog restaurant that ran from August 2015 to November 22, 2023 in a 1930s roller rink on Banks Avenue in Asheville's South Slope, opened by pitmaster Elliott Moss with Meherwan Irani's Chai Pani restaurant group. Pasture-raised pigs from western North Carolina farms smoked over wood from ten at night to eight in the morning; the plate carried South Carolina hash over rice — the pig's organs and fatty trimmings cooked down to a gravy — beside the chopped hog, with a fried-chicken sandwich, smoked baked beans and pimento cheese, lard-crust pies and banana pudding under meringue. The rink's murals stayed on the walls.

Elliott Moss grew up watching his grandfather smoke whole hogs, and brought that South Carolina whole hog to the mountains. He and Meherwan Irani, both James Beard nominees, opened Buxton Hall in August 2015 in a building that had been a roller rink in the 1930s and then the Standard Paper Sales Company. Bon Appétit ranked it ninth among the country's new restaurants in 2016 and named its fried chicken sandwich the sandwich of the year. The pandemic closed it from March to July 2020; a fire later forced another closure and new equipment. Moss left as pitmaster in July 2022 and chef Nick Barr took the kitchen. The Smoke Sheet reported on November 8, 2023 that the last day of service would be November 22. Chai Pani, Irani's Indian restaurant, moved from Battery Park Avenue into the 8,000-square-foot space and reopened there on May 21, 2024.

Whole hogs from pasture farms smoked overnight, ten to eight, over wood, then were chopped in the eastern way. The hash — organs and trimmings cooked to a gravy — went over rice as it does in the Pee Dee. The kitchen fried chicken for a sandwich, smoked the baked beans and the pimento cheese, baked pies on lard crusts and topped the banana pudding with meringue.

Closed since November 22, 2023. Chai Pani, its co-owner's Indian restaurant, has occupied the rink at 32 Banks Avenue, Asheville, since its reopening there on May 21, 2024.

Buxton Hall Barbecue to Eastern North Carolina barbecue: the chopped whole hog was cooked the eastern way, in a city that had not had one.

Buxton Hall Barbecue to whole hog: the cut, pasture-raised, overnight over wood.
