title: Cannon's BBQ
text:
A small barbecue house in a converted mobile home at a five-way crossroads in Little Mountain, Newberry County — the Dutch Fork, the German-settled land between the Broad and Saluda rivers where the Midlands mustard sauce is at home. The Cannons cooked over wood coals they burned down themselves and chopped the pork for a sauce with a concentrated yellow-mustard taste; the ribs fell off the bone, and the hash — the Midlands' stew of pork and onion, here tinged bright yellow with mustard — is what Robert Moss remembered it for. It has closed: Moss, writing in March 2020, called it recently closed.

Little Mountain sits off Interstate 26 at exit 91, and Cannon's sat a few miles from the exit in a modified mobile home at a 'five points' intersection, with an overfilled dumpster and wood strewn about the lot when Destination BBQ came in March 2014 — the wood being the point, since the Cannons burned their own coals. The reviewers found the pork chopped finer than they liked, the ribs falling off the bone, the hash good and the sauce 'typical of the Midlands: mustard based', with a very concentrated yellow-mustard flavor. Robert Moss, telling the story of hash and rice in 2020, used it as his example of the mustard-yellow hash: 'At the recently-closed Cannon's BBQ in Little Mountain, S.C., the hash was tinged bright yellow with mustard.' *Tradition holds —* the Cannon brothers ran it about fifteen years and served the last plates on July 4, 2019, a closing the Columbia station WLTX reported that June.

Pork chopped and sauced with a yellow-mustard sauce, ribs that fell from the bone, and hash — pork and onion cooked down to a spoonable stew — tinged bright yellow with mustard and served over rice, all cooked over wood coals the family burned down on the lot. The building was a mobile home fitted out as a dining room, the lot a woodyard.

Closed. Robert Moss described it as recently closed in March 2020; no reopening is recorded in this project's sources as of September 15, 2026. The coordinates here are the town's, not the building's.

Cannon's BBQ to South Carolina mustard barbecue: its style: Dutch Fork mustard, in the sauce and in the hash.

title: Carolina Bar-B-Que
text:
A mustard-sauce buffet house on South Main Street in New Ellenton, Aiken County, founded by Willie Mae Walker and her son Jess. She was born Willie Mae Baltzegar, daughter of the Rowesville pitmaster Willie Baltzegar, which puts a pit-cooking line behind the place two generations deep. Pork shoulders cook over wood in smokers out back — not open-pit whole hog. The buffet was twelve dollars in April 2025 and the hash is rust-orange and thick enough to lift on a fork. Thomas Zeigler has run it since about 2022.

Willie Mae Walker came out of Rowesville, where her father Willie Baltzegar cooked, and she and her son Jess opened in New Ellenton — 1969 by two accounts, 1968 by a third. Naming her as a founder is not a courtesy: the sources put her first, with her son second, which is unusual enough in this trade to be worth saying once. Jess 'Bubba' Walker carried it on. Then the place slipped. Michael Stern, writing for The Food Section on April 22, 2025, said it had been losing its footing four or five years earlier — the food not up to standard and the staff getting cranky — before Thomas Zeigler took the business over about three years before he wrote, tweaked a few recipes and turned it round. Destination BBQ's page, updated April 2025, still names Bubba Walker as the owner, so the two listings disagree and the later, purpose-built piece is followed here. Southern Living put it on the South's Top 50 barbecue list in 2016, a list Robert Moss compiled, and the Barbeque Association gives it the hundred-mile designation. The Campaign for Real Barbecue certified it. Destination BBQ traces the hash recipe to the Dukes family tradition, which is the Orangeburg line reaching west.

Pork shoulders only — no ribs — cook over wood in smokers behind the building, which is not the open-pit whole-hog method of the Pee Dee and is described that way by the writers who visit. The sauce is the Midlands mustard. The buffet is all you can eat, twelve dollars in April 2025. The hash is rust-orange, thick, with an organ-meat sweetness, ladled over rice; one writer put it slightly thicker than Maurice's and a little less tart.

Open Wednesday 11 to 1:30 and Thursday to Saturday 11 to 8, closed Sunday to Tuesday, at 109 South Main Street, New Ellenton. Cards and cash. A search result circulating a South Main address in the eight hundreds is not supported by any page read here.

title: Clyde Cooper's BBQ
text:
Raleigh's downtown barbecue house since New Year's Day 1938, when Clyde Cooper opened on East Davie Street with fifty dollars borrowed from a brother-in-law; it moved around the corner to 327 South Wilmington Street in 2014 when the old building was lost to development, carrying the awning and the front door with it. It cooks pork shoulders — hand-trimmed, never whole hog — in pits on the upper floor, chops them and dresses them with Cooper's tangy sauce, which the city's tourism office calls a blend of eastern and Lexington ways. Fried chicken, Brunswick stew, collards, hushpuppies, boiled potatoes and banana pudding fill out the board; fried pork skins ride on the tray.

Clyde Cooper opened on January 1, 1938 in an 1884 building at 109 East Davie Street, and for fifty years he alone held the key. He cooked at first behind his house on Chapel Hill Road until the health department stopped him and the pits went upstairs, built to order by Nunnery-Freeman. The restaurant's own history says he was among the first Raleigh business owners to let Black customers in through the front door, in the early 1960s. After decades of being asked, he sold around 1988 to a builder named Tony; Debbie Holt, who had managed the place for him for five and a half years, took it over around 2008. Clyde Cooper died on February 12, 1998, short of a hundred. Holt told the Southern Foodways Alliance in November 2011 that she was fighting a developer's plan for a multistory apartment building on the Davie Street site — 'Ain't all about the money. It's about saving it for people and generations to come.' The building was lost; in 2014 the restaurant moved to South Wilmington Street, where the old awning hangs over the lunch counter and the old door hangs on the wall. In 2023, marking 85 years, Visit Raleigh noted it had at last begun taking credit cards.

Pork shoulders are trimmed by hand and cooked in the upstairs pits, then served chopped, sliced or coarse; the sauce is tangy rather than sweet, on Cooper's recipe. A tray — barbecue, slaw, hushpuppies and fried pork skins — cost $11 in 2023. Fried chicken, ribs and brisket, Brunswick stew, collards, boiled potatoes, several kinds of fried pork skins and banana pudding are the rest of the menu.

title: Cook's Barbecue
text:
A pork-shoulder pit off Valiant Drive south of Lexington, Davidson County, built by hand in 1969 by Doug Cook on a cul-de-sac plot down the road from his house — a pit and kitchen, a wooden chopping block, a drive-up window — with a dining room he framed from oaks felled on the lot. His son Brandon, born a year after the restaurant, came back as pitmaster in 2001 and kept the original brick pit and the hickory coals. In an October report DavidsonLocal recorded that the restaurant, by then trading as Cooks & BBQ Still Smoking, had announced on July 28 that it was closed indefinitely and would be sold; no reopening is on this disk.

Doug Cook built his stand in 1969 with his own hands; when customers wanted somewhere to sit he cut trees from the oak grove around it and framed a dining room. Brandon Cook grew up in the place — crawling into the fireplace as a child, flirting with the waitresses as a teenager — and learned under his father to tend the pits, shovel the cherry-red hickory coals and cook Lexington-style shoulders. He returned in 2001 as pitmaster and told the Southern Foodways Alliance's Rien Fertel in November 2011, 'Believe it or not, I'm related to half of the people around here that run the barbecue places, so yeah, I eat a bunch of it.' Customers dip their plates rather than pour sauce. DavidsonLocal, in an October roundup of Davidson County barbecue houses changing hands, reported that Cooks & BBQ Still Smoking on Valiant Drive had posted on July 28 that it was closed 'indefinitely' and was to be sold, with no buyer announced.

Shoulders cook over hickory coals in the original brick pit, the coals shoveled in from the fireplace; the meat is chopped on the wooden block and served Lexington style, with the dip beside the plate for dipping rather than poured over.

Closed. DavidsonLocal reported the indefinite closure and a planned sale; listings still showed it closed in September 2026 and no reopening is recorded on this disk. The building sits at 366 Valiant Drive, Lexington.

title: Cooper's Country Store
text:
A whitewashed general store on US 521 near Salters, south of Kingstree in Williamsburg County, that sells hardware, groceries, gasoline, diesel, propane, plow points, cast-iron cookware, live crickets — and, from a small meat counter at the back, whole-hog barbecue cooked over wood embers, hash, boiled peanuts and salt-cured country hams. Theron Burrows opened it as an Esso station in 1937; George Cooper built the pit after 1974; his nephew Russell Cooper has run it since 2003. It is a store, not a restaurant, and the barbecue is one more thing it keeps.

In 1937 the federal government built Highway 521 from Manning to Georgetown, and Theron Burrows, a tobacco and cotton farmer, opened an Esso service station and store on the new road. When he died in 1974 his daughter Adalyn and her husband George Cooper took it over as Cooper's Country Store. George watched families along the highway selling barbecue from car trunks and built his own pit — chickens on one half, hogs on the other. He ran the store twenty-nine years and in 2003 sold it to his nephew Russell Cooper, who told Rien Fertel of the Southern Foodways Alliance in June 2012: 'We keep all the meats. We keep all the hams. We got a full line of groceries and we got a full line of hardware. We got gasoline. We got propane. We got diesel fuel. You name it, we got it.' Garden & Gun sent Hunter Kennedy in 2014 and found the two-storey porte cochère over the pumps, the wood-panelled aisles, the plow points and cant hooks, and the Southampton-style country hams the same family has cured for the store for nearly sixty years, sold by the slice or whole and shipped across the country. A lunch buffet was added in March 2024.

Whole hogs cook over wood embers until the meat pulls with tongs; when the hog is flipped, the pitmaster Laverne Darby — more than thirty-five years at the pit — mops it with the vinegar sauce, which Russell Cooper describes as 'downright vinegar and salt and pepper', with black pepper, crushed pepper and ground red pepper. The hash is not ground but stringy, pulled meat cooked down. Barbecue and hash are sold from the meat counter at the back, with the hams, house-cured bacon, smoked tails and hocks; barbecue sandwiches and boiled peanuts too. The lunch buffet runs Wednesday to Saturday, 10:30 to 2.

Open Monday to Saturday, 7 a.m. to 7 p.m., closed Sunday; lunch buffet Wednesday to Saturday, 10:30 a.m. to 2 p.m. 6945 SC Highway 521, Salters. The coordinates here are the highway at Salters Depot, not the building. Checked September 15, 2026 against Destination BBQ.

title: Dukes Bar-B-Que
text:
The name on a dozen or more buffet houses across the Midlands and Lowcountry, all descended from the sons of Manuel Dukes of Orangeburg County, who learned pit cooking from a Rowesville pitmaster and catered the county's gatherings. In Orangeburg itself the line is Earl Duke's: he opened downtown at Chestnut Street and Columbia Road in 1955 and later moved to Whitman Street, and his sister's family runs a second Dukes on Chestnut Street. Both sell from a buffet line: chopped pork in a mustard-and-ketchup 'rust' sauce, hash over rice — the Midlands' stew of pork and onion — fried and barbecued chicken, and a loaf of sliced white bread at the end.

Manuel Dukes was born in rural Orangeburg County around 1875. His sons became the county's pitmasters, catering barbecues, and historians have suggested that their German descent explains the mustard in the sauce. Willie Baltzegar, a Rowesville pitmaster, taught them. In the 1950s the sons and daughters opened restaurants: Danny Dukes first, in Cope and Branchville; Earl Duke in Orangeburg in 1955, at Chestnut Street and Columbia Road, later moving to Whitman Street beside the Pepsi plant; a sister, Elma, and her husband Harry Ott on Spruill Street in North Charleston; and others in Aiken, Elloree, Smoaks, Ridgeville, Blackville and New Ellenton. The name spread past the family, and by 2017 some Dukes were family-owned and others sold. Earl's Whitman Street house passed to Harold Kittrell, a carpenter, and then to his son Tony, who told the Southern Foodways Alliance in June 2012 that 'the barbecue, hash, and rice, our sauce, sweet tea, and sliced bread are just what people come here for' and gave the sauce its name: rust gravy — sweet, ketchup-based, orange-yellow, thicker than most. The Otts opened in St. Matthews in 1965 and moved to Chestnut Street in Orangeburg ten years later; their descendants cook fifty to fifty-five pigs a week in the pit out back, Wednesday to Friday, for a buffet that is 'just barbeque, hash, rice and slaw with loaves of bread at the end'.

A buffet, all you can eat, paid at the register; in March 2011 the Charleston City Paper gave the price as $10 for adults and $6 for children. Chopped pork from shoulders and hams is dressed with the rust sauce; hash — pork simmered down with onion into a reddish stew — is ladled over white rice; fried chicken, barbecue chicken, collards, butter beans, black-eyed peas, mac and cheese, fried okra, hushpuppies, corn nuggets and a loaf of Sunbeam bread fill the rest of the line. Most Dukes houses stopped burning logs decades ago and cook on gas-fired cookers with wood chips for smoke; the Chestnut Street house cooks its hogs in a pit behind the building, and takes cash only.

Two houses in Orangeburg. Chestnut Street (789 Chestnut Street NE) opens Thursday to Saturday, 11 a.m. to 7 p.m. Whitman Street (1298 Whitman Street SE) lists Thursday to Saturday, 11 to 8, but its own site on September 15, 2026 reads 'temporarily closed. We plan to reopen soon.'

title: Fuzzy's Bar-B-Q
text:
A pork-shoulder house on Highway Street in Madison, Rockingham County, opened in 1954 by T.H. 'Fuzzy' Nelson and in the Nelson family since. Shoulders cook over hickory coals in pits behind the building; the tray is the Piedmont tray, chopped or coarse-chopped pork with the dip — the thin vinegar-and-ketchup sauce of the region — red slaw and hushpuppies. It holds True 'Cue certification, which turns on wood or charcoal being the only heat under the meat, and it is a stop on the North Carolina Barbecue Society's Historic Barbecue Trail. Breakfast is served from early morning, which few barbecue houses do.

T.H. Nelson, called Fuzzy, opened on the road through Madison in 1954, and the family kept it. The restaurant's own page calls itself a Nelson family restaurant operated by Fuzzy's son and daughter, Phil and Debbie, with Hilda Vestal managing after more than seventeen years; a visitor writing in April 2016 instead named a son, Fred, as the one running it, and the two accounts are not reconciled here. The building was rebuilt around 1978 and photographs of the first one hang inside. The pits stayed outdoors and the wood stayed in them. Both rosters of the Historic Barbecue Trail read for this project carry Fuzzy's — the older twenty-three-stop list and Visit NC's twenty-stop page of 2026 — which makes it one of the few pits to survive every revision of that list, while the Campaign for Real Barbecue certified it separately. *Inference —* the double listing is why Fuzzy's appears in nearly every written account of the trail, though its own advertising runs to one page and a telephone number. That page also claims notice from The New Yorker, from PM Magazine and from a Congressional barbecue contest. No issue, date or citation is given for any of the three, and none is repeated here as established.

Pork shoulders cook over hickory coals in pits behind the building, the fire tended through the cook rather than set and left. The meat is chopped or coarse-chopped and dressed with the dip; red slaw — cabbage cut fine and dressed with the same sauce, which is why it is red — and hushpuppies fill the tray. The kitchen serves breakfast from early morning as well, so the room is working hours before the barbecue houses down in Lexington open their doors.

Open at 407 North Highway Street, Madison. Three sources give three sets of hours: the restaurant's page says Monday to Saturday from seven in the morning and Sunday from seven, the NC Pork Council says Tuesday to Saturday from six and closed Sunday and Monday, and it lists a different street besides. Check before driving.

title: Grady's Barbecue
text:
A whole-hog pit at a country crossroads in Dudley, Wayne County, south of Goldsboro, opened on July 4, 1986 by Steve and Gerri Grady and run by Gerri and their son Scottie since Steve's death in August 2025. Hogs cook over oak and hickory coals; the barbecue is chopped by hand and served with stewed collards, cabbage, slaw and potato salad, and tea Gerri brews on the stove. The Assembly reported in February 2026 that it is, by most accounts, the one Black-owned brick-and-mortar whole-hog restaurant at the top of North Carolina's best-of lists, and one of the last of its kind. It opens four days a week.

Steve Grady's brother started the restaurant on a Friday in 1986 and quit by Saturday; he disliked the smoke. Steve and Gerri, married that same year, bought it with bank loans and the backing of the boss at the sawmill where Steve worked. Both had grown up on farms at Seven Springs. Steve had learned whole hog from his father and grandfather, who cooked a couple of pigs a year in pits dug in the ground for holidays; Gerri learned to cook at nine or ten from her mother and grandmother and then her mother-in-law, and told ABC11 in 2021, 'This is cooking the old fashioned way. It's a dash of this and a dash of that. There are no measurements.' Steve cut oak and hickory from storm-downed trees across Wayne County and stacked it beside the building where customers could see it. USA Today and GQ wrote the place up; the Gradys spoke for the North Carolina Barbecue Society and gave the Southern Foodways Alliance an oral history in December 2011. In June 2020 Steve was hospitalized with COVID-19; the restaurant reopened that July on its 34th anniversary. In 2024 the NC BBQ Hall of Fame and the American Royal both inducted him. Stephen Grady died on August 26, 2025; Gerri and Scottie kept the pit going.

Steve started the charcoal fires at eleven at night and came back at four in the morning to put the hogs on over hickory and oak; by eight the barbecue was ready. The meat is hand-chopped and dressed with a spicy vinegar sauce, and the plate carries slaw, hushpuppies — fried cornmeal fritters — and the day's vegetables, stewed collards, cabbage and potato salad, peeled and chopped by hand that morning.

Open four days a week at 3096 Arrington Bridge Road, Dudley, run by Gerri Grady and her son Scottie since Steve Grady's death in August 2025. Days and hours are from Our State (2013) and The Assembly (February 2026); check before driving.

title: Henry's Smokehouse
text:
An Upstate barbecue house at 240 Wade Hampton Boulevard on the edge of downtown Greenville, opened by Beau Hammond — in 1991 by the company's own account, in 1992 by the Greenville Journal's — in a small building that had been other eateries before. It cooks pork butts twelve hours and ribs six to eight over hickory logs in open pits, hand-pulls and chops the pork, and serves it with two sauces, a mild tomato-based one in the Piedmont manner and a spicy mustard one, with hash and rice on the side. A second house is in Simpsonville and a food truck, Henry's Hog Hauler, travels; the Barbeque Association lists it as 100-Mile Barbecue.

Beau Hammond opened Henry's with a menu so short that the sides were coleslaw and simmered green beans, and a rule he kept repeating: 'You want to be fair to the customer first. The money will come after that.' The house grew, added stores in Simpsonville and on Woodruff Road, and passed to Tiger O'Rourke and Bo Wilder, partners who added hand-cut fries in O'Rourke's years. Playboy ranked it first in the world in June 2002, a line the house still quotes; it took the Upstate readers' award seventeen years running; and in 2024 Southern Living picked it for the state. John Malik, writing in the Greenville Journal in October 2025, found a pulled-pork sandwich with fries and half-and-half tea at about $13 and the fire still built every day: 'You have to baby great barbecue. The fire changes every day... The result of great smoked pork should stay the same.'

Pork butts cook twelve hours and ribs, St. Louis cut, six to eight, in open pits over hickory logs — cured oak and pecan too, by Malik's account — at low temperatures, the fire built and tended all day. The pork is pulled by hand from the bone and chopped; the sauces are a mild tomato-based one and a spicy mustard; hash and rice, a stew of pork over rice, is on the menu with the hand-cut fries. About $13 for a sandwich, fries and tea in October 2025.

Open Monday to Saturday 11 a.m. to 8 p.m. and Sunday 11 to 3 at 240 Wade Hampton Boulevard, Greenville, with the same hours at 123 North Main Street, Simpsonville, per the company's site on September 15, 2026.

title: Hite's Bar-B-Que
text:
A take-out barbecue stand on Dreher Road in West Columbia, open only on Friday and Saturday, where the Hite family has cooked whole hogs and hams over oak and hickory coals since 1957. It sells chopped pork, ham, ribs, pork skins, chicken, hash and rice and slaw by the plate and the pound, with a yellow mustard sauce applied lightly; there is no dining room, only picnic tables by a pond. The hash — the Midlands' stew of pork and onion — is made in cast-iron kettles over wood embers. It is not Jackie Hite's of Batesburg-Leesville, some twenty-five miles west, which closed in 2018.

John D. Hite farmed on Dreher Road — minnows, hogs, corn and sweet potatoes — and in 1957 began selling barbecue as a side project, a farmer looking for extra income. The stand stayed a two-day business beside the farm and passed to his grandson David Hite, who runs it with the family recipes and, in the words of the restaurant's site, 'the age-old process for cooking barbeque'. Destination BBQ describes that process: coals rendered in a modified campfire fashion, then shoveled, 'payload after smoky payload', under whole hogs and hams until the meat is lacquered with smoke. The hash is cooked the old way in cast-iron kettles over wood embers, and the stand makes an onion sausage that Destination BBQ calls unique to the Midlands. *Inference —* the Dreher Road Hites and Jackie Hite of Leesville share a Lexington County surname and a mustard sauce; no source in this project links the two businesses.

Whole hogs and hams cook on a pit over oak and hickory coals. The meat is chopped and lightly dressed with a mustard sauce whose base is a strong yellow mustard. Orders are plates — pork, rib or chicken with hash, rice, slaw and rolls — or sandwiches, or meat by the pound, all to go; picnic tables by the pond are the only seating. Hash simmers in cast-iron kettles over wood embers; pork skins and onion sausage are the extras.

Open Friday and Saturday only. The restaurant's site gives 10 a.m. to 6 p.m. both days; Destination BBQ recorded 8 a.m. to 7 p.m. Friday and 8 to 6 Saturday. Take-out only. 240 Dreher Road, West Columbia. Checked September 15, 2026.

title: Home Team BBQ
text:
A Charleston barbecue company that began in November 2006 when Aaron Siegel, a Culinary Institute-trained cook from Atlanta, turned Bunch's, a mid-century gas station at 1205 Ashley River Road in West Ashley, into Fiery Ron's Home Team BBQ. It cooks pulled pork, ribs, brisket and smoked chicken wings with an Alabama white sauce, runs a bar known for American whiskey and frozen drinks — the Game Changer is its signature — and books live Americana, blues and bluegrass. Seven locations by 2026: West Ashley, Sullivan's Island (2009), downtown Charleston (2016), Aspen (2016), Columbia (2019), Greenville (2021) and north Mount Pleasant (2022), with more than six hundred employees.

Aaron Siegel grew up in Atlanta without barbecue, went to the University of Georgia and then, in January 1997, to the Culinary Institute of America at Hyde Park; he interned at Nava in Atlanta under Kevin Rathbun, cooked in Aspen at a white-tablecloth restaurant and a burrito shop, and moved to Charleston in 2002. In 2006, with little money and much help from friends and family, he and his partners Taylor Garrigan, Tony McKie and Madison Ruckel opened in the old gas station on Ashley River Road; Garrigan was the opening sous chef and is an operating partner now. Sullivan's Island came in 2009; downtown at 126 Williman Street and Aspen, Colorado, in 2016; Columbia in 2019, Greenville in 2021, north Mount Pleasant in 2022. McKie curates the music. The company gives to Hogs for a Cause, has run the Rock the Block fundraiser since 2017 and started the Holy Smokes festival in 2021. 'There wasn't a place where you could go have a good time and hang out for a few hours, watch a game, catch a music show' with the family, Siegel told the City Paper before the twentieth anniversary in July 2026.

Low and slow, in the company's phrase, on smokers at each store: pulled pork, ribs, brisket, smoked wings tossed in Alabama white sauce — *Tradition holds —* a mayonnaise-based sauce from north Alabama — pulled-pork sandwiches, barbecue tacos, tots and queso, a kids' menu. The bar carries a wide American whiskey list, frozen cocktails and craft beer; live Americana, blues and bluegrass play at several stores.

Open at seven locations: the original at 1205 Ashley River Road, Charleston (West Ashley); Sullivan's Island; 126 Williman Street downtown; north Mount Pleasant; Columbia; Greenville; and Aspen, Colorado — per the company's site and the City Paper in July 2026. Checked September 15, 2026.

title: Hursey's Bar-B-Q
text:
The Burlington, Alamance County, barbecue business of the Hursey family: Sylvester and Daisy Hursey began smoking pork over a backyard pit in 1945 with a sauce of their own, moved to a cafe in Gibsonville with two big pits behind it, and built a Burlington restaurant on Rauhut Street in 1957; their son Charles took over the Burlington trade in 1966, and his sons Chuck and Chris manage it now, a fourth generation coming on. It smokes more than 1,200 pork shoulders a week over hickory, plus hams, for five restaurants, a catering house and a wholesale trade; broasted chicken and hot apple turnovers are the other things it is known for.

The family's telling starts in the mid-1940s with Sylvester Hursey and a friend cooking their first pig after a night out; in 1945 he and Daisy set up a homemade pit in the yard and sold to neighbors, using his father's way with hickory-smoked pork and a sauce they kept to themselves. When the yard was too small they bought a cafe on Piedmont Street in Gibsonville and built two large pits behind it. The family says the state issued them its first license to wholesale barbecue — in 1949 by the company's history, in 1945 by Our State's 2014 account. Sylvester built the Rauhut Street restaurant in Burlington in 1957; Charles Hursey went full-time in 1960 out of high school and took over Rauhut Street in mid-1966, expanding the wholesale plant on Highway 87 North. Our State in 2014 found Charles, about seventy, and his wife Ellen at the register, and counted five addresses in Burlington, Graham and Mebane. The company lists a win at a North and South Carolina cook-off held in Washington, D.C., and a National Golden Chicken Award among its credentials.

Pork shoulders, more than 1,200 a week, and hams are hickory-smoked and served chopped or sliced with the family's Old-Fashioned Barbecue Sauce and hushpuppies; broasted chicken — pressure-fried — and hot apple turnovers are the other things people drive for. The wholesale kitchen also makes hot-dog chili by the ton: Our State reckoned 200,000 hot dogs' worth in ten days.

Open daily 11 to 9 at 1834 South Church Street, Burlington, per OpenStreetMap (2026); four more Hursey's stand in Burlington, Graham and Mebane (Our State, 2014).

title: Jack Cobb & Son Barbecue Place
text:
A Black-owned whole-hog counter on South Main Street in Farmville, Pitt County, that Jack Cobb and his son Rudy built as a cinder-block storefront in 1971 and closed in the autumn of 2018. Hogs cooked all night over oak, pecan and hickory coals banked around them; Rudy Cobb shovelled glowing coals in from the hearth and would not use gas. There were no chairs and no tables, only a counter, three days a week. Barbecued chicken and barbecued turkey shared the board with the pork.

Jack Cobb made tobacco hogsheads for A.C. Monk & Co. for about fifty years and cooked barbecue on Saturdays. When his son Rudy came home from Vietnam in 1966 — North Carolina A&T, then combat — the business faced the plain arithmetic of a segregated town. Our State put it in 2013: white customers wanted Jack's barbecue but would not walk into a Black-owned business. So Jack and Rudy carried it out to the cars. A hundred plates a trip, barbecue and cornbread and slaw, sixty-five cents each. Rudy dated the turn to 1966 or 1967 and remembered how he ended the deliveries: he used to carry it to their houses, and when there got to be too many he told them they had to come get it — nobody would bother them, he would be there. He told Rien Fertel for the Southern Foodways Alliance on November 30, 2011 that he was the principal owner, born September 1941, and that he still cooked with wood and did not use gas. Jack died in September 1989, having blessed his son's decision to stop turning the hogs overnight. Rudy's own sons did not want it and no buyer came. He closed in 2018: it was like losing a wife or a son, he told WRAL.

Whole hogs — always whole hogs — cooked overnight on oak, pecan and hickory, the wood banked around the pit so it lit through the night, the coals shovelled in from the hearth. Decades of it stained the white walls grey. The pork came chopped with a vinegar sauce, and the hushpuppies were made to Rudy's stepmother Lillian Blunt Cobb's recipe. Barbecued chicken and barbecued turkey were the other meats. There was nowhere to sit: you took your food and went.

Closed. The last service was in the autumn of 2018 — WNCT reported in August that the closing had been put off to October 18 while buyers were sought, and WRAL confirmed the closure the following July. The building stands at 3883 South Main Street, Farmville.

Jack Cobb & Son Barbecue Place to whole hog: the cut, and the only one — always whole hogs, in the owner's words.

title: Jackie Hite's Bar-B-Q
text:
A whole-hog buffet house on East Railroad Avenue in Leesville, across the tracks from the town, that James Lee 'Jackie' Hite opened in May 1979 and ran until his death in September 2016; his family closed it in 2018. Hogs cooked whole over hickory coals, the coals made in a burn barrel — a steel drum in which the logs burn down — and the chopped meat was dressed with a mustard, vinegar and pepper sauce and set on a buffet with fried chicken, hash and rice, collards, field peas and creamed corn, paid for on the way out. Hite was also Leesville's mayor and fire chief.

Jackie Hite's father was a plumber, a fisherman and a part-time barbecue man, and the son learned the pit helping him cook for the annual Firemen's Ball. Hite went into Leesville's public life from 1966 — fire chief, water commissioner, councilman, magistrate, and three terms as mayor — and in May 1979 opened the restaurant across the railroad tracks. He cooked hogs whole over hickory as his father had, and told Rien Fertel of the Southern Foodways Alliance in June 2012, five years after open-heart surgery and with constituents asking him to run for mayor again: 'Once you been there, you can't get it out of your blood', and 'We just never done nothing but what we're doing and that's why it's so hard.' He died in September 2016 after weeks of failing health; WIS called him a Midlands barbecue legend, and the restaurant had then been open more than thirty-five years. *Tradition holds —* his family kept the pits going two more years and closed the doors on September 23, 2018, the anniversary of his burial, saying it was what Jackie Hite himself would have wanted.

Whole hogs over hickory coals, the wood burned down in a burn barrel and shoveled under the meat — *Tradition holds —* on pits of concrete block. The chopped pork got a sauce a visitor called 'like straight mustard': mustard seed and vinegar. Service was a buffet: fried chicken, hash and rice, coleslaw, collards sweet and smoky, salad, creamed corn, mac and cheese, field peas. Guests ate first and paid on the way out. The last listed hours were Wednesday and Thursday 9 to 2, Friday and Saturday 9 to 3, Sunday 9 to 2, cash or card.

Closed since 2018. The building stands at 460 East Railroad Avenue, Leesville (Batesburg-Leesville); Destination BBQ marks it permanently closed. Nothing continues under the name as of September 15, 2026, so far as this project's sources show.

title: Keaton's Barbecue
text:
A chicken house in the crossroads community of Cleveland, Rowan County, west of Salisbury, where since 1953 the chicken has been fried (or baked) and then dipped whole in a hot vinegar-and-tomato barbecue sauce — 'dipped chicken', a North Carolina barbecue of its own kind. Burette Walker 'B.W.' Keaton, a Black railroad man laid off in 1953, started it in a shack and turned down moves to Statesville and Charlotte; he died in 1989, and his niece Kathleen Murray has run it since 1991. Half or whole, white or dark, hot or mild, with a slice of white bread and a hot vinegar slaw.

B.W. Keaton lost his railroad job in 1953 and started selling chicken from a shack on Cool Springs Road. The lore, as Our State tells it: the Schlitz Brewing Company offered $10,000 for the sauce recipe and Keaton countered at $100,000; a shotgun lived under the checkout counter; no weapons, no swearing, no photographing the staff; no utensils, because he did not believe in them. He refused offers to relocate to bigger towns. David Cecelski wrote it up for the North Carolina Folklife Institute in December 2010 as a place found on the back roads between Statesville and Winston-Salem, the chicken fried or baked and then dipped in the hot vinegar-tomato sauce, with a slaw of cabbage in a spicy red dressing of vinegar, tomato, cayenne and celery seed. Keaton died in 1989; Kathleen Murray, his niece, took over in 1991. Cash orders want exact change in small bills; cards are taken over five dollars.

Chicken is fried or baked, then dipped in the hot vinegar-tomato sauce and served with a white-bread bun — half or whole bird, white or dark meat, hot or mild sauce. The sides are secondary; the slaw is cabbage in a spicy red vinegar-tomato dressing. Plastic forks are now available; the founder did not provide them.

Open Tuesday 11 to 2 and Wednesday to Saturday 11 to 2 and 5 to 8, closed Sunday and Monday, at 17365 Cool Springs Road, Cleveland — hours as the restaurant's site listing and Our State give them, with the warning that they vary. Cash preferred.

title: Kepley's Bar-B-Q
text:
A High Point, Guilford County, barbecue stand in a surplus World War II Quonset hut — a half-cylinder of corrugated steel — opened in June 1948 by Hayden Kepley on North Main Street and closed on February 8, 2025 after 77 years. Bob Burleson came to work there as a sixteen-year-old curb boy the year it opened, bought it with Charlie Johnson when Kepley retired in 1962, and ran it until his death in May 2022 at ninety; his daughter Susan Burleson closed it when she could not staff the hours. It served chopped, vinegary pork with tangy red slaw on a bun, hushpuppies, and 85-cent coffee with refills.

Hayden Kepley bought an Army Quonset hut in 1948 and started selling barbecue from it; Bob Burleson, newly motherless at sixteen, arrived that summer as a curb boy. In 1962 Kepley sold to Burleson and his son-in-law Charlie Johnson; Johnson retired in 2001 and Susan Burleson became her father's co-owner, then sole owner after he died in May 2022. The menu board was hand-painted wood and did not change for decades; the hut got green awnings outside and wood paneling within. The High Point Enterprise reported in January 2025 that after four longtime waitresses retired Susan Burleson could not find people willing to work the hours — 'I would have to work up here all day and night, and I'm just too old to do that' — and would not sell, because new owners 'would run it the way they want to run it, and it just wouldn't be Kepley's anymore.' The last day was February 8, 2025. Stephanie Hunt, who grew up nearby, wrote its farewell in Garden & Gun two days before.

Pigs roasted slowly — the sources read do not say over what fuel — and the pork chopped and dressed vinegary, served on a bun under red slaw with hushpuppies on the side; coffee 85 cents with free refills, in 2025. Kepley's shipped barbecue nationwide from the hut.

Closed since February 8, 2025. The Quonset hut stands at 1304 North Main Street, High Point; OpenStreetMap still carried the listing, with a 1948 start date, in February 2026.

title: Lewis Barbecue
text:
A Central Texas-style barbecue restaurant at 464 North Nassau Street on the upper peninsula of Charleston, opened in June 2016 by John Lewis, a pitmaster from El Paso who cooked in Austin with Franklin Barbecue and then as a partner in La Barbecue, welding his own smokers along the way. The meat is sold by the pound from a counter: prime brisket, beef ribs, pork spare ribs, turkey breast, pulled pork, 'Texas hot guts' sausage and a green-chile cheddar sausage, with sides from Texas — pinto beans, green chile corn pudding — and from here, collards. A second Lewis opened in Greenville in August 2022 and a third in Atlanta in December 2025.

John Lewis grew up in El Paso and moved to Austin at eighteen; a New Braunfels smoker, a birthday present, started the habit. He competed on the barbecue circuit in Denver, came back to Austin to cook with Franklin Barbecue, and partnered with LeAnn Mueller to open La Barbecue, where the brisket made his name. He moved to Charleston in 2015 and opened Lewis Barbecue in June 2016; Rodney Scott's whole hog arrived on King Street eight months later. Lewis welds his own custom smokers. The Greenville store followed at 214 Rutherford Street in August 2022; in December 2025, after six years of looking, he opened at Ansley Mall in Atlanta with six smokers on the roof, an open-air smokehouse above the Beltline. The Charleston house holds a Michelin Bib Gourmand. Lewis's own line, to Rough Draft Atlanta: 'I think beef is better than pork.'

Everything is sold by weight or the link, cut to order at the counter: USDA prime brisket at $35 a pound, pulled pork $19, turkey breast $22, spare ribs $24, hot-guts sausage $8 a link and green-chile cheddar $7 — the Charleston menu as posted on September 15, 2026. Sides are creamy potato salad, tangy coleslaw, cowboy pinto beans, green chile corn pudding, collard greens, mac and cheese and fries. Beef ribs and oxtail come off the smokers too.

Open Tuesday to Saturday 11 a.m. to 10 p.m., Sunday and Monday 11 to 9, at 464 North Nassau Street, Charleston, per the restaurant's site on September 15, 2026. Greenville (214 Rutherford Street) and Atlanta (1544 Piedmont Avenue) are open as well.

title: Lexington Barbecue
text:
The pork-shoulder pit on Smokehouse Lane in Lexington, Davidson County, that Wayne Monk opened in 1962 at 26 after working under Warner Stamey, and that he owns with his son Rick. Shoulders cook nearly half a day over oak and hickory coals under four brick chimneys whose white smoke shows from the road; the meat is served chopped or sliced with the 'dip', the thin vinegar-and-ketchup sauce of the Piedmont, and with red slaw dressed with the same. Locals call it the Honeymonk, after Monk and his early partner Sonny Hunneycutt. The James Beard Foundation named it an America's Classic in 2003.

Wayne Monk worked under Warner Stamey, the man who carried the Lexington method out of the Weaver and Swicegood stands of the 1920s, and in 1962, at 26, opened his own place with Sonny Hunneycutt. The partner left; the joined name, Honeymonk, stayed on the town's tongue, and DavidsonLocal, reporting Monk's induction into the NC Bar-B-Q Hall of Fame on March 1, 2024, tied the name to the two surnames. Wikipedia records the 1962 founding and the James Beard Foundation's America's Classic award of 2003, the same year the Skylight Inn in Ayden got one — the two North Carolinas honored together. Our State counts about a thousand customers a day. Wayne and Rick Monk own it together, and the restaurant's own page lists Rick as owner.

Pork shoulders cook nearly half a day over oak and hickory coals. The plate is barbecue — chopped, coarse-chopped or sliced — with red slaw, hushpuppies and fries; a tray drops the bread. The dip is thin, vinegar with ketchup, spices and sugar, and the slaw is dressed with it, which is why it is red. Onion rings and barbecue beans are on the board.

Open Tuesday to Saturday 10 to 9, closed Sunday and Monday, at 100 Smokehouse Lane, Lexington, per the restaurant's site in September 2026. OpenStreetMap lists Monday hours as well; the restaurant's own page is followed here.

title: Luella's Bar-B-Que
text:
An Asheville barbecue house on Merrimon Avenue with a second room at Biltmore Park, opened in 2007 by Jeff Miller and named for his grandmother and his daughter. Jeff and Ashley Miller own it. Pork butts, ribs, whole chickens, brisket and turkey come off a smoker that a 2011 account had running hickory coals around the clock; the sauce is the Coastal Plain's vinegar rather than a mountain sweet one. Macaroni and cheese is on the board because the daughter it is half named for likes it.

Jeff Miller opened Luella's in 2007, naming it for his grandmother and for his six-year-old daughter. The first room was in south Asheville by two 2017 accounts, and Merrimon Avenue came in 2009, mid-recession; he later bought the Merrimon property. Explore Asheville's profile of him says he owns the business with his wife Ashley Miller, and a 2017 piece has the two of them beginning a hunt for a second site in 2014; the Biltmore Park room opened in spring 2016 and the business marked ten years in 2017. The restaurant's own pages name only Jeff, as owner and pit boss, which is the asymmetry a reader should know about before deciding what the ownership line means. The fire is the other open question. The only description of it found anywhere is from Our State in August 2011, which watched the kitchen manager open the heavy doors of a smoker cycling meat over hickory coals twenty-four hours a day. Every page since — the restaurant's own, the tourism listings, the 2017 features — is silent on fuel, and none says gas or electric either. *Inference —* silence across fifteen years of copy is not a change of method; it is copy that stopped mentioning the method.

Pork butts, racks of ribs, whole chickens, beef brisket and turkey go through the smoker; the chopped pork comes with an eastern vinegar-based sauce, which is a Coastal Plain sauce carried into the mountains. Ribs are cut St. Louis style. The sides are the reason the daughter's name is on the sign: the macaroni and cheese is hers. Both rooms run eleven to nine, seven days.

Open at 501 Merrimon Avenue and at 33 Town Square Boulevard in Biltmore Park, both eleven to nine daily, per the restaurant's own pages read on September 16, 2026. No independent report from 2026 confirms trading, and nothing on this disk records how Hurricane Helene touched either room.

title: Maurice's Piggie Park BBQ
text:
A chain of eight barbecue restaurants around Columbia run from the original drive-in at 1600 Charleston Highway, West Columbia, where Maurice Bessinger and his brother Joe Jr. opened in 1953. Pork hams cook twenty-four hours over hickory coals at the West Columbia pits and go out daily to the 'Pit-Stop' locations; the meat is served chopped, in sandwiches and plates, with the yellow mustard sauce the company bottles as Southern Gold — sold for decades as Carolina Gold. Maurice's sons Lloyd and Paul, his daughter Debbie and his grandchildren run it. The name also carries a 1968 Supreme Court case and the flag fight of 2000.

Joe Bessinger opened his first restaurant in Holly Hill in 1939 with a mustard sauce of his own. His son Maurice, born in Orangeburg County in 1930, came home from the Korean War in 1952 and with his brother Joe Jr. opened Maurice's Piggie Park, a drive-in, in West Columbia in 1953; by 1964 there were four. That year Anne Newman, the wife of a Black minister, was refused entry, and Matthew J. Perry filed a class action under Title II of the Civil Rights Act of 1964; Bessinger answered that his religion compelled him to oppose integration. The district court held the Act reached his sandwich shop but not the drive-ins; the Fourth Circuit reversed; and in Newman v. Piggie Park Enterprises, 390 U.S. 400 (1968), the Supreme Court held 8–0 that a plaintiff who wins such an injunction ordinarily recovers attorney's fees. Bessinger ran for the legislature in 1964 and for governor in 1974; by 1999 his was the largest barbecue business in the country, with Carolina Gold in some 3,000 groceries. On July 1, 2000, the day the Confederate flag came off the State House dome, he raised it over his restaurants. Bi-Lo, Food Lion, Harris Teeter, Kroger, Piggly Wiggly, Publix, Sam's Club, Wal-Mart and Winn-Dixie dropped the sauce; he sued them for $50 million and lost at the state Supreme Court in 2007. His brothers' Charleston restaurants were reported as independent concerns, 'sans the politics'. His children took the company, took the last flags down in 2013, and sell the sauce as Southern Gold. Maurice died on February 22, 2014. On October 26, 2024 a three-alarm fire destroyed the pits, kitchen and offices beside the West Columbia restaurant; the restaurant and its sign survived, three locations reopened within a week on rented smokers, and Lloyd Bessinger said: 'we want to be positive, we want to help people.'

Pork hams — not whole hogs — cook twenty-four hours over hickory wood coals at the original West Columbia pits, the company says, and the barbecue is delivered daily to the other locations, the 'Pit-Stops' where customers drive in. The meat is chopped for sandwiches and plates and dressed with the family's yellow mustard sauce, whose bottled recipe lists mustard, brown sugar, soy sauce and vinegar. The company sells the sauce by the bottle, the half gallon and the gift box.

Open: eight locations — West Columbia (Charleston Highway), Irmo, downtown Columbia on Elmwood Avenue, Devine Street, Clemson Road, O'Neil Court and two in Lexington — per the company's site on September 15, 2026. The West Columbia restaurant reopened within a week of the October 2024 fire; the pit house and offices behind it are being rebuilt.

Maurice's Piggie Park BBQ to South Carolina mustard barbecue: the style it made national: the Midlands mustard sauce, bottled and shipped.

Maurice's Piggie Park BBQ to mustard-based barbecue sauce: its Southern Gold, formerly Carolina Gold — the bottled mustard sauce of the 1990s supermarkets.

Maurice's Piggie Park BBQ to Carolina Gold: the name it sold the sauce under until the family renamed it Southern Gold.

Maurice's Piggie Park BBQ to Maurice Bessinger: its founder, 1953 to his death in 2014, and the reason the name carries a court case and a flag.

Maurice's Piggie Park BBQ to Bessinger's Bar-B-Q: the Charleston brothers' house: the same sauce lineage, a separate business.

Maurice's Piggie Park BBQ to political barbecue: its founder stood for the legislature in 1964 and for governor in 1974, and flew the Confederate flag over the restaurants from 2000 to 2013.

title: McCabe's Bar-B-Q
text:
A family buffet house on North Brooks Street in Manning, Clarendon County, where the McCabes cook whole hogs, shoulders and hams together for ten to twelve hours over wood coals, on pits David McCabe built in a screened room off the back porch. The pulled meat is mixed and dressed with a vinegar-and-pepper sauce, slightly sweet with a little heat — the Pee Dee's sauce, not the Midlands' mustard — and set out with hash and rice, perloo, fried chicken and a table of vegetables. Open Friday and Saturday middays, cash only, closed for January. Southern Living has listed it among the South's top fifty barbecue houses.

Two sons of Jessie McCabe opened the restaurant some thirty years before Gwen Fowler wrote it up for the state tourism office, and almost everyone working in the small place was a McCabe. Mrs. McCabe, ninety at the time, still cooked the sides — rice and hash, perlo, green beans, turnip greens, cabbage, sweet potatoes, peas, coleslaw, hushpuppies — and her fried chicken went faster than it could be fried. The pork cooked on pits in a screened room in the back, and there was one sauce, vinegar and pepper, slightly sweet. Garden & Gun wrote the place up in its June/July 2010 issue; the South Carolina Barbeque Association put it on its 100-Mile list, the houses worth a hundred-mile drive; Southern Living named it among the South's top fifty. David McCabe, who runs it now, cooks whole hog, shoulders and hams together for ten to twelve hours on pits he built himself over coals he makes himself, and keeps the sauce as 'the big secret': 'vinegar-based with salt, pepper, and ketchup... and our secret ingredient.'

Whole hogs, shoulders and hams share the pits for ten to twelve hours; the meat is picked and mixed, then dressed with the vinegar-pepper sauce — vinegar, salt, pepper, ketchup and the secret. The buffet: hash and rice, perloo (rice cooked with chicken, the Pee Dee's chicken bog under its other name), fried chicken, green beans, greens, cabbage, sweet potatoes, peas, okra, tomatoes, butter beans, coleslaw and hushpuppies. Cash only.

Open Friday and Saturday, 11 a.m. to 2 p.m., closed the month of January; the state tourism office's older listing gave Thursday to Saturday. 480 North Brooks Street, Manning. Cash only. Checked September 15, 2026 against Destination BBQ's page, which carries a March 2026 menu.

McCabe's Bar-B-Q to vinegar-and-pepper sauce: its sauce — vinegar, salt, pepper and a little ketchup — the Pee Dee's, not the mustard of the Midlands an hour west.

McCabe's Bar-B-Q to South Carolina mustard barbecue: the neighbouring style: Manning's sauce is vinegar, the Midlands' is mustard.

McCabe's Bar-B-Q to whole hog: whole hogs on the pit with shoulders and hams, all mixed in the pull.

title: Melton's Barbecue
text:
The Rocky Mount whole-hog house that Wikipedia records as North Carolina's first sit-down barbecue restaurant. Bob Melton, a horse trader, cooked hogs for friends in an open pit by the Tar River, sold meat by the pound, and in 1924 (some accounts say 1922) opened a shed of a restaurant that grew room by room. It served finely chopped whole hog with a vinegar sauce, boiled potatoes, slaw, corn sticks, hushpuppies and Brunswick stew, and sent barbecue out by bus to parties across the state. Floods from Hurricanes Fran and Floyd drove it out of the river bottom, and it closed in 2005.

Robert Benjamin Melton traded horses in Rocky Mount and cooked whole hogs on the banks of the Tar River for his friends; by 1922 he was selling barbecue there, and in 1924 he built the shed that Wikipedia and UNC's North Carolina Miscellany call the state's first indoor, sit-down barbecue restaurant. In 1929 a plate with boiled potatoes cost 45 cents and a sandwich 15. Food writer Beth Tartan recorded that a Raleigh hostess with company coming would call and say 'Ride me a party,' and Melton's would put barbecue and fixings on the bus. Life magazine called him the King of Southern Barbecue in 1958, the year he died; his partners W.B. Melton, T.O. Fulghum and Add Smith carried on. By the time John Egerton visited for Southern Food (1993) the pits had gone from charcoal to gas with wood chips, a change he judged for the worse. The low ground flooded: after Hurricane Fran the restaurant reopened in ten days and customers came by boat for a stretch, and a plaque later marked the high-water line. Hurricane Floyd in 1999, the 75th-anniversary year, put water over the ceiling and silt through the building. The restaurant moved to a strip mall, could not make the numbers in a shrinking local economy, and closed in 2005.

Small hogs of 80 to 90 pounds, cooked whole over charcoal in the early decades and over gas with wood chips by the 1990s, chopped fine — 'the consistency of chopped peanut butter,' a 1988 Boating writer said — and seasoned with a vinegar sauce. The sides were boiled potatoes, slaw, corn sticks, hushpuppies and Brunswick stew, the plate of the Coastal Plain.

Closed since 2005. The original site was in the Tar River bottom at Rocky Mount; the map point marks the town, not the building.

title: Melvin's Legendary Bar-B-Que
text:
A Charleston mustard-sauce house with rooms on Folly Road on James Island and on Houston Northcutt Boulevard in Mount Pleasant, opened in 1982 by Melvin Bessinger with his son David after Melvin left the partnership with his brother Thomas at Bessinger's. David Bessinger runs it now, and the thing that distinguishes it is a reversal: in 2015 he took out the gas-assisted pits and went back to cooking over wood alone. Pork shoulders go twenty-four hours at about two hundred degrees over smouldering hickory.

The line starts at the Holly Hill Cafe, where Joseph Bessinger — Big Joe — was cooking in 1939, and it runs out through his sons into four or five Lowcountry and Midlands businesses that share a mustard sauce and not much else. Melvin left the partnership with his brother Thomas at Bessinger's on Savannah Highway and opened his own on Houston Northcutt Boulevard in 1982, with James Island following in 1984. The Southern Foodways Alliance recorded David Bessinger on June 26, 2012, and he put the family plainly: as far as why they all got into the restaurant business, he thought it trickled down from one generation to another — it was in the blood. The turn came in 2015. Southern Living reported on October 1 of that year that David had made a weighty decision, installed new pits and gone back to the family's wood-cooking roots; the company's own history says he discontinued the gas-assisted pits and brought back smoking over all wood. *Inference —* that is a rare direction of travel. Most of the Carolinas' movement over seventy years has run from wood to gas, one pit at a time, and it is nearly always one-way. The Campaign for Real Barbecue certified both houses afterwards.

Pork shoulders, not whole hogs, cook about twenty-four hours at two hundred degrees in metal boxes the size of a pair of refrigerators, over smouldering wet hickory logs. Since 2015 the fire is wood alone; before that the pits were gas-assisted. The sauce is the Midlands mustard, which the Alliance's oral history records the Bessinger and Sweatman families as having worked out between them. Hash is not on the menu in any source read.

Open Monday to Saturday, 10:30 a.m. to 9 p.m., closed Sunday, at 538 Folly Road on James Island and at 925 Houston Northcutt Boulevard, Mount Pleasant. The map point here is the James Island house.

title: Midway BBQ
text:
A hash house and meat market on Main Street in Buffalo, a mill village in Union County in the Upstate, in business since about 1941 and the last of the nearly fifty hash houses the county once had. Hash here is the Upstate's kind: beef, butter, onion, salt and pepper cooked down slowly in three hundred-gallon pots, sold over rice and by the quart, and it outsells the barbecue three or four to one. The barbecue is hickory-smoked shoulder and ham, chopped; a creamy, spicy chicken stew goes out by the hundred gallons a day; and the front of the building is a butcher's counter with sawdust on the floor.

Jack O'Dell opened Midway some time around 1941 — 'the date is sketchy', the family says. Union County was hash-eating country and O'Dell's was one of nearly fifty hash houses; the others closed and Midway stayed. His daughter Amy Allen owns it; her husband Jay Allen has managed it since 1994, and it was Jay whom Rien Fertel recorded for the Southern Foodways Alliance on June 12, 2012, at what the interview page lists as 811 Hash Boulevard. Jay's arithmetic: catering, three parts hash to one of barbecue; in the store, four to one. 'Without hash, we're done. We're closed.' The slogan calls Buffalo the hash and chicken stew capital of the world.

Hash: beef, butter, onion, salt and pepper, slow-cooked in three 100-gallon pots into a thick stew and ladled over white rice — no pork, no mustard, the Upstate's version. Chicken stew, creamy and spicy, a hundred gallons a day. Barbecue: shoulder and ham smoked over hickory, chopped or pulled, and chopped barbecue chicken. A full-service meat counter sells across the front of the store.

Open Tuesday to Friday 10 a.m. to 6 p.m. and Saturday 10 to 4, closed Sunday and Monday, per the company's site on September 15, 2026. 811 Main Street, Buffalo, Union County.

Midway BBQ to hash and rice: the reason the place exists: beef hash, the Upstate's kind, three or four to one against the barbecue.

Midway BBQ to pork shoulder: shoulder and ham, hickory-smoked and chopped, are the barbecue.

title: Morris Barbeque
text:
A Saturday-only whole-hog house on Morris BBQ Road outside Hookerton, in Greene County, in business since 1956; the county named the road for it. William Morris Jr., grandson of the founder Willie McKinley Morris, cooks the hogs, chops the meat and works the counter. The pig goes on a gas machine built in Wilson in the early 1970s, its burners set off to one side rather than under the meat. Doors open at eight for take-out and half past nine for the dining room, and the barbecue is usually gone by one.

Willie McKinley Morris — Pop — peddled barbecue through Hookerton from a cart as early as 1931, in what the family's history page calls the Hoover days; that page says a mule, the Southern Foodways Alliance transcript says a horse and buggy. A country store came first, the kind of place for a Coca-Cola and a pack of Nabs, and the barbecue business dates itself from 1956. Frances Morris, called Nannie, died in 1974. Pop died in 1991 and left the business to his grandson William Morris Jr., born in March 1956, the year it opened. Rien Fertel recorded Morris for the Alliance on November 26, 2011, and Morris described the cooker himself: gas, built in Wilson by a company no longer in business, bought around the early seventies, the burners offset from the hog. His own history page does not say that. It describes his grandfather's pit of charcoal, corncobs and oak wood and then says the tradition continues with very little change. On July 10, 2026 a storm dropped a large tree on the back of the building. The pit was undamaged. Repairs pushed past a Labor Day reopening, and no date had been set when WCTI reported on September 2, 2026 — the first run of consecutive missed Saturdays in some seventy years.

Whole hogs — hams and shoulders chopped together — cook about six and a half hours, and the chop is judged by a committee of six, with Morris's daughter Ashley Morris Godley taking the final say. Orders go up on a board: telephone ahead and the name is written down, first come first served, and paying in advance holds the tray. Skins, ribs and bone trays have to be ordered ahead; the skins are the first thing gone each week.

Closed since the storm of July 10, 2026, with no reopening date in the reports read through September 2, 2026. The restaurant's own site still advertises its usual Saturday hours, which is stale copy rather than news. 891 Morris BBQ Road, Hookerton. Check before driving.

Morris Barbeque to whole hog: the cut — hams and shoulders from the same pig, chopped together.

title: Parker's Barbecue
text:
A large eastern barbecue house on U.S. 301 south of Wilson, opened in August 1946 by brothers Graham and Ralph Parker and their cousin Henry Parker Brewer, and owned since 1987 by Donald Williams, who started there in 1963, with partners Eric Lippard and Kevin Lamm. It cooks about 150 whole hogs and fries about 8,000 chickens a week for some 20,000 customers, on gas cookers the founders installed in the 1950s. The barbecue is chopped fine and dressed with vinegar and red pepper; young staff in white paper caps seat the room; cash or check only.

The restaurant opened in August 1946 just off Highway 301 as a family destination for pit-cooked barbecue and fried chicken, the owners' history says. The day that set it on its feet came in 1954, when the Ralston Purina plant opened in Wilson and Parker's served 17,000 plates at 75 cents each in four hours. In the 1950s the cookers went from wood coals to gas, for a temperature that could be regulated. Donald Williams came to work in 1963 and bought the business when Graham and Ralph Parker retired in 1987. June Brunson worked there more than 62 years, until her death in 2020; Richard Ward, who came on opening day, was still a customer at 100 in 2013. Ralph Parker, the last of the founders, died on July 4, 2013 at 89. Williams and Kevin Lamm gave the Southern Foodways Alliance an oral history in November 2011, in which Lamm said the owners knew they were consistent because customers told them the place had not changed across decades. Three or four employees have been there more than forty years. On Mother's Day the kitchen uses 45 pigs and 26 chicken fryers.

Hogs are dressed and cooked whole in a cinder-block building behind the restaurant, on gas cookers, and the meat is chopped fine and seasoned with a vinegar-and-red-pepper sauce. Barbecue is served from nine in the morning. Plates come with hushpuppies and slaw, and the menu runs to fried chicken, fish, string beans and, in season, oysters battered or stewed. Waiters in white caps seat and serve; the owners greet at the door.

Open seven days, 9 a.m. to 7 p.m. for dine-in and to 7:30 for take-out, at 2514 U.S. Highway 301 South, Wilson, per the restaurant's site in September 2026. Cash or check; an ATM is on site. A separate Parker's operates in Greenville; the relationship is not documented here.

title: Red Bridges Barbecue Lodge
text:
The Shelby, Cleveland County, pork-shoulder house of the Bridges family, begun in 1946 by Red Bridges, an Army cook home from the war, and his wife Lyttle, and run by their daughter Debbie Bridges-Webb with her children Natalie Ramsey, who runs the front, and Chase Webb, who tends the pits overnight. Shoulders cook seven to eight hours a side over hickory and oak — no gas, no electric, the family told WBTV in 2026 — and the recipes are the ones the Bridges started with. The lodge on U.S. 74, across from the Cleveland Mall, marked eighty years in June 2026.

Red Bridges came home from the Army, where he had cooked, and in 1946 began selling barbecue sandwiches from a livestock yard, the family told the Southern Foodways Alliance; the restaurant's own history calls that first venture Dedmond's Barbecue. In 1949 it became Red Bridges Barbecue Lodge, and the lodge building dates from 1953. Red died in 1966 and Lyttle ran the business after him — 'probably the first female barbecue entrepreneur in North Carolina,' her grandchildren said in 2011. Debbie, their daughter, owns it now; Natalie Ramsey and Chase Webb told the Alliance's Rien Fertel that nothing would change, 'because you don't find pit-cooked barbecue hardly anymore.' WBTV, marking the eightieth year in June 2026, found server Wanda Montgomery in her 44th year and the family planning to put the sauce in grocery stores.

Pork shoulders smoke seven to eight hours on each side over hickory and oak coals, Chase Webb at the pits through the night. The barbecue is chopped or sliced and dressed with the family's sauce, unchanged since 1946 by the family's account; the plate is the Piedmont plate, red slaw and hushpuppies beside the meat.

Open Wednesday to Sunday at 2000 East Dixon Boulevard (U.S. 74), Shelby, across from the Cleveland Mall, per WBTV in June 2026.

title: Rodney Scott's Whole Hog BBQ
text:
A whole-hog restaurant at 1011 King Street on the Charleston peninsula, opened in February 2017 by Rodney Scott of Hemingway and the restaurateur Nick Pihakis in a former fried-chicken house, with seats for about 128, a drive-through and delivery. It cooked whole hogs over hardwood coals and served the pulled pork with a hot vinegar sauce beside spare ribs, fried catfish, a rib-eye sandwich and banana pudding. Sister restaurants followed in Birmingham in 2019 and in Atlanta and a second Alabama town in 2021. Every location closed in May 2026 amid lawsuits and liens against Pihakis's restaurant group, and the King Street doors have stayed shut since.

Rodney Scott was born in Philadelphia in 1971 and raised at his parents' store and pits in Hemingway, where he cooked his first hog at eleven. A customer, Nick Pihakis of the Jim 'N Nick's chain, told him he was undercharging; after the Hemingway cookhouse burned in November 2013 it was Pihakis's Fatback Collective that staged the Bar-B-Que in Exile dinners to rebuild it. The two opened Rodney Scott's Whole Hog BBQ in February 2017 in the old Chick's Fry House on upper King Street. In May 2018 the James Beard Foundation gave Scott its chef award for the Southeast, the second pitmaster to win one; the Chef's Table: BBQ episode about him in 2020 set sales records three days running, with hour-long lines; Food & Wine put the restaurant among the forty most important of the past forty years. Birmingham opened in 2019, Atlanta and a fourth Alabama site in 2021, and a cookbook with Lolis Eric Elie came out the same year. On May 3, 2026 the King Street restaurant closed at 5 p.m. 'until further notice', in general manager Sam Ayala's words, days after a meat supplier sued Pihakis Restaurant Group for $394,238.74 and a landlord filed more than $12 million in liens; every Rodney Scott's closed with it. In June Scott cooked a pop-up at Munkle Brewing under the name Pitmaster Scott and said reopening in Charleston was his first priority.

Whole hogs cooked over hardwood charcoal, pulled, and seasoned with a spice rub that includes MSG — Scott calls it a 'flavor maker' — and a hot vinegar sauce. Past the hog: spare ribs, fried catfish, a rib-eye steak sandwich, banana pudding. The room seated about 128, with a drive-through window and delivery.

Closed. The King Street restaurant shut at 5 p.m. on May 3, 2026 'until further notice' and had not reopened when this record was written on September 15, 2026; the Birmingham, Atlanta and other Alabama locations closed the same week. Rodney Scott has said he means to reopen in Charleston. Address of record: 1011 King Street.

title: Sam Jones BBQ
text:
A whole-hog restaurant in Winterville, Pitt County, opened on November 10, 2015 by Sam Jones, grandson of the Skylight Inn's founder Pete Jones, with his partner Michael Letchworth, and a second house in downtown Raleigh since February 2021. Whole hogs are smoked on site over wood, chopped and served daily; the menu runs longer than the Skylight's, with ribs, smoked chicken and turkey, cornbread, slaw and collards, banana pudding, and in Raleigh a full bar. Winterville is seven miles from the Skylight Inn in Ayden; Raleigh is the family's first restaurant outside Pitt County.

Sam Jones grew up in the Skylight Inn, which his grandfather Pete Jones opened in Ayden in 1947; he left the family business as a teenager and came back, telling the Southern Foodways Alliance in 2011 that returning was like a flag-bearer keeping the standard up on the field. In 2014 he and Michael Letchworth, who had worked at the Skylight since 2004, signed for a loan and began building in Winterville; Sam Jones BBQ opened on November 10, 2015. The restaurant's own history counts Southern Living's 2012 list of ten Southern pitmasters among its credentials. In 2019 Jones and Daniel Vaughn published Whole Hog BBQ: The Gospel of Carolina Barbecue, which writes the family method down. The Raleigh restaurant at 502 West Lenoir Street opened softly in February 2021 in a building that had been Dusty's Garage, keeping the old floor and hanging family photographs; it seats about 140 inside and out, with a private room upstairs and a bar. INDY Week reported in May 2021 that three hogs a day went on at about one in the afternoon, cooked at 250 degrees until ten, were held overnight, and had their skin crisped the next morning.

Whole hogs of about 180 pounds cook some sixteen hours in wood-fired pits; the meat is chopped with the crisp skin through it and dressed in the eastern way, with vinegar, salt and pepper. A tray — the eastern plate, barbecue with slaw and bread and no plate under it — comes with cornbread. Beyond the hog there are ribs, smoked turkey and chicken, collards, a sweet slaw and banana pudding, and in Raleigh a bourbon old-fashioned infused with pig fat and named Jay the Butcher.

Open, both houses. Winterville: 715 West Fire Tower Road, Monday to Saturday 11 to 9, Sunday 11 to 8:30. Raleigh: 502 West Lenoir Street, the same hours. Hours as posted on the restaurant's site in September 2026.

title: Scott's Bar-B-Que
text:
A whole-hog pit behind a country store on the Hemingway Highway in Williamsburg County, in the Pee Dee. Roosevelt and Ella Scott opened the store in 1972 and the barbecue began as a weekend sideline; it grew into the business, and into the pit where their son Rodney Scott learned the trade before he opened his own restaurant in Charleston in 2017. Whole hogs cook eight to twelve hours over coals burned down from hickory, oak and pecan, and the meat is pulled and dressed with a thin sauce of vinegar and pepper. It sells by the plate and the sandwich, cash only, four days a week.

Roosevelt and Ella Scott came from Philadelphia to the Pee Dee in 1972 with their infant son, farmed tobacco and raised hogs near Nesmith, and opened a variety store and gas station on the Hemingway highway. Ella and the family smoked a hog on weekends; demand climbed from one or two a week to four or six, and Rodney cooked his first pig at eleven and joined full time at seventeen. John T. Edge profiled the store in 2009, and when Rien Fertel recorded Rodney for the Southern Foodways Alliance in June 2012 the pits were turning eight to ten hogs a night. On November 27, 2013, at 4 a.m., a pit flared while two employees roasted fourteen pigs in the wooden cookhouse beside the store; the cookhouse burned, no one was hurt, and the store kept cooking on other pits. Rodney answered with the Bar-B-Que in Exile Tour: fundraising dinners in Birmingham, Charleston and elsewhere, staged with the Fatback Collective — the chefs and restaurateurs around Nick Pihakis of Jim 'N Nick's — to raise $100,000 and rebuild in metal, so the pits could be insured. Rodney had taken the business over in 2011; in 2017 he left to open Rodney Scott's Whole Hog BBQ in Charleston with Pihakis. Roosevelt Scott died on December 10, 2020. Ella Scott died in 2023, the store closed for five months, and in May 2024 her brother Sam Wilson and Rodney's son Dominic Scott reopened it.

Hogs are split and cooked eight to twelve hours at around 250 degrees over coals of hickory, oak and pecan, shoveled under the meat through the night; *Tradition holds —* the coals come from a burn barrel, a steel drum in which the logs burn down. The cooked meat is pulled from the bones and seasoned with the family's sauce, which Rodney Scott gives as 'vinegar, pepper, some more pepper, some love'. Orders are a whole-hog plate or a sandwich; the SCETV crew in 2021 filmed the same wood-burning pit and the same counter. The rebuilt pit house is metal.

Open at 2734 Hemingway Highway, Hemingway. Destination BBQ lists Wednesday to Saturday from 9:30 a.m., closing between 5 and 7 p.m., cash only. Run since May 2024 by Sam Wilson and Dominic Scott. Checked September 15, 2026 against the sources named; check before driving.

title: Scott's Famous Barbecue
text:
The Goldsboro barbecue of the Rev. Adam Scott, a Black cook and preacher who catered barbecues from the 1910s, sold from the back door of his house on Brazil Street from the early 1930s, and whose son A. Martel Scott patented the family's vinegar sauce as Scott's Famous Barbecue Sauce in 1946. The company dates the sauce to 1917 and sells about a million bottles a year. The restaurants — three around Goldsboro by 1950 — are closed: after a first closure in 2001 the family ran on Thursday and Friday lunches for a while, then stopped to make sauce.

Adam Scott was born in 1890 and took his first cooking job in 1911 at the Elberon Hotel in Atlantic City; back in Goldsboro he catered barbecues from about the mid-1910s, and between 1931 and 1933 opened a back-door restaurant at his home on Brazil Street — two hogs a week on Saturdays at first, later four to seven a day, with an enclosed porch for a dining room. His first customers were mostly white. In 1933 he cooked barbecue for Franklin Roosevelt in the White House Rose Garden. He said the final recipe for the sauce came to him in a vision. In the 1940s he moved to Winston-Salem to cook for R.J. Reynolds, and his son Alvin Martel Scott, born 1913, patented Scott's Famous Barbecue Sauce in 1946 and put it in stores. By 1950 there were three Scott's around Goldsboro — Martel's on the Mount Olive highway, Ed Scott's on the Wilson highway, Adam's on the Raleigh road — and the Green Book, the travel guide for Black motorists, listed a Scott's at 404 Gulley Street from 1950 to 1955. Martel ran the business until his death in 1992; his wife Ann chaired the company until hers in 2009. Adam Scott died in 1983 at 93. The restaurant closed in 2001, reopened on Thursday and Friday lunches when customers kept calling, then closed for good; the Scotts' children and grandchildren make the sauce. The National Barbecue Hall of Fame inducted Adam Scott in 2022.

Hogs cooked at the house, two a week and then several a day, chopped and dressed with the vinegar sauce; the later restaurants served chopped pork with hushpuppies and fried chicken. What survives is the sauce: vinegar, salt and spices, no tomato, fat-free and sugar-free, sold in grocery stores across the east and by the case online.

Closed. The Scott family's sauce company continues in Goldsboro; the restaurant's last address is not confirmed on this disk, so the map point marks the town.

title: Shealy's Bar-B-Que
text:
A buffet house on East Columbia Avenue in Batesburg-Leesville, Lexington County, opened in June 1969 by Victor and Sara Shealy with their teenage children Tommy and Nancy, and family-run since. It is the barbecue buffet in its fullest form: pork shoulders smoked by the thousand each week and served chopped with mustard sauce — vinegar and tomato sauces alongside — hash over rice, fried chicken, ribs, country-fried steak and more than forty home-cooked sides, with a salad bar and a dessert bar, all you can eat. The South Carolina House marked its fiftieth anniversary with a resolution in 2019.

Victor and Sara Shealy barbecued whole hogs in their back yard on weekends in the early 1950s, and word of Victor's sauce spread until they were cooking four or five hogs a week. They quit their jobs, borrowed about $20,000 to buy a building, and in June 1969 opened Shealy's Bar-B-Que House with Tommy and Nancy, then teenagers, working beside them. *Tradition holds —* Sara put the food on a buffet from the first year, and the family counts it among the first barbecue buffets in the state. On April 30, 2019 the South Carolina House of Representatives adopted a resolution for the fiftieth anniversary, naming the 'all-you-can-eat buffet' of 'renowned barbeque and over forty home-cooked sides'. The house stands at the western edge of the Midlands mustard belt; *Inference —* by the map, a quarter mile across the railroad from where Jackie Hite's cooked whole hogs until 2018.

Everything is on the line: chopped pork and ribs with a choice of mustard, vinegar or tomato sauce; hash — the thick pork gravy of the Midlands — over white rice; fried chicken by the heap, and off the menu the pulley bone, the wishbone piece; country-fried steak with milk gravy, lima beans, creamed corn, collards, mac and cheese, green and butter beans, mashed potatoes, a salad bar and a dessert bar. A 2015 review put the buffet under $15 a head with a drink. Carry-out plates go from 10 a.m.

Open Monday, Tuesday and Thursday to Saturday, buffet 11 a.m. to 9 p.m., carry-out 10 to 8:30; closed Wednesday and Sunday. 340 East Columbia Avenue, Batesburg-Leesville — OpenStreetMap records the building at number 240. Checked September 15, 2026.

title: Short Sugar's Pit Bar-B-Q
text:
A drive-in barbecue on South Scales Street in Reidsville, Rockingham County, opened in June 1949 by the Overby brothers and named for the one who died two days before the opening, and closed in January 2025 after 75 years. It cooked over hickory coals in two small pits visible from the counter — hams for sliced barbecue, shoulders for chopped — and dressed the meat with a thin dark sauce built on Worcestershire and sugar rather than the ketchup of the Piedmont dips, a sauce that fit neither of North Carolina's camps. Curb service ran to the end.

Johnny, Clyde and Eldridge Overby meant to open the Overby Brothers Drive-In in June 1949; two days before opening Eldridge was killed in a car crash, and his brothers named the place for him alone, by his nickname, Short Sugar — a small man, whether friendly or fetching Our State leaves open. In 1982 Short Sugar's won the Barbecue Bowl, the first restaurant from either Carolina to do so. The Wilson family ran it in its later decades: David Wilson, whose wife was an Overby daughter, and his son John David, who told the Southern Foodways Alliance in 2011 that a barbecue place with no pit in sight was 'an insult to those families who still do it the way it's supposed to be done.' A dining room was added about the 1980s to the 1950s drive-in. Hobbled by the pandemic closures and then by the economy, it served its last plates in mid-January 2025; a Reidsville writer who went by on January 16 found it shut, and The State You're In wrote the farewell the next day.

Two small hickory-coal pits behind the counter; hams for the sliced, shoulders for the chopped, cooked fresh to order rather than held. The sauce was thin and dark, sugar and Worcestershire, runny and salty-sweet, with less ketchup or tomato paste than the Piedmont dips; it went on sandwiches sliced or chopped, and the kitchen sold it by the gallon.

Closed since mid-January 2025. The building stands at 1328 South Scales Street, Reidsville; no successor is recorded on this disk.
