title: Shuler's Bar-B-Que
text:
An all-you-can-eat barbecue house on Highway 38 between Latta and Sellers, in Dillon County in the Pee Dee, opened in 1996 by Norton and Lynn Hughes and named for Norton's father Shuler Hughes, who made the sauce in 1956, and for their grandson of the same name. Pork cooks over wood coals; the buffet runs to more than twenty items and includes liver hash over rice. It is open Thursday to Saturday. The Barbeque Association gives it the hundred-mile designation.

Shuler Hughes made the sauce in 1956. His son Norton learned the method from him and put it plainly to a visiting writer in February 2016: low and slow, and cook on wood — that was what his father taught him. Lynn Hughes traded a master's degree in education and teaching to start the restaurant with her husband in 1996, which is the sentence the business's own page uses and the reason a woman is named as an owner here rather than as a helper. The name skips a generation twice: it is the founder's father's given name and their grandson's. In 2014 the business appeared on CNBC's The Profit, and it has taken the Dillon Herald's readers' award for barbecue every year since 2008 by its own account. Payment is where the sources disagree — a visiting writer in 2016 recorded cash only and no credit cards, and Destination BBQ's page says cards and cash — so nothing is tagged here either way. A separate Shuler's Barbecue at Lake City is permanently closed and is not this business.

Pork cooks low and slow over wood; chicken and ribs share the pits. The buffet is all you can eat and runs past twenty items, and the liver hash — hash made with the liver in it, as the Pee Dee makes it — goes over white rice. The house phrase for the buffet is to eat until it hurts. Whole hog is not claimed by any source read; the pit is described as shoulder-based.

Open Thursday to Saturday, 11:30 a.m. to 8 p.m., at 419 Highway 38 West, between Latta and Sellers. The map point is the town of Latta, not the building: no street-level coordinate for the highway address came back from the geocoder.

Shuler's Bar-B-Que to Pee Dee whole-hog barbecue: the region it cooks in, and the vinegar-leaning country north of the Midlands mustard belt.

title: Skylight Inn BBQ
text:
A whole-hog pit in Ayden, Pitt County, opened by Walter B. 'Pete' Jones on July 8, 1947 and run by his family since. Hogs cook, heads on, over coals burned down from oak and hickory logs; the meat is chopped on a block with the crisp skin chopped through it, dressed with vinegar, salt, pepper and Texas Pete, and served on a tray with slaw and a square of dense cornbread. A wood-and-aluminum copy of the U.S. Capitol dome sits on the roof.

The Jones family counts its barbecue back to 1830 and Skilton Dennis, who *tradition holds* sold barbecue from a covered wagon near Ayden — a claim painted on the billboard outside and repeated by the press, with no document behind it that this project has seen. Pete Jones opened the Skylight at eighteen, in 1947, having learned whole hog at his uncle Emmitt Dennis's City Cafe; he gave the place beer and a jukebox, it ran late with rowdy crowds, and the late nights ended when the town set a 7 pm curfew. In 1979 a National Geographic article called the restaurant 'the barbecue capital of the world'; the dome went up in 1984 as the family's answer, and 'Capital of 'Cue' has been on the sign since. The James Beard Foundation named it an America's Classic in 2003. Pete Jones died in 2006; the family kept the pits. *Tradition holds —* his son Bruce and nephew Jeff Jones run the Skylight, and grandson Samuel Jones opened Sam Jones BBQ in Winterville in 2015, then a second in Raleigh, cooking the same whole hog with a longer menu.

Whole hogs, heads still on, cook over charcoal the pit crew makes by burning oak and hickory logs in fireplaces beside the pits. The chop takes in tenderloin, inner meat and crisped skin together. The plate is a tray: barbecue, slaw, cornbread; the sandwich is the same on a white roll. The cornbread is stone-ground cornmeal, water and pork drippings baked flat — denser and chewier than a skillet cornbread. Barbecue chicken is the one other meat.

Open Monday to Saturday, lunch through early evening, at 4618 S Lee Street, Ayden. Cash and cards. The dome, the block and the cleavers are all still in use.

Skylight Inn BBQ to Eastern North Carolina barbecue: the style it is the standing example of: whole hog, wood coals, vinegar and pepper, white slaw.

Skylight Inn BBQ to whole hog: the cut it has never departed from; the skin goes into the chop.

Skylight Inn BBQ to cornbread: its cornbread is its own — a dense pork-fat cake, the one side that visitors argue about.

Skylight Inn BBQ to Pete Jones: its founder, who cooked here from 1947 until his death in 2006.

Skylight Inn BBQ to Sam Jones: the grandson who carried the method to his own restaurants and wrote it down in a book.

Skylight Inn BBQ to Sam Jones BBQ: the family's second pit, in Winterville, opened 2015.

title: Smithfield's Chicken 'N Bar-B-Q
text:
A quick-service chain of eastern North Carolina barbecue and fried chicken — 41 restaurants across the state as of March 2024, and an online store — begun by Junius and Maggie Moore in downtown Smithfield, Johnston County, in 1977 as Smithfield Bar-B-Q. It sells the eastern pairing over a counter, chopped pork and fried chicken, from the coast to the Triangle, and it stands in Wikipedia's list of the state's notable barbecue restaurants beside Melton's and the Skylight Inn. It is the chain form of the tradition, described here the same way as a wood pit.

Junius and Maggie Moore opened Smithfield Bar-B-Q in downtown Smithfield in 1977 and soon a second in Clayton, the next town toward Raleigh; a third followed at Salter Path on the Bogue Banks in 1979. Through the early 1980s the company opened across eastern North Carolina, and in the 1990s it reached the Raleigh-Durham area. By March 2024 Wikipedia counted 41 locations statewide. OpenStreetMap in 2026 carries a dozen of its restaurants from Leland to Rocky Mount, tagged for barbecue and chicken, with a brand entry on Wikidata (Q7545474); its mappers have spelled the name three ways — Bar-B-Q, Barbeque, BBQ — as the signs themselves have. The chain's own site did not render for this project, so what it says of its cooking is not on disk.

Counter service: chopped eastern barbecue and fried chicken, alone or together on a plate, to eat in or take out, with an online store for shipping. The cooker and the sauce are not described in the sources read for this record; a customer should look at the plate and the map, not this page, for either.

Open; 41 restaurants in North Carolina as of March 2024 (Wikipedia). The map point marks Smithfield, the town of the first restaurant, and not a headquarters.

title: Speedy Lohr's Barbecue
text:
A wood-burning pork house on NC 8 south of Lexington, Davidson County, run by Randy and Amy Lohr, who bought the building in June 2013 from Whitley's Barbecue and carried the family name onto it. Randy's father was Sherman Paul 'Speedy' Lohr, who started the first Speedy's on Highway 52 and learned under Warner Stamey. The pits burn wood and the family says plainly that they always will. The tray is the Piedmont tray, chopped shoulder with the dip and red slaw; pork-skin sandwiches come out on Thursdays.

There are three businesses in the Carolinas carrying the Lohr name and they do not cook alike, which is the first thing to settle. This is the NC 8 house. Amy Lohr set out the line herself, in a comment on a visiting writer's post on February 2, 2023: her father-in-law founded the original Speedy's on Highway 52, and Randy bought this building in 2013. She wrote, of the pits, that they still cook over them with wood, have never stopped and never will, Lord willing — which is as direct a statement of method as a pit gives, and it comes from an owner rather than from a listing. Highway work had already cost the family twice: Randy's father's place went in an earlier expansion of Highway 8, and a Speedy Lohr's at Southmont closed in 2005 for the same reason. Then in 2015 this building caught fire and closed. It reopened in August 2016, thirteen months and about $200,000 later, with the pits rebuilt to code. Randy and Amy's son Luke is the named successor, and a visiting writer recorded in 2018 that he means to keep cooking with wood. The Campaign for Real Barbecue certified the pit.

Pork cooks over wood in pits behind the building, rebuilt after the 2015 fire. The meat is chopped and served the Piedmont way, with the dip — thin vinegar reddened with ketchup — and red slaw dressed from the same jug. Pork-skin sandwiches are a Thursday item rather than an everyday one.

Open at 3664 NC Highway 8 South, Lexington, and carried on Visit Lexington's current barbecue list. The map point here is the town, not the building: no street-level coordinate for the address came back from the geocoder. Hours are not on this disk. Check before driving.

title: Speedy's Barbecue
text:
A Lexington pork-shoulder house that Paul 'Speedy' Lohr opened as a drive-in in 1963 and the Dunn family has run since the early 1970s. Roy and Ella Dunn hold it now. The pork cooks in five electric cookers that look like large rotisserie ovens — not over wood, which is why the house appears on no wood list and on no trail, and which makes it a plain case of how much of the Piedmont cooks. The tray is the Piedmont tray: chopped shoulder, the dip, red slaw, hushpuppies.

Roy Dunn started at Speedy's as a curb boy. In the early 1970s Paul Lohr sold the business to Roy and a cousin, and the Dunn brothers have run it together since 1978; a local paper gives the purchase year as 1970 and Our State as the early seventies, a small gap left open here. What the Dunns bought included the name, which is why a Lexington driver can pass two Speedys in twenty minutes and find two different fires. Our State's writer stood in the kitchen in September 2013 and described what is actually there: the pork cooking slowly inside five electric cookers that look like giant rotisserie ovens. A visiting writer put it flatly in July 2016 — Speedy's of Lexington cooks over electricity, not wood. Neither the Historic Barbecue Trail, which requires wood or charcoal, nor the Campaign for Real Barbecue, which requires the same, lists the house, and both absences follow from the cookers rather than from anything about the food. In about 2023 the restaurant left Winston Road after some sixty years and moved to Piedmont Drive, pushed out by the state highway widening that also took Smiley's down the road.

Shoulders — a short shank is the cut the kitchen prefers — cook slowly in five electric cookers. The meat is chopped and served with the dip, the thin vinegar-and-ketchup sauce of the Piedmont, with red slaw dressed from the same jug and hushpuppies on the tray. The room runs eleven to eight, six days a week.

Open Monday to Saturday, 11 a.m. to 8 p.m., at 408 Piedmont Drive, Lexington, the address it moved to after roughly sixty years on Winston Road. OpenStreetMap last checked the listing on August 10, 2025.

title: Stamey's Barbecue
text:
The Greensboro pork-shoulder house of the Stamey family, opened by Warner Stamey in 1953 as a drive-in on High Point Road (now West Gate City Boulevard) and run by his grandson Chip since 1993, with a second restaurant on Battleground Avenue. Fifteen-pound shoulders cook eight to ten hours over hickory coals; the barbecue is chopped or sliced and served with the dip, the thin red vinegar sauce of the Piedmont, red slaw and hushpuppies — which the family says Warner Stamey was the first to put beside barbecue in North Carolina. The name reaches back to a Lexington stand of 1938.

Charles Warner Stamey, born in 1911, the youngest of eleven, learned pit-cooking in Lexington under Jess Swicegood and Sid Weaver, the men who set up the town's first stands, and took the method home to Shelby in the 1930s. In 1938 he came back to Lexington and bought Swicegood's stand, renaming it Stamey's; Wayne Monk trained under him there before opening Lexington Barbecue in 1962. In 1953 Stamey moved to Greensboro and opened a drive-in on High Point Road; the present building replaced it in 1979. He handed the business to his son Charles in 1957, and Charles's brother Keith joined in 1970; the second generation opened the Battleground Avenue restaurant, which burned in 2016 and reopened with a drive-through in July 2017. Chip Stamey left another career to take over in 1993 and told the Southern Foodways Alliance in November 2011 that the shoulders still cook over hickory and the barbecue is still served with dip rather than squirted with sauce. The American Royal put Warner Stamey in its barbecue hall of fame in 2020.

Shoulders of about fifteen pounds cook eight to ten hours over hickory coals. The meat is chopped or sliced and served on a tray or a bun with red slaw and hushpuppies; the dip goes on at the table, not in the kitchen. Warner Stamey's hushpuppies — fried cornmeal fritters — became the bread of the Piedmont plate.

Open. Battleground Avenue: 2812 Battleground Avenue, Greensboro, Monday to Saturday 11 to 9, per OpenStreetMap (checked August 2026). The 1953 site on West Gate City Boulevard is the other restaurant.

title: Stephenson's Bar-B-Q
text:
A family barbecue house on N.C. 50 at Willow Spring, in western Johnston County south of Raleigh, opened in July 1958 by hog farmer Paul Stephenson and run since his death by his son Andy. It cooks pork shoulders over hardwood charcoal — whole hogs at the start, shoulders later for leaner meat — and barbecue chicken with a tangy sauce, with hushpuppies and collards from the recipes of Paul's wife Jean, a home-economics teacher. It serves about 600 meals a day and closes on Sundays.

Paul Stephenson raised shoats — young pigs — on a Depression-era farm. A man bought fourteen of them one day, and when Stephenson asked what for, he said the barbecue man wanted them. Stephenson did the arithmetic: a hundred-pound pig sold for $11.50, and cut into three-ounce sandwiches at 35 cents each it was worth a good deal more. He taught himself to cook a pig, put up a building on his own land, and sold his first barbecue in July 1958. He cooked over hardwood until the energy crisis of the mid-1970s, when the family switched to hardwood charcoal; Andy Stephenson, who took over after his father died about 2008, told Our State in 2014 that charcoal cooks slower and needs checking less often than wood. The whole hog gave way to shoulders for the reason customers everywhere gave, leaner meat. Jean Stephenson worked out the collards and the hushpuppies.

Shoulders cook over hardwood charcoal; the barbecue is chopped and sauced in the eastern way, and the barbecue chicken gets a tangy sauce of its own. Plates carry hushpuppies — fried cornmeal fritters — and collards, both to Jean Stephenson's recipes. The kitchen turns out about 600 meals a day (Our State, 2014).

Open, closed Sundays, at 11964 N.C. Highway 50 North, Willow Spring, per Our State (2014). The map point marks the community, not the building.

title: Sweatman's Bar-B-Que
text:
A whole-hog barbecue house in an old farmhouse on Eutaw Road outside Holly Hill, in Orangeburg County, the mustard belt of the Midlands. Harold 'Bub' Sweatman and his wife Margie opened it in 1977 and it has served two days a week since: Friday and Saturday, pulled pork from whole hogs, ribs, hash over rice — hash being the Midlands' stew of pork and onion — and a spicy-sweet mustard sauce, with pork skins when the hogs give them. The open block pits became gas-and-wood smokers; the buffet that made the name ended after the pandemic; the family sold in 2011, and new owners took over in 2026.

Bub and Margie Sweatman first opened a small barbecue restaurant in Holly Hill in 1959. It did not last, and for years they cooked hogs only for friends and family. In 1977 they bought an old farmhouse in Eutawville, a rural community close to Holly Hill, and opened Sweatman's Bar-B-Que in its rooms; it has not closed since. The sauce belongs to a shared story: Joseph 'Big Joe' Bessinger, who opened the Holly Hill Café in 1939, worked out a mustard-based sauce with the Sweatman family — both families of German descent — and the Bessingers came to call theirs the Golden Secret. When Rien Fertel came for the Southern Foodways Alliance in June 2012 he recorded the cook Douglas Oliver, who said that whatever the economy did, 'everybody going to eat barbecue, especially if it's good; they're going to eat what we got, they'll be back.' Margie Sweatman died in 2003 and Bub in 2005; the family ran the house until 2011, when close family friends Lynn and Mark Behr bought it. In the Behr years the open concrete-block whole-hog pits gave way to Southern Pride smokers, and after COVID-19 the buffet ended. In 2026 the Patel family took over.

Whole hogs, oak- and hickory-smoked, pulled and dressed with the house mustard sauce, with vinegar and red sauces alongside. The plate is pork or ribs with hash and rice and sides; pork skins are fried when there are skins; banana pudding ends it. The old pits were open beds of concrete block over wood coals; the hogs now cook in Southern Pride smokers — *Tradition holds —* cabinet cookers fired by gas with wood for smoke.

Open Friday and Saturday, 11:30 a.m. to 8 p.m., at 1427 Eutaw Road, Holly Hill, per the restaurant's site on September 15, 2026; Destination BBQ's 2026 page lists Thursday to Sunday instead. New owners since 2026. Check before driving.

title: Tarheel Q
text:
A pork-shoulder pit on US 64 west of Lexington, Davidson County, cooking on brick masonry pits behind the building. Leon and Becky Simmons have owned it since December 2017. Smoke shows from the stacks when wood and pork go on together; the tray is the Piedmont tray, chopped shoulder with the dip, red slaw and hushpuppies, and a weekend pork-and-chicken special ran at $11.95 in April 2026. It carries True 'Cue certification, which turns on wood or charcoal being the only heat under the meat. It is not a stop on the Historic Barbecue Trail.

The founding year and the first owner are not on this disk; the business is older than the current owners, who took it over in December 2017. Leon and Becky Simmons had worked for the Lohrs about twenty-five years before that, a visiting writer recorded in 2019 — and Paul 'Speedy' Lohr had learned under Warner Stamey, so the line back to Lexington's teaching pit runs through two hands rather than one, and no source read states a Stamey line for Tarheel Q itself. In December 2018 the Simmonses opened a second house, Arcadia Q, on NC 150, taking over from Roger and Lisa Lohr; it closed in late August, and the manager Toni London reopened the room days later under her own name for it, Southern Fire Pit Barbecue and Home Cooking. The hardest thing in the record is older. In the summer of 2015 a Salmonella Typhimurium outbreak traced to Tarheel Q sickened 280 people across twenty-one North Carolina counties and six states and killed one; state health officials declared it over on July 8, 2015, and a wrongful death suit followed that August. The restaurant is open, and John Tanner ate there and wrote it up on April 18, 2026.

Pork shoulders cook on brick masonry pits out back, wood and meat going on together through the day; the smokestacks run hard in the afternoon. The meat is chopped and served the Piedmont way, with the dip — thin vinegar reddened with ketchup — and red slaw dressed from the same jug. Barbecue chicken shares the weekend special with the pork.

Open Monday to Saturday, closed Sunday, at 6835 West US Highway 64, Lexington. Last confirmed by a visiting writer's meal on April 18, 2026. The restaurant's own site refused the fetch, so the hours here come from a listing rather than from the house.

title: The Fiction Kitchen
text:
A vegetarian and vegan restaurant in Raleigh whose menu carries a Southern-style pulled barbecue made without pork, served with the slaw and the sides a Carolina plate expects. Carolina Morrison opened it in 2012 on money raised through Kickstarter, ran it downtown for a decade, and reopened it at Gateway Plaza after a move in 2023. It is in this catalogue because it is one of the ways barbecue is cooked and eaten in North Carolina now, and because it is one of the few places in either state a published list names as LGBTQ-owned.

Morrison crowdfunded the restaurant in 2012 and built it into a fixture of the state capital over more than a decade. When the downtown lease ended early in 2023 the restaurant ran as a pop-up while the new room was fitted, and reopened at Gateway Plaza alongside two other tenants. Cardinal & Pine named it in a list of eight LGBTQ-owned North Carolina businesses, introduced as 'the LGBTQ-owned bars and restaurants that deserve your patronage in June and beyond', and pointed readers at the pulled barbecue.

*Inference —* a vegan pulled barbecue in Raleigh is not a pit and does not claim to be one. It sits here for the same reason a gas cooker and a bottled dip sit here: this catalogue describes what is cooked and sold under the word, and lets the reader decide what to drive to.

The barbecue is the kitchen's own preparation rather than a pit product; the plate is built the way a Carolina plate is built, with slaw and sides. Check the menu before going, as it changes.

Open at Gateway Plaza, Raleigh. Hours are on the restaurant's own site; check before driving.

title: True BBQ
text:
A Black-owned pit on D Avenue in West Columbia, opened in 2010 by the brothers Ernest and Milton Zanders after years of selling from street corners and events. The wood-fired pits are visible from the front parking lot. Hash and rice is what the place is known for and what it sells by the pint and the quart alongside pulled pork, ribs, pork chops, brisket and chicken. It is open four days, Thursday to Saturday and no more. A second True BBQ trades in Myrtle Beach.

Ernest Zanders started the business and Milton, his brother, took over as head cook. They built it up selling barbecue on street corners and at events before they took a building in West Columbia in 2010; a 2026 local piece says fifteen years rather than sixteen, which is the sort of drift an anniversary line picks up. The hardest stretch is recent and it is in the record because Hannah Wade put it there for the Post and Courier's Free Times on June 25, 2022: a relative, Bryan Williams, died of a heart attack in early October 2021, and just before Christmas that year Milton's wife had her fourth stroke. The restaurant kept its doors. Wade also reported that national attention came when Eater named the hash the best in the state — the original Eater piece and its year are not on this disk, so that reaches this record at one remove. The Campaign for Real Barbecue certified the pits for burning wood rather than gas, and the directory EatOkra lists the business as Black-owned. The Free Times profile itself, which names both brothers and the head cook, never uses the phrase.

Wood-fired pits sit where a customer can see them from the parking lot. Pulled pork, ribs, pork chops, brisket and chicken come by the plate; the hash — the Midlands stew of pork cooked down — goes over white rice and also sells by the pint and the quart to take home. Cards and cash are both taken. There is no buffet.

Open Thursday to Saturday, 11 a.m. to 8 p.m., closed Sunday to Wednesday, at 1237 D Avenue, West Columbia. A second True BBQ trades in Myrtle Beach and is also on the wood-certified list.

title: Wilber's Barbecue
text:
A whole-hog pit on U.S. 70 east of Goldsboro, Wayne County, opened in 1962 by Wilberdean 'Wilber' Shirley and cooked the same way since: split hogs over oak coals in open pits in a cinder-block cookhouse behind a red-brick restaurant with knotty-pine walls and red-checked tablecloths. It closed in March 2019 over unpaid taxes and reopened in July 2020 under Goldpit Partners, a group of Goldsboro natives who bought it and restored the building. The pork is hand-chopped on oak blocks and seasoned with vinegar and spices; fried chicken, collards, fried okra and hushpuppies come alongside.

Wilber Shirley learned the trade at Griffin's Barbecue in Goldsboro and in 1962 bought the former Hill's Barbecue on Highway 70 and put his name on it. He told the authors of Holy Smoke that he cooked 'split halves of whole hogs over oak coals in closed pits,' and that the grease hitting the coals made the smoke flavor. Staff split and cut oak all year; on a Labor Day weekend the pits held up to 130 pigs, and the dining rooms seated more than 300. Shirley worked twelve or thirteen hours a day, six days a week, for more than forty years, with some ninety employees. In March 2019 the restaurant was shut for nonpayment of taxes. Willis B. Underwood III, an insurance salesman and lifelong regular, gathered other customers into Goldpit Partners, bought the place, kept the paneling and the tablecloths, and reopened it in July 2020 — curbside only at first, Wednesday to Sunday, with a shortened menu. 'I just didn't want to see the smoke die,' he told Our State. Shirley's son-in-law Dennis Monk took a management role, and Shirley, who turned ninety in June 2020, advised. He died in April 2021. Pitmaster Jackie Martin, at the pits nearly forty years, works from two in the afternoon to five or six in the morning.

Whole hogs cook all night over oak embers on open pits — nine hours by one account, twelve or more by another — then are hand-chopped on oak blocks and seasoned with vinegar and spices. The plate is barbecue with fried okra and slaw; the sandwich is barbecue and slaw; the 'Bone Box' is a tray-sized pig pickin', the meat left on the bone for pulling by hand. Sides run to hushpuppies, collards, cabbage, macaroni and cheese and fried chicken; the desserts — pecan pie, coconut and carrot cake, banana pudding, Wilber's cookies — are made in the house.

Open Wednesday to Saturday 11 to 7 and Sunday 11 to 3, at 4172 U.S. Highway 70 East, Goldsboro, per the restaurant's site in September 2026. Goldpit Partners own it.

title: Adam Scott
text:
The Rev. Adam Scott (1890–1983) was a Black cook and Holiness minister in Goldsboro who by his company's date went into the barbecue business in 1917, cooking whole hogs in his back yard and selling chopped pork with a vinegar sauce through the back door; between 1931 and 1933 the house on Brazil Street became a restaurant. He said the sauce came to him in a dream; his son A. Martel Scott patented it in 1946, and the family still bottles it. David Cecelski's account has him catering a barbecue for President Franklin Roosevelt at the White House in 1933.

Adam Scott was born in Goldsboro in 1890, the son of Joseph Scott, who was born in Oberlin, Ohio, and the grandson of Charles and Mary Scott, who had likely been enslaved in Johnston County. His first cooking job was at the Elberon Hotel in Atlantic City in 1911. Back home he catered barbecues from about the mid-1910s — 1917 is the company's founding date — and between 1931 and 1933 opened a restaurant at his home on Brazil Street: two hogs a week at first, cooked Friday night and sold Saturday through the back door, then four to seven hogs a day, with an enclosed porch for a dining room. His first customers were mostly white; he ran a separate cafe for Black customers elsewhere in town. The sauce, sugar-free and fat-free, took him three years to settle, and he said the precise ingredients were revealed to him in a dream. *Tradition holds —* in 1933 he catered barbecue in the White House Rose Garden for President Franklin Roosevelt; Cecelski tells it as fact, without a document behind it, and this record has seen none. He was a minister of the United Holy Church of America, by 1938 pastor of three churches and its general treasurer, and he closed on Sundays. In the 1940s he moved to Winston-Salem to cook for R.J. Reynolds and other private clients; his son Alvin Martel Scott, born 1913, took the Goldsboro business, patented Scott's Famous Barbecue Sauce in 1946, and by 1950 there were three Scott's around town, one run by Adam on the Raleigh road. He died in 1983 at ninety-three and is buried in Elmwood Cemetery under the word 'Elder'. The American Royal made him a legacy inductee of its Barbecue Hall of Fame in 2022.

Dead: 1983, at ninety-three, in Goldsboro. The restaurants closed after 2001; the sauce is made by his descendants and sold in eastern North Carolina groceries and online, and the American Royal's Barbecue Hall of Fame lists him as a 2022 legacy inductee.

title: Adrian Miller
text:
A Denver writer and lawyer, the 'Soul Food Scholar' of his own site, whose Black Smoke: African Americans and the United States of Barbecue (UNC Press, 2021) is the history of the Black cooks, pitmasters and restaurant owners behind American barbecue and of their absence from its legends. It won the James Beard Foundation's 2022 Media Award for Reference, History, and Scholarship, his second after Soul Food (2013; award 2014). A former special assistant to President Clinton, he directs the Colorado Council of Churches and is a certified barbecue judge.

Miller left the White House when the Clinton administration ended — he had been special assistant to the president and deputy director of the President's Initiative for One America — and between jobs took up food writing after reading John Egerton's Southern Food. Soul Food: The Surprising Story of an American Cuisine, One Plate at a Time (UNC Press, 2013) took him to 150 restaurants in 35 cities and won the 2014 Beard award for reference and scholarship; The President's Kitchen Cabinet (2017) named 150 African Americans who had cooked in the White House. Black Smoke came out in April 2021: essays on how barbecue was built on Black labor, enslaved cooks and then paid ones, and on how the menus, the television and the legends that followed left them out, with profiles of forgotten cooks and twenty-two recipes. The Beard Foundation gave it the Media Award for Reference, History, and Scholarship in Chicago on May 12, 2022. Miller sat on the board of the Southern Foodways Alliance from 2004 to 2010 and received its Ruth Fertel Keeper of the Flame award in 2018; he is a certified Kansas City Barbeque Society judge and was a consultant on Netflix's Chef's Table: BBQ. *Tradition holds —* the cooks at the eastern Carolina trenches were Black men for most of two centuries, enslaved and then paid; Black Smoke is the book this catalogue cites for that labor and its erasure.

Executive director of the Colorado Council of Churches since June 2013, in Denver. His 2025 book with Deborah Chang, Cooking to the President's Taste: Asian Heritage Chefs in White House History (White House Historical Association), followed Black Smoke; in 2026 he earned a James Beard Media Award nomination for feature reporting.

Adrian Miller to pitmaster: Black Smoke tells the history of the Black pitmasters the word was late to name.

Adrian Miller to Eastern North Carolina barbecue: his book is the record this catalogue cites for the Black cooks at the eastern pits and their erasure from the menus and legends.

title: Bob Garner
text:
A North Carolina television reporter and writer who has covered the state's barbecue since 1994, when he began short features on it for UNC-TV's magazine program North Carolina Now. His first book, North Carolina Barbecue: Flavored by Time (John F. Blair, 1996), toured the state's pits; a one-hour television special followed, and with it the name 'the barbecue man'. Bob Garner's Guide to North Carolina Barbecue (2002) and Bob Garner's Book of Barbecue (2012) came after. He writes restaurant pieces for Our State magazine and divides his time between Burlington and Raleigh.

Garner learned to cook over a fire in the Boy Scouts and, as a young married man, learned whole pigs from his wife's brothers — she was a farm girl from northeastern North Carolina — and he dates his conversion to the smell of the juices dripping onto the coals. The UNC-TV features began in 1994; the 1996 book went across the state pit by pit, and after the special based on it he was 'the barbecue man' on the state's public television. He was executive producer and host of the UNC-TV series Carolina Countryside, appeared on Food Network, the Travel Channel and Good Morning America, and made a special, A North Carolina Pig Pickin', with his youngest son, Everett. The 2002 Guide described a hundred restaurants from the mountains to the coast; the 2012 Book of Barbecue folded both earlier books into one, with recipes, tips and profiles of pitmasters — a pitmaster being the person who tends the pit. For Our State he wrote up Lexington Barbecue, Stamey's, B's, Wilber's, Short Sugar's and the Skylight Inn, among others; his 2012 Lexington Barbecue piece records the shoulders roasting ten hours over oak coals, fresh coals shovelled under the meat every half hour, and the crust, the 'brown', lifted off and saved for special orders. Asked by the blog BBQ Jew in 2011 whether wood was required, he answered that he preferred live coals but had eaten too much good barbecue cooked otherwise to be dogmatic, and named Smithfield's Chicken 'N Bar-B-Q and Ken's Grill in LaGrange among the gas-and-electric places he eats at. His five favourites that year were The Pit in Raleigh, Lexington Barbecue, Bridges in Shelby, Grady's in Dudley and B's in Greenville.

Still on the state's public television: he visited Sam Jones BBQ in Raleigh for North Carolina Weekend in August 2021 and named his places in a 2023 NC Weekend segment. Our State keeps his restaurant pieces online. No 2025 or 2026 activity was found for this record (checked September 15, 2026).

title: Bob Melton
text:
R. B. 'Bob' Melton (died 1958), a horse trader raised on a Nash County farm, cooked whole hogs for friends in an open pit on the Tar River at Rocky Mount, began selling barbecue there in 1922, and in 1924 built the shed that Wikipedia and UNC's North Carolina Miscellany call the state's first indoor, sit-down barbecue restaurant. He served finely chopped whole hog with a vinegar sauce, boiled potatoes, slaw, corn sticks, hushpuppies and Brunswick stew, and sent barbecue across the state by bus. Life magazine called him the King of Southern Barbecue in 1958, the year he died.

Melton had been cooking since he was twelve, the Miscellany says, and traded horses for a living. By 1922 he was selling barbecue from pits on the Tar River bank; two years later he built the restaurant, a large shed that grew room by room, and Rocky Mount took to it. In 1929 a plate with boiled potatoes cost 45 cents and a sandwich 15. The food writer Beth Tartan recorded the catering: 'When a woman who lives in Raleigh is having company, she calls up Bob Melton's and says: "Ride me a party."' The bus carried the barbecue and fixings. In later years he retired from the pits and greeted at the door; in 1958 Life magazine called him the King of Southern Barbecue, and he died that year. His partners W.B. Melton, T.O. Fulghum and Add Smith carried the restaurant on — by 1993 on gas and wood chips rather than charcoal, a change John Egerton noted with regret in Southern Food — until the Tar River put it under: Hurricane Fran's flood, then Hurricane Floyd in 1999, the seventy-fifth anniversary year, with water above the ceiling. The restaurant moved to a strip mall and closed in 2005. *Inference —* the vinegar-sauced whole hog on Melton's menu is the eastern style as it is still described, which is why the tradition dates its restaurant history from his shed.

Dead: 1958, at Rocky Mount. The restaurant outlived him by forty-seven years and closed in 2005; the riverside building is gone.

Bob Melton to Melton's Barbecue: the shed he built by the Tar River in 1924, the state's first sit-down barbecue restaurant.

Bob Melton to Eastern North Carolina barbecue: the style's first restaurant menu was his: whole hog, vinegar sauce, boiled potatoes, corn sticks.

Bob Melton to whole hog: the cut, small hogs of 80 to 90 pounds chopped fine, 'the consistency of chopped peanut butter'.

Bob Melton to Down East: he cooked whole hog in an open pit by the Tar River before he sold it.

title: Bum Dennis
text:
Latham Wade 'Bum' Dennis (June 12, 1937 – December 9, 2022) opened Bum's Restaurant in downtown Ayden in 1963 with his wife Shirley and cooked whole hogs over wood coals there for the rest of his working life, with a table of vegetables beside the barbecue that few eastern pits keep. He was of the Dennis family that counts Skilton Dennis's 1830 wagon as the start of the trade, and a kinsman of Pete Jones of the Skylight Inn. His son Larry, at the pit since he was nine, runs the restaurant.

His mother could not settle on a name for weeks, and people said a man without a name would grow up to be a bum; she named him Latham, and Bum stuck. He was born in Pitt County on June 12, 1937, finished Ayden High School in 1956 and joined the Navy that year. In 1963 he and Shirley opened the restaurant that carries his nickname; he cut the wood for the pits, opened for breakfast at 5:30 and closed at nine every day but Sunday. The family's barbecue, he and Larry told Rien Fertel for the Southern Foodways Alliance in December 2011, runs back through six generations of Dennises to the wagon of 1830. 'People have been cooking with wood for 500,000 years,' Larry told Our State. 'We just never stopped.' Bum's own account of the trade, as he gave it to Fertel: 'In this type restaurant business, what you got to do you got to love it and it's a way of life. You get up every morning and that's what you do.' When Daniel Wallace visited for Our State in 2014 Bum had retired but came in to serve breakfast around five, silver handlebar moustache and all, and Shirley sat at her table with her friend Hilda Worthington; Larry arrived at four to burn oak and pecan down to coals and did everything but kill the pig. Bum died at his home, Raven Hall, on December 9, 2022, at eighty-five.

Dead: December 9, 2022, at home in Ayden, aged eighty-five. Larry Dennis runs Bum's Restaurant at 566 East Third Street; the Dennis family's whole hog and vegetable table continue there.

title: Dennis Rogers
aliases: the oracle of the holy grub
text:
Dennis Rogers (October 10, 1942 – August 8, 2020), a News & Observer columnist for more than thirty years, raised in Wilson and an Army veteran, who wrote about small-town eastern North Carolina and its soldiers and, in barbecue, spoke for the east: whole hog with vinegar and pepper and nothing else. He called himself the 'oracle of the holy grub' in a long mock war of columns with Jerry Bledsoe of Greensboro over ketchup in the sauce. His columns were collected in Home Grown (1979), Second Harvest (1981), Crossroads (1984) and It's Bad News When the Bartender Cries (1988).

The war ran in print for decades, Rogers from Raleigh for the whole hog of Wilson, Greenville and Goldsboro, Bledsoe from Greensboro for the Piedmont's shoulder and red dip, each with a self-conferred title. Rogers's line, in one column, was that people who would put ketchup in the sauce they feed to innocent children are capable of most anything, and that the eastern purveyors of pure barbecue would not be roadkill for their western kin. When the 2005 bills over the Lexington Barbecue Festival's title brought the argument to the General Assembly, ABC's World News Tonight put the two men on air: Rogers said of the eastern sauce, 'It doesn't need anything else', and that somebody who would put ketchup on barbecue and give it to a child was capable of pretty much anything; Bledsoe answered that America loves ketchup and that Rogers had ruined any chance of the state being distinguished in its barbecue. In January 2007, after thirty years as a columnist, Rogers gave up the column at 64 for a new beat — the home front and the war's weight on eastern North Carolina, reported from Sanford — telling WRAL, 'I'm not dead yet!' and that he could not walk away with the soldiers' stories untold. He retired later that year, kept a website of his and his wife's RV travels, wrote a novel, acted in local theatre and rode motorcycles. He died in his sleep on August 8, 2020, at 77, after a long illness.

Died August 8, 2020, at 77. His column collections, published by the News & Observer between 1979 and 1988, survive in libraries and used bookshops; his family promised a barbecue in his memory once the pandemic allowed.

Dennis Rogers to Eastern North Carolina barbecue: the style he spoke for: the whole hog of Wilson, Greenville and Goldsboro.

title: Ed Mitchell
text:
Ed Mitchell (born 1948 or 1949) is a whole-hog pitmaster from Wilson who began cooking pigs behind his family's grocery store in the early 1990s, turned the store into Mitchell's Ribs, Chicken & Bar-B-Q, co-founded The Pit in Raleigh in 2007, and has argued for pasture-raised heritage hogs since the 2000s. The Southern Foodways Alliance recorded him in 2007; the American Royal put him in its Barbecue Hall of Fame in 2022. His book, Ed Mitchell's Barbeque, written with his son Ryan Mitchell and Zella Palmer, came out from Ecco in 2023.

He cooked his first pig at fourteen or fifteen, at a family gathering in Wilson where the men had passed the moonshine and fallen asleep; his grandfather woke to a cooked hog, asked who had done it, and poured him a glass. 'Growing up, all our lives on any celebration... it had to be accompanied by barbecue,' he told Amy Evans of the Southern Foodways Alliance in September 2007. After his father died — in 1991, by his own account in WALTER magazine; 1990 by the Alliance's — his mother asked for barbecue, he cooked a pig behind Mitchell's Grocery, customers asked for it, and by 1992 the store was Mitchell's Ribs, Chicken & Bar-B-Q. From 2002 he headlined New York's Big Apple Barbecue Block Party each year; in 2003 he began cooking free-range pigs. The Wilson restaurant closed in 2004 or 2005 amid a state tax case. In 2007 he opened The Pit in Raleigh with a real-estate developer and left it in May 2011; Que, in Durham's American Tobacco campus, ran less than a year from 2014. He cooks hot and fast, a bank of coals around the hog, 500 degrees falling to 250, with a rub of salt, black and red pepper and onion powder and a sauce of cider vinegar, crushed red pepper, salt, sugar and black pepper; he wants the whole hog because a sandwich needs shoulder, ham and belly together. With Ryan he has worked with True Made Foods on sauces since 2018 and announced The Preserve, a Raleigh restaurant with LM Restaurants, in 2019. 'I barbeque not because I love hoisting 150-pound hogs over my shoulders, but because I want to keep the tradition of my African American ancestors alive,' he wrote in 2023.

Living. He has not run a restaurant since Que closed in 2015; he ships barbecue from a smokehouse in Micro, Johnston County, through Goldbelly, sells sauces with True Made Foods, and works with his son Ryan. The Preserve, announced for Raleigh in 2019, had not opened as of July 2024.

Ed Mitchell to Eastern North Carolina barbecue: the style he cooks and speaks for: whole hog over wood, a vinegar-and-pepper sauce, from Wilson.

title: Elliott Moss
text:
Elliott Moss is a chef and whole-hog pitmaster from Florence, in the Pee Dee of South Carolina, who grew up watching his grandfather smoke hogs, moved to Asheville in 2007 to open The Admiral, and in August 2015 opened Buxton Hall Barbecue there with Meherwan Irani's Chai Pani group, bringing wood-cooked whole hog and South Carolina hash to the mountains. He left Buxton Hall in July 2022; it closed in November 2023. In 2025 he and his wife Jennifer opened Elliott's Barbecue Lounge inside Seminar Brewing in Florence, which Southern Living named the South's best new barbecue restaurant for 2026.

Moss, 'a son of the low country of Florence, S.C.' in the Asheville chamber's words, learned smoke from his grandfather's whole hogs. He came to Asheville in 2007 to help open The Admiral, whose cooking put him on the James Beard Foundation's semifinalist list for Best Chef: Southeast in 2013. A first deal for a barbecue place fell through; Meherwan Irani of Chai Pani reached out within forty-eight hours, and Buxton Hall Barbecue opened in August 2015 in a 1930s roller rink on Banks Avenue on the South Slope: pasture-raised hogs from western North Carolina farms smoked over wood from ten at night to eight in the morning, hash and rice made from the pig's organs and trimmings, a fried chicken sandwich, pies on lard crusts. 'When I'm in here, I cut all the lights off except this little lamp,' he told Our State in 2016, 'and it's just like I'm outside, cooking a pig, standing in front of the burn barrel.' Bon Appétit put the restaurant ninth among the country's new restaurants in 2016 and named the sandwich its fried chicken sandwich of the year; the Beard Foundation listed him as a semifinalist again in 2017. He left Buxton Hall in July 2022, opened two West Asheville restaurants, Regina's and Little Louie's, in the summer of 2023 and left them within six weeks, and in March 2024 announced on Instagram that after seventeen years he and Jennifer were leaving Asheville to keep cooking whole hog somewhere else. The somewhere was home: Elliott's Barbecue Lounge opened inside Seminar Brewing at 551 West Lucas Street, Florence, in the spring of 2025 — pasture-raised whole hog 'cooked Pee Dee burn barrel-style', in Robert Moss's words for Southern Living, with collards, hash and rice and a buttered, grilled bun.

Living. He and Jennifer Moss run Elliott's Barbecue Lounge in Florence, South Carolina, open since spring 2025; Southern Living ranked it 36th among the South's fifty barbecue restaurants in 2025 and its best new barbecue restaurant in 2026.

Elliott Moss to Buxton Hall Barbecue: the Asheville restaurant he opened in 2015 and left in July 2022, fifteen months before it closed.

Elliott Moss to whole hog: the cut he has cooked from Asheville to Florence: pasture-raised, overnight, over wood.

Elliott Moss to hash and rice: he put South Carolina hash on an Asheville plate and asked what other pits did with those parts of the pig.

Elliott Moss to burn barrel: the barrel he described standing in front of in the dark at Buxton Hall, and the method named for his Florence hog.

title: Jerry Bledsoe
aliases: the world's leading, foremost barbecue authority
text:
Jerry Carroll Bledsoe (July 14, 1941 – December 31, 2025), a Greensboro newspaper columnist and author, born in Danville, Virginia and raised in Thomasville, who wrote for the Greensboro Daily News, later the News & Record, for twenty-three years and became a true-crime writer with Bitter Blood (1988), a number-one New York Times bestseller. In barbecue he was Lexington's man: the self-styled 'world's leading, foremost barbecue authority' in a decades-long mock war of columns with Dennis Rogers of the Raleigh News & Observer over ketchup in the sauce.

Bledsoe delivered the Thomasville Tribune at nine, served three years in the Army after high school, and worked at papers in Kannapolis and Charlotte before the Greensboro Daily News, where his columns of the 1970s and 1980s made his name; he was later a contributing editor at Esquire. The barbecue war was one of those columns' running jokes: Bledsoe for the Piedmont's chopped shoulder with its red dip, Rogers for the east's whole hog and clear vinegar, each claiming a title — Bledsoe the world's leading, foremost barbecue authority, Rogers the oracle of the holy grub. Bledsoe wrote that Rogers had ruined any chance of the state being distinguished in its barbecue; Rogers wrote that people who would put ketchup in sauce fed to innocent children were capable of most anything. The joke outlived the columns. When bills to make the Lexington Barbecue Festival the state's official barbecue festival divided the General Assembly in 2005, ABC's World News Tonight came to Greensboro, and Bledsoe gave them 'America loves ketchup' and called vinegar an astringent thing that ruins the taste buds. In 1996 he wrote 'Slaw Crazy', an essay holding that barbecue is always served with slaw in North Carolina and always has been. Bitter Blood, on the Lynch–Newsom–Klenner murders of 1984–85, was followed by Blood Games (1991), Before He Wakes (1994) and Death Sentence (1998); he founded Down Home Press to publish books about North Carolina, and in later years wrote for the Rhino Times, including a long series on the Greensboro police. He died on December 31, 2025, at 84.

Died December 31, 2025, at 84. The Rhino Times, where he last wrote, marked his death the next day; The Assembly's tribute, 'A Hell of a Writer', ran on January 12, 2026.

Jerry Bledsoe to Lexington-style barbecue: the style he championed in print from Greensboro.

Jerry Bledsoe to Lexington dip: 'America loves ketchup': his defence of the red sauce, to ABC in 2005.

Jerry Bledsoe to Eastern North Carolina barbecue: the other side; he wrote that Rogers had ruined the state's chances of distinction in barbecue.

Jerry Bledsoe to Dennis Rogers: his opponent for decades, the Raleigh columnist and 'oracle of the holy grub'.

Jerry Bledsoe to Lexington Barbecue Festival: whose fight over an official title in 2005–07 brought the columnists' war back into the news.

Jerry Bledsoe to slaw: his 1996 essay 'Slaw Crazy': barbecue is always served with slaw in North Carolina, and always has been.

title: Jess Swicegood
text:
Jess Swicegood ran a barbecue stand a few yards from Sid Weaver's tent by the Lexington courthouse in the 1920s, taught Warner Stamey pit cooking alongside Weaver, and sold Stamey the business in 1938 — for $300, by Robert Moss's account — when Stamey came back from Shelby and renamed it Stamey's. Through that sale the Swicegood stand is the ancestor of Stamey's in Greensboro and, through Stamey's pupil Wayne Monk, of Lexington Barbecue. He is spelled Jess and Jesse in the sources, and no dates of birth or death are on record here.

The sources agree on the order: Weaver's tent in 1919, Swicegood's stand beside it within the decade, then the two of them together. Moss's history, as the Barbecue Bros relay it, says Weaver 'later teamed up with Jess Swicegood and those two men perfected Lexington-style barbecue and helped spread the technique across the Piedmont of North Carolina'. Stamey's history and the American Royal's 2020 bio put Swicegood first in the pair that taught Warner Stamey when he was a high-school boy boarding with his sister, and the Southern Foodways Alliance's note on Stamey's calls the two 'pit-cooking pioneers'. In 1938 Stamey moved back to Lexington, bought out his mentor and renamed the operation Stamey's; Wayne Monk worked under Stamey in downtown Lexington for several years before he opened Lexington Barbecue in 1962. *Inference —* a stand that changed hands for $300 was a tent or a shed, not a building; the first permanent barbecue restaurant in town was Alton Beck's, in 1938, the same year.

Dead, on no date this record can name. The Lexington stand he sold in 1938 carried the Stamey name into the 1950s; the Stamey family's restaurants are in Greensboro, and Lexington Barbecue, opened by Stamey's pupil Wayne Monk in 1962, cooks a mile or two from where his stand stood.

Jess Swicegood to Lexington-style barbecue: the style's second name after Weaver's: his stand and Weaver's tent are where it was worked out.

Jess Swicegood to Sid Weaver: the tent his stand stood beside; Weaver was first, by a few years.

Jess Swicegood to Warner Stamey: his pupil, who bought him out in 1938 and put his own name over the door.

Jess Swicegood to Stamey's Barbecue: the name on his old stand from 1938, carried to Greensboro in 1953.

Jess Swicegood to Lexington Barbecue: Wayne Monk trained at the stand Stamey bought from him; the pit is his grandchild.

title: Jim Early
text:
James Howard Early Jr. (1939–2021), a Winston-Salem lawyer and cook who founded the North Carolina Barbecue Society in 2006 and led it until his death. His self-published guide, The Best Tar Heel Barbecue: Manteo to Murphy (2002), came out of a search through all hundred counties for pits still cooking pork over wood coals; the society's Historic Barbecue Trail is that list under rules he wrote — wood or charcoal on grates, a house sauce, fifteen years' cooking, no more than two stops in a town.

Early was born in Henderson, grew up in Winston-Salem, took his bachelor's and law degrees at Wake Forest, and practiced law for years before barbecue took over. The search behind the book covered 22,000 miles and about 4,000 hours across the state's hundred counties; he found fewer than thirty restaurants still cooking over wood coals, six of them Black-owned and three owned by women. The society he founded in 2006 set itself to preserve the state's barbecue history and, in its own words, to secure North Carolina's place as the Barbecue Capital of the World; the less formal motto was to cook and eat barbecue as often as possible, preferably among friends. It ran two-day cooking boot camps three times a year — Tanglewood Park in May, Sugar Mountain in July, Castle Hayne in September — teaching whole hog, pork butt, ribs, chicken, brisket and Early's pimento cheese; CNN put the school on a 2012 list of ten cooking schools worldwide, the only one in the United States. He published a monthly magazine, Pigtails, and a second book, Jim Early's Reflections: The Memories and Recipes of a Southern Cook. In September 2017 he closed his law office to run the society full time. He took no side in the east–west argument, and told Our State in 2016 that '99.99 percent of places' now cooked with gas or electricity; the Trail bypasses all of them. He died on June 21, 2021, at 82, weeks after a stroke.

Died June 21, 2021. The society's two web addresses did not resolve when this project checked on September 15, 2026; its Facebook page carries on as a forum, and the Trail's list is reprinted by Our State and others. His 2002 guidebook is held by libraries and sold used.

title: Joe Bessinger
text:
Joseph Jacob 'Big Joe' Bessinger, a farmer from Orangeburg County, traded the family cow, a mule and fifty dollars for a cafe in Holly Hill and opened it in 1939 serving pork with a mustard-based sauce — the Golden Secret, his family calls it, worked out with the Sweatman family on shared German roots. Five of his sons opened barbecue restaurants on it: Maurice and Joe Jr. at West Columbia in 1953, Melvin and Thomas in Charleston from 1955, and, by two accounts, Robert. Some name him the inventor of South Carolina's mustard sauce; the evidence names no one.

Big Joe was one of fourteen children of Mack Bessinger and raised eleven of his own — Maurice was the eighth — on a farm near Orangeburg with his wife Genora. In 1939 he gave up farming, sold a cow, and opened the Holly Hill Café; Melvin, ten, was taught to make the sauce, and Maurice, nine, went to work in the restaurant. Robert Moss's 2011 history in the Charleston City Paper puts the move to Holly Hill in the 1940s; the family's own dates say 1939. After the war Melvin's Army pay went into a second Holly Hill restaurant, Eat At Joe's, in 1946, where Thomas started cooking at fourteen. Then the sons scattered with the recipe. Maurice and Joe Jr. opened Maurice's Piggie Park at West Columbia in 1953; Melvin closed Eat At Joe's in 1955 and moved to Charleston with Thomas, where Thomas opened his own place in 1960 and the brothers opened Piggy Park Drive-In on Savannah Highway in 1961, renamed Bessinger's in 1971; Melvin crossed the Cooper River to Mount Pleasant in 1982. Moss writes that three sons — Melvin, Thomas and J.D. — opened Piggy Park drive-ins around Charleston; West Of lists Thomas, Melvin, Maurice, J.D., Woodrow and Robert as owners of competing restaurants, with Robert's Bar B Que in North Charleston. The businesses were separate: when Maurice raised Confederate flags in 2000 the Charleston brothers were reported as independent concerns, 'sans the politics'. His grandson David Bessinger told the Southern Foodways Alliance in 2012: 'It's just in our blood.' *Inference —* the 'Joe Jr.' of Wikipedia and Maurice's obituary and the 'Joe David' or 'J.D.' of the Charleston writers are one son.

Dead; no source read for this record gives the year. The sauce he served in 1939 is on the tables of Maurice's Piggie Park, Bessinger's and Melvin's, and bottled by Maurice's heirs as Southern Gold.

Joe Bessinger to Maurice Bessinger: his eighth child, who started in the Holly Hill kitchen at nine and took the sauce to the supermarkets.

Joe Bessinger to Maurice's Piggie Park BBQ: the West Columbia chain of his sons Maurice and Joe Jr., from 1953; his recipe is on its label.

Joe Bessinger to Sweatman's Bar-B-Que: the Holly Hill family he worked the mustard sauce out with; their pit opened in 1977.

Joe Bessinger to mustard-based barbecue sauce: his Golden Secret of 1939, the earliest name attached to the Midlands sauce.

Joe Bessinger to South Carolina mustard barbecue: the style his sons carried from Orangeburg County to Columbia and the coast.

Joe Bessinger to Carolina Gold: the name his son Maurice sold the family sauce under.

Joe Bessinger to Dutch Fork: the German-settled country whose roots the family and the Sweatmans credit the sauce to.

title: John Shelton Reed
text:
A sociologist of the American South, born 1942, who taught at the University of North Carolina at Chapel Hill from 1969 until 2000 and retired as William Rand Kenan Jr. Professor. With his wife Dale Volberg Reed and William McKinney he wrote Holy Smoke: The Big Book of North Carolina Barbecue (UNC Press, 2008); alone, Barbecue: A Savor the South Cookbook (2016) and On Barbecue (2021). In 2013 he and Dan Levine founded the Campaign for Real Barbecue, which certifies restaurants that cook their local style over wood alone. He lives in Chapel Hill.

Reed came to barbecue after a career on the South itself: MIT, a Columbia doctorate in 1971, the Center for the Study of the American South, which he helped found, and the quarterly Southern Cultures, which he co-edited. Holy Smoke, written with Dale and William McKinney, gives North Carolina's two styles their history, their recipes and their people, and in it the Reeds lamented how much of the state's barbecue was cooked on gas. In 2011 he wrote the introduction to the Southern Foodways Alliance's North Carolina barbecue oral histories, opening with George Washington's diary for May 27, 1769 — a barbecue in Alexandria and a night away — and the point that until the early twentieth century barbecue was for harvests, fundraisers and rallies, never home cooking. The campaign came two years later: a retired professor 'with time on my hands', in his words, and Dan Levine, 'Porky LeSwine' of the blog BBQJew, set out to find and list the places still cooking entirely with wood, Levine as Chief Smoke Detector, Reed as Éminence Grease. On April 23, 2014, in the Raleigh News & Observer, they offered a prize — an apron, later a cap as well — to anyone who could name the statute, regulation or official that forbade a restaurant to cook with wood, since owners so often said the health department had made them switch; two years on nobody had claimed it, and Daniel Vaughn in Texas and Robert Moss in South Carolina had found the same in their states. Reed allows that gas is cheaper, easier and more consistent. Dale Volberg Reed died in 2018. On Barbecue (University of Tennessee Press, 2021) collects his essays, reviews and op-eds on the subject, and in 2023 the governor gave him the Order of the Long Leaf Pine.

Retired, in Chapel Hill; co-founder and Éminence Grease of the campaign, whose site listed about seventy North Carolina restaurants in January 2018 and remains active in 2026. His own site lists The Ramos Gin Fizz (LSU Press, 2025) and a revised 1001 Things Everyone Should Know About the South, due in 2027.

title: Lake High
text:
Lake E. High Jr. of Columbia, a wine judge and, in his own account, a born critic, who founded the South Carolina Barbeque Association with the psychologist Walter Rolandi in 2004 to train judges and promote the state's barbecue, and wrote its history: A History of South Carolina Barbeque (The History Press, 2013). His account gives South Carolina all four of the barbecue sauces he counts — vinegar-and-pepper, mustard, light tomato and heavy tomato — each with a region and a date, and the association publishes them as a map.

High was 74 when South Carolina Living profiled him in September 2015 as 'the guru of 'que': a master judge of the association he founded, certified as well by the Kansas City Barbeque Society, the Memphis Barbecue Network and the American Wine Society, who said he had probably eaten more barbeque than anyone in the state. When he and Rolandi founded the association the state had two cook-offs a year; by 2015 it had thirty-seven, more per head than any other state, and the association had certified more than 800 judges. His book, published in June 2013 while he was the association's president, runs from the 1500s — Native Americans cooking pork on frames after the Spanish brought the pig, and, in his telling, Europeans learning barbecue at the sixteenth-century colony of Santa Elena at what is now Port Royal — through the 1920s, when the craft settled into restaurants, to the cook-off era. The sauce account, posted on the association's site over his name as founder, runs in order of age: vinegar-and-pepper first, hundreds of years old; mustard from the German settlers of the 1730s to 1750s, distinct to South Carolina; light tomato, vinegar-and-pepper with ketchup, from around 1900; heavy tomato, the newest, of the last sixty years. Only South Carolina, he holds, has all four. Robert Moss, another South Carolinian, counts two: sweet mustard and spicy vinegar. In 2015 High told the magazine, 'Barbeque is a noun, not a verb. It's something Southerners eat, not do.' In August 2018 the co-founders named Jim Wellman of Lexington president and Don Adkins of Seneca vice president.

The association is active in 2026 with a full cook-off calendar; its site names High as founder and 'a professional wine judge' and lists no current officers. His book remains in print with The History Press. No later interview with High was found for this record (checked September 15, 2026).

Lake High to South Carolina Barbeque Association: co-founded it in 2004 with Walter Rolandi; its president when his book appeared in 2013; its historian.

title: Maurice Bessinger
text:
Lloyd Maurice Bessinger Sr. (July 14, 1930 – February 22, 2014) opened Maurice's Piggie Park, a drive-in, in West Columbia in 1953 with his brother Joe Jr., built it into a chain, and bottled his father's mustard sauce as Carolina Gold for supermarkets nationwide. He refused Black customers until the suit that became Newman v. Piggie Park Enterprises (1968), ran for the legislature in 1964 and for governor in 1974, and raised the Confederate flag over his restaurants on July 1, 2000, the day it came off the State House dome. His children took the last flags down in 2013.

Bessinger was born on the family farm near Orangeburg on July 14, 1930, the eighth of eleven children of Joseph Jacob and Genora Thomas Bessinger, and started cooking at nine in his father's Holly Hill restaurant in 1939. He served in the Army in the Korean War, came home in 1952, and with Joe Jr. opened the first Piggie Park drive-in in West Columbia in 1953; there were four by 1964. That year Anne Newman, the wife of a Black minister, was refused entry, and Matthew J. Perry filed a class action under Title II of the Civil Rights Act of 1964; Bessinger answered that his religious beliefs compelled him to oppose integration. The district court held the Act reached his sandwich shop but not the drive-ins; the Fourth Circuit reversed; and in 1968 the Supreme Court held 8–0 in Newman v. Piggie Park Enterprises, 390 U.S. 400, that a plaintiff who wins such an injunction ordinarily recovers attorney's fees. He chaired George Wallace's 1964 campaign in the state, lost a House race that year by about a hundred votes, and took 2.5 percent in the 1974 Democratic primary for governor. By 1999 the sauce — mustard, brown sugar, soy sauce and vinegar, sold as Carolina Gold — had made his the largest barbecue business in the country. On July 1, 2000 he raised Confederate flags over them and called the flag a Christian symbol; his restaurants distributed a tract arguing that slavery is not inherently evil; Bi-Lo, Food Lion, Harris Teeter, Kroger, Piggly Wiggly, Publix, Sam's Club, Wal-Mart and Winn-Dixie dropped the sauce, and his $50 million suit against them failed at the state Supreme Court in 2007. He published an autobiography, Defending My Heritage, in 2001. He died on February 22, 2014, at eighty-three.

Dead: February 22, 2014, West Columbia, aged eighty-three. His sons Lloyd and Paul, his daughter Debbie and his grandchildren run Maurice's Piggie Park; the flags came down by 2013 and the sauce is sold as Southern Gold.

Maurice Bessinger to South Carolina mustard barbecue: the style he made a national product and the name that carries its court case.

Maurice Bessinger to political barbecue: he ran for the House in 1964 and for governor in 1974, and chaired George Wallace's state campaign.

title: Pete Jones
text:
Walter B. 'Pete' Jones (died 2006) opened the Skylight Inn in Ayden, Pitt County, in the summer of 1947 — at seventeen by his family's count, eighteen by Wikipedia's — and cooked whole hogs over wood coals there for nearly sixty years. He learned the trade at his uncle Emmitt Dennis's City Cafe, counted his barbecue back to a Dennis ancestor's wagon, and put a copy of the U.S. Capitol dome on his roof after National Geographic called the place the barbecue capital of the world. The James Beard Foundation made the restaurant an America's Classic in 2003.

Pete Jones told Bob Garner that he sat in school as far back as the fifth or sixth grade and daydreamed about having his own barbecue place. He got it at seventeen: he built the Skylight while working for his uncle Emmitt Dennis at the City Cafe, where he cooked whole hog, and opened on July 8, 1947. He gave the place beer and a jukebox to set it apart from Ayden's other barbecue stands, thought about adding a dance hall, and ran late with rowdy crowds until the town's 7 pm curfew ended the late nights. The cooking did not change: whole hogs, heads on, over coals burned down from oak and hickory in fireplaces beside the pits, chopped with the crisp skin through the meat. He could not read or write, Kathleen Purvis records in Garden & Gun. In 1979 a National Geographic article called the restaurant the barbecue capital of the world; the dome went up in 1984, silver-painted wood, so that people could find the place — 'A place like this don't need any sign,' he told Garner. By the restaurant's own account he cooked at a congressional event attended by President Reagan and Vice President Bush in 1982, and in 2003 the James Beard Foundation named the Skylight an America's Classic. His line on fuel — 'If it's not cooked with wood, it's not barbecue' — is the one the Campaign for Real Barbecue prints on its wood page. He died in February 2006; his son Bruce, his nephew Jeff and his grandson Sam kept the pits.

Dead. Pete Jones died in February 2006 by the restaurant's account; Wikipedia gives the year, and Bob Garner's 2012 profile prints 2005. The Skylight Inn is run by his son Bruce, his nephew Jeff and his grandson Sam Jones.

Pete Jones to Skylight Inn BBQ: the pit he opened in 1947 and ran until his death; the dome on its roof was his answer to National Geographic.

Pete Jones to whole hog: the only cut he cooked, heads on, the skin chopped into the meat.

Pete Jones to pitmaster: he ran the Skylight's pits for most of sixty years before the word was in the dictionaries.

title: Rien Fertel
text:
A New Orleans writer and historian — a Tulane doctorate in history, 2013 — who recorded the Southern Foodways Alliance's barbecue oral histories in North Carolina in 2011 and South Carolina in 2012, then spent five years following the whole-hog pitmasters of Tennessee and the Carolinas for The One True Barbecue (Touchstone, 2016): part travelogue, part memoir, about the cooks who fire, flip and chop 200-pound pigs in smoke-filled pit houses, from Rodney Scott of Hemingway and Sam Jones of Ayden to Ricky Parker of Lexington, Tennessee.

Fertel's first bite of whole hog was at Siler's Old Time BBQ in Henderson, Tennessee, in 2008, and the cook who held his attention was Ricky Parker of Scott's-Parker's in Lexington, Tennessee, who died of liver disease at fifty-one; Fertel went back to see Parker's sons at the pits. For the Southern Foodways Alliance he recorded the North Carolina set in November and December 2011 — Chip Stamey in Greensboro, Sonny Conrad at the Barbecue Center, David Wilson at Short Sugar's, Brandon Cook at Cook's, Debbie Holt at Clyde Cooper's, the Parker's crew in Wilson, Samuel Jones at the Skylight Inn on November 29, Bum and Larry Dennis in Ayden, Stephen and Gerri Grady in Dudley — and the South Carolina set in June 2012: Douglas Oliver at Sweatman's, Tony Kittrell at Dukes, Jay Allen at Midway, Jackie Hite, Russell Cooper at Cooper's Country Store, the Browns in Kingstree, David Bessinger at Melvin's, and Rodney Scott in Hemingway, where the pits were turning eight to ten hogs a night. The One True Barbecue follows the whole-hog line from those pits: Scott, who went on to a Charleston restaurant and a James Beard award; Jones, the Skylight's grandson; Keith 'Pop' Ward, who tends Wilber's pits through the night in Goldsboro; Oliver at Sweatman's; three places named Scott's; and a new generation, Tyson Ho at Arrogant Swine in Brooklyn and Elliott Moss at Buxton Hall in Asheville. Robert Moss reviewed it for Southern Living, and John Shelton Reed wrote that it 'should be read by anyone who thinks barbecue is about sticky red sauce'. Fertel holds that most barbecue writing is hyperbole.

Visiting professor of history at Tulane and book critic for the Times-Picayune/Advocate; his fourth book, Brown Pelican (LSU Press, 2022), left barbecue behind. He calls New Orleans home and lives part of the time in a century-old church in St. Martinville, Louisiana.

title: Robert F. Moss
text:
A food writer and historian in Charleston — a Furman graduate with a doctorate in English from the University of South Carolina — who is contributing barbecue editor for Southern Living and was restaurant critic for the Post and Courier. Barbecue: The History of an American Institution (University of Alabama Press, 2010; revised and expanded 2020) is a documentary history of the subject built from newspapers, letters, diaries and travel narratives; Barbecue Lover's the Carolinas (2015) is his guide to both states. He counts South Carolina's sauces as two, mustard and vinegar, where the state's association counts four.

Moss's history reads the colonial and early-republic barbecue out of the record: whole hogs cooked as a ritual in the British colonies by the eighteenth century, the communal feast spreading from Virginia into the Carolinas in the mid-1700s, the political barbecue as an institution of the new republic, and the restaurants of the twentieth century. The second edition, published October 6, 2020, added colonial material, profiles of early restaurateurs and African American cooks, and a final chapter, 'The Second Golden Age of Barbecue', on the wood-cooked places that opened across the country in the 2010s. On South Carolina hash he went to the newspapers — 'rich hash' at a barbecue at Matthews' Spring, in the Abbeville Press and Banner of 1854 — and traced the name to haslet, the old word for the viscera: the head, liver and lights the whole hog left behind. When the Post and Courier reported in 2020 that hash was fading, he answered in Southern Living that new places were putting it on their menus, and used the recently closed Cannon's in Little Mountain as his example of the Midlands' mustard-yellow kind. He has tested Summerville's claim to sweet tea (2013) and told the story of hushpuppies (2023). When John Shelton Reed's campaign asked in 2014 for any regulation that forbade wood cooking in North Carolina, Moss looked in South Carolina and reported in the Columbia Free Times that there was none there either. He reviewed Rien Fertel's The One True Barbecue for Southern Living in 2016. His other books are Southern Spirits (2016), The Lost Southern Chefs (University of Georgia Press, 2022) and The Roffignac (LSU Press, 2024).

Based in Charleston; contributing barbecue editor for Southern Living and a frequent contributor to Charleston Magazine, Garden & Gun, Serious Eats and The Local Palate. His site, robertfmoss.com, carries his features on hash, hushpuppies and the revised history.

title: Rodney Scott
text:
Rodney Scott (born November 1, 1971) is a whole-hog pitmaster from Hemingway, in the Pee Dee of South Carolina, who cooked his first pig at eleven at his parents' store, took the business over in 2011, and in February 2017 opened Rodney Scott's Whole Hog BBQ in Charleston with Nick Pihakis. In 2018 the James Beard Foundation named him Best Chef: Southeast, the second pitmaster to win a Beard chef award. His book with Lolis Eric Elie, Rodney Scott's World of BBQ, came out in 2021. Every Rodney Scott's location closed in May 2026; he cooks pop-ups as Pitmaster Scott.

Roosevelt and Ella Scott moved from Philadelphia to the Pee Dee in 1972 with their infant son, farmed and raised hogs near Nesmith, and opened a gas station and variety store on the Hemingway highway; the barbecue began as a weekend hog. Rodney cooked his first at eleven and was full time at seventeen, when the store cooked four to six a week. 'My whole life has been barbecue,' he told Rien Fertel for the Southern Foodways Alliance in June 2012, by which time the pits held eight to ten hogs a night. John T. Edge had profiled the store in 2009, and Nick Pihakis of the Jim 'N Nick's chain, a customer, told him he was undercharging. On November 27, 2013 the wooden cookhouse burned; Scott took his hogs on the road — the Bar-B-Que in Exile Tour, staged with Pihakis's Fatback Collective — to rebuild in metal. After a quarrel with his father in 2016 he left Hemingway, and in February 2017 he and Pihakis opened Rodney Scott's Whole Hog BBQ in a former fried-chicken house on upper King Street, Charleston. In May 2018 the James Beard Foundation gave him its Best Chef: Southeast award; the Chef's Table: BBQ episode about him in 2020 set the restaurant's sales records three days running. Birmingham followed in 2019, Atlanta and a second Alabama town in 2021, and the book with Lolis Eric Elie the same year. On May 3, 2026 the King Street restaurant closed 'until further notice' amid suits and liens against Pihakis Restaurant Group, and the other locations with it; in June he cooked at Munkle Brewing under a new name, Pitmaster Scott. Roosevelt Scott died in 2020 and Ella in 2023; the Hemingway store reopened in May 2024 under her brother Sam Wilson and Rodney's son Dominic.

Living. His Charleston restaurant has been closed since May 3, 2026; he cooks pop-ups in Charleston as Pitmaster Scott, has said that reopening there is his first priority, and was announced in July 2026 as a headliner of the Pair'd Margaret River Region Festival in Western Australia.

title: Sam Jones
text:
Samuel 'Sam' Jones is the grandson of Pete Jones and a third-generation pitmaster of the Skylight Inn in Ayden, where he sold chopped pork as a child. With Michael Letchworth he opened Sam Jones BBQ in Winterville on November 10, 2015, and a second restaurant in Raleigh in February 2021. His book with Daniel Vaughn, Whole Hog BBQ: The Gospel of Carolina Barbecue (2019), writes the family method down. He was a James Beard semifinalist for Best Chef: Southeast in 2018, and Sam Jones BBQ holds a Michelin Bib Gourmand from the first Michelin Guide American South (2025).

At four, Sam Jones told a reporter that he wanted to be a trash man and the Prince of Barbecue; his father Bruce joked about putting hog grease in his milk bottle. He grew up in the Skylight Inn, quit it at fifteen, and came back after a college paper on barbecue told him what his work was. He described the return to Rien Fertel of the Southern Foodways Alliance in November 2011 as a flag-bearer's job, keeping the standard up on the field: 'I don't want our style of barbecue to be one of them things where you read about it in the history books. I want it to be one of them things where you can go get it and taste it and see it.' Southern Living put him among ten Southern pitmasters in 2012. A cooking event in Charleston in 2013 turned him toward a place of his own; in 2014 he and Michael Letchworth signed for a loan, and Sam Jones BBQ opened in Winterville on November 10, 2015, with a longer menu than the Skylight's — ribs, turkey, chicken, banana pudding — around the same wood-cooked hog. The James Beard Foundation listed him as a semifinalist for Best Chef: Southeast in 2018; Whole Hog BBQ, written with Daniel Vaughn of Texas Monthly, came out from Ten Speed Press in 2019. The Raleigh restaurant opened in a former garage on West Lenoir Street in February 2021. He has served as Ayden's fire chief, lives on the farm he grew up on with his wife Sarah and two daughters, and told Garden & Gun in 2019: 'Today I'm proud to be from Ayden, North Carolina.'

Living. He runs Sam Jones BBQ in Winterville and Raleigh with Michael Letchworth and the Skylight Inn with his father Bruce and Jeff Jones; a stall in Raleigh's Morgan Street Food Hall is planned for the end of 2026, and Sam Jones BBQ holds a Bib Gourmand from the first Michelin Guide American South, November 2025.
