title: Sid Weaver
text:
Sid Weaver sold barbecue from a tent across from the Davidson County courthouse in Lexington from 1919 — cooked in the alley behind, sold to people on their way to court — and is the first name in every account of Lexington-style barbecue. Jess Swicegood set up beside him within the decade; the two taught Warner Stamey, and Weaver's hand Alton Beck built the town's first permanent barbecue restaurant in 1938. What is known of him is the tent, the date, the pupils and the sauce that came out of those stands: vinegar and pepper with ketchup, the Piedmont's dip.

Our State's Jeremy Markovich calls him Lexington barbecue's Abraham, 'first cooking up his barbecue in the alley outside and selling it from a tent to people heading over to the old courthouse in 1919'. Robert Moss's history, as the Barbecue Bros summarize it, has him first and Jess Swicegood joining him later, the two working out the shoulder-and-dip style and spreading it across the Piedmont. Stamey's own history puts both men 'selling pork out of tents across from the courthouse' when Warner Stamey, boarding with his sister for high school in the late 1920s, came to learn from them; the American Royal's 2020 citation for Stamey says they taught him everything there was to know about pit cooking. Alton Beck, who had worked for Weaver, opened the first bricks-and-mortar barbecue restaurant in town on West Center Street in 1938, rebuilt it in 1949, and retired after thirty-one years; the wood pits found behind a wall of Lexington's city hall in 2015 are thought to be his. *Tradition holds —* Weaver later built a small cafe of his own near the square. No birth date, death date or photograph of Weaver is in any source read for this record.

Dead, on no date this record can name. The stands are gone; Lexington counted more than twenty barbecue restaurants in 2003, and the Lexington Barbecue Festival has closed Main Street each October since 1984, a few blocks from where the tent stood.

title: Skilton Dennis
text:
Skilton Dennis is the ancestor the Dennis and Jones families of Ayden name as the start of barbecue for sale in North Carolina: by their account he sold smoked hog meat and cornbread from a wagon in 1830, and Otter Dennis, of the same family, founded the town. The 1830 is painted on the Skylight Inn's billboard as one of its four tenets and was recorded from Bum and Larry Dennis by the Southern Foodways Alliance; Bob Garner's 2012 profile of Pete Jones puts the covered wagon in the mid-1800s. No document has been produced.

The claim is the families'. Pete Jones, who opened the Skylight Inn in 1947, learned the trade from the Dennis side of his family and liked to say that barbecue ran in his blood; his great-great-grandfather, he told Bob Garner, sold barbecue from a covered wagon in Ayden in the mid-1800s. The billboard outside the Skylight sets the tradition at 1830. Bum Dennis and his son Larry gave Rien Fertel the same story for the Southern Foodways Alliance in December 2011: Skilton Dennis selling smoked hog meat and cornbread from a wagon in 1830, and Otter Dennis founding the 'enigmatically-named' town. John Tanner's post on Bum's death counts the wagon-seller as a great-great-great-grandfather, 'add 4 or 5 more greats' — the arithmetic of a family story, not of a record. The Alliance's page for Sam Jones says the Dennis clan's history shows them as the first in North Carolina to serve pit barbecue publicly. *Inference —* Ayden was incorporated only in 1891, around a railroad depot on William Henry Harris's farm; a wagon in 1830 would have served the farms and churches of what became southern Pitt County, not a town. *Inference —* this project has seen no census, deed or grave for a Skilton Dennis selling barbecue in 1830; the date is held here as the families' and nothing more.

Dead, on no date this record can name. The two families that tell his story cook whole hog in Ayden: the Joneses at the Skylight Inn, opened 1947, and the Dennises at Bum's Restaurant, opened 1963, a few blocks apart.

title: Warner Stamey
text:
Charles Warner Stamey (born 1911), the youngest of eleven children, learned pit-cooking as a high-school boarder in Lexington from Jess Swicegood and Sid Weaver at their tents across from the courthouse, sold barbecue in Shelby through the 1930s, came back in 1938 to buy Swicegood's stand and rename it Stamey's, and in 1953 opened the Greensboro drive-in his family runs. His restaurant credits him with putting hushpuppies beside barbecue in North Carolina. Wayne Monk, Red Bridges and his brother-in-law Alston Bridges learned under him; the American Royal made him a legacy inductee of its Barbecue Hall of Fame in 2020.

Stamey was born in 1911 — in Lincoln County, by Cleveland County's local history — and moved to Lexington to live with his older sister while he attended high school. There he hooked up with Jess Swicegood and Sid Weaver, who were selling pork out of tents across from the courthouse, and they taught him pit cooking. With a diploma and $350 he went to Shelby and sold barbecue to growing crowds; he married Mary Linda Bridges in 1933, and the county history has Stamey's Barbecue at 230 South Washington Street in 1937. Her brother Alston Bridges learned smoking from him and managed his Log Cabin Barbecue in Lexington for two and a half years; Red Bridges, no relation, learned from him too and opened at the same Washington Street address about 1949. In 1938 Stamey sold the Shelby operation, went back to Lexington, bought Swicegood's and put his own name on it — for $300, Robert Moss's history says. Wayne Monk worked under him there for several years before opening Lexington Barbecue in 1962. In 1953 Stamey opened a drive-in on High Point Road in Greensboro, his sixth restaurant by the American Royal's count, with call-in service; four years later he handed it to his son Charles, and Charles's brother Keith joined in 1970. The hushpuppy — the fried cornmeal fritter of the fish camps — went onto the barbecue tray under him: Keith said his father picked the idea up from a friend's fish camp, the Friendly Road Inn in Greensboro, and the restaurant's history says he introduced it to North Carolina barbecue diners. Chip Stamey, his grandson, left another career to take the Greensboro house in 1993, and told the Southern Foodways Alliance in 2011 that his rule is to keep everything the same.

Dead; his death year is not confirmed by any source this record cites. The American Royal inducted him as a 2020 legacy member of its Barbecue Hall of Fame, and the fourth generation of Stameys runs the two Greensboro restaurants.

title: Wayne Monk
text:
Wayne Monk opened Lexington Barbecue beside U.S. 29/70 in Lexington, Davidson County, in 1962, at twenty-six, after years as a carhop and then a pit hand under Warner Stamey, and he owns it with his son Rick. The pit cooks pork shoulders over oak and hickory coals and serves them with the dip, the Piedmont's thin red vinegar sauce; locals call it the Honeymonk, from his name and his early partner Sonny Hunneycutt's. He cooked for the heads of government at the 1983 economic summit in Williamsburg, and the James Beard Foundation named the restaurant an America's Classic in 2003.

Monk was a teenage carhop at a Lexington barbecue place, worked for Holland Tussey, and spent several years working directly under Warner Stamey at Stamey's in downtown Lexington — Stamey had bought Jess Swicegood's stand there in 1938 — so that his own pit stands two teachers from the courthouse tents of 1919. At twenty-six, in 1962, he bought a roadside parcel beside U.S. Highway 29/70 that had been Tussey's, built onto the small cafe on it, and opened Lexington Barbecue #1 with Sonny Hunneycutt; the partner left, and the joined name, Honeymonk, stayed on the town's tongue. In 1983 a politically connected local attorney asked whether he would cook for President Reagan, and he served barbecue to the heads of government at that year's economic summit in Williamsburg, Virginia, Margaret Thatcher and François Mitterrand among them. The James Beard Foundation made the restaurant an America's Classic in 2003, the same year as the Skylight Inn in Ayden. Garden & Gun found three generations at the pits in 2015: Wayne; Rick, who started at thirteen and is pitmaster, bookkeeper or janitor as the day requires; and Rick's son Nathan, who began in the kitchen at about sixteen. 'It's not a job. It's a way of life,' Rick said. The American Royal inducted Wayne Monk into its Barbecue Hall of Fame on September 14, 2019 — he 'set the standard that practically defines North Carolina barbecue', the citation said — and the new North Carolina Bar-B-Q Hall of Fame inducted him at Burlington on March 1, 2024.

Living: no death notice was found in the sources read for this record (September 2026). The restaurant's site names him as founder and lists Rick Monk as owner; Lexington Barbecue is open Tuesday to Saturday at 100 Smokehouse Lane, Lexington.

title: Wilber Shirley
text:
Wilberdean 'Wilber' Shirley (1930–2021) learned barbecue at Griffin's in Goldsboro, bought the former Hill's Barbecue on U.S. 70 east of town in 1962 and put his name on it, and cooked split whole hogs over oak coals there for more than forty years. Wilber's fed presidents, governors and senators and, on a holiday weekend, up to 130 pigs. It closed in March 2019 over unpaid taxes; a group of customers bought it and reopened it in July 2020, while he lived. He died on April 5, 2021, at ninety.

'I went to work at a place called Griffin's Barbecue... That's how I first learned to cook it,' he told John Shelton Reed and Dale Volberg Reed for Holy Smoke. In 1962 — July 24, 1961, by WRAL's obituary — he bought Hill's Barbecue on Highway 70 and renamed it. 'Split halves of whole hogs over oak coals in closed pits,' he said of his method: 'That grease hitting those coals makes the smoked flavor. You can't spray it on there, paint it on there, put it on there.' The pits ran overnight, from about ten at night to ten in the morning; in season the place cooked 100 to 125 pigs a week, and Our State counts 130 on a Labor Day weekend and dining rooms for more than 300. 'I work seven days a week,' he said. 'Some weeks I come in eight days a week.' A waitress had been there more than thirty years, a cook since before he bought the place. Presidents George H.W. Bush and Bill Clinton, Governors Terry Sanford and Jim Hunt and Senator Jesse Helms ate there. The restaurant was shut in March 2019 for nonpayment of taxes. Willis B. Underwood III, an insurance salesman who had eaten there all his life, gathered other regulars into Goldpit Partners, bought it, and reopened it in July 2020 for curbside orders: 'I just didn't want to see the smoke die.' Shirley, a longtime member of First Free Will Baptist Church in Goldsboro, died at a retirement community in Kinston on April 5, 2021. The Campaign for Real Barbecue quotes him on its wood page: cooking whole hogs over hardwood coals overnight 'is not easy or cheap, but it is the right way, and something we as a community take a lot of pride in'.

Dead: April 5, 2021, at Kinston, aged ninety. Wilber's Barbecue is open under Goldpit Partners at 4172 U.S. Highway 70 East, Goldsboro, cooking whole hogs over oak; his portrait hangs in the dining room.

title: Campaign for Real Barbecue
text:
A campaign, founded in 2013 by the sociologist and barbecue writer John Shelton Reed and the blogger Dan Levine, that certifies restaurants which cook the barbecue style traditional to their area and rely solely on wood for heat, and gives them a certificate and a decal. It began in North Carolina — about seventy places certified by January 2018 — and has regional 'smoke detectors' for South Carolina, Kentucky, Georgia, Alabama and the Virginia–Washington region under a True 'Cue USA program. Its three stated goals are to celebrate wood-cooking, to honor the places that keep it, and to teach eaters the difference between wood-cooked barbecue and what it calls 'faux 'cue'.

Reed and his wife Dale wrote Holy Smoke (2008) and in it lamented how much North Carolina barbecue was cooked on gas. In 2013 he and Dan Levine — 'Porky LeSwine' of the blog BBQJew, the campaign's 'Chief Smoke Detector' to Reed's 'Eminence Grease' — founded the campaign to find and list the places still cooking entirely with wood or charcoal. On April 23, 2014, in the Raleigh News & Observer, they issued the True 'Cue Challenge: a prize to anyone who could name the statute, regulation or official that forbade a restaurant to cook with wood, since owners so often said the health department had made them switch. Two years on, Reed wrote, no one had claimed it, and Daniel Vaughn in Texas and Robert Moss in South Carolina had found the same in their states; one state official mentioned environmental concerns, and Reed allows that gas and electricity are cheaper, easier and more consistent. The campaign draws its line with care: it certifies only wood-for-heat, but has 'no beef' with cooks who use gas or electricity for ignition and temperature control so long as wood smoke reaches the meat, and reserves 'faux 'cue' for meat cooked with no smoke at all. Its Pledge is for those who hold that if it is not cooked with wood it is not barbecue. Its wood page quotes a federal meat-labeling rule defining barbecued meat as cooked by the direct action of dry heat from burning hardwood, and gathers witnesses from Pete Jones to Rodney Scott, Wilber Shirley and Aaron Franklin, with Alton Brown's joke that gas lets you control the heat, 'but you're going to go to hell'.

A restaurant is certified once the campaign confirms it cooks its region's style with wood as the only heat; it receives a certificate and a window decal and is listed on truecue.org by state. Eaters sign the Pledge; the site sells merchandise; regional smoke detectors handle the other states.

Active; the site lists certified places by state and runs the True 'Cue USA program. About seventy North Carolina restaurants held certificates in January 2018; no current count is posted.

title: North Carolina Barbecue Society
text:
A non-profit founded in 2006 in Winston-Salem by Jim Early, a lawyer and cook, to promote North Carolina's barbecue culture and, in its own words, to secure the state's place as the Barbecue Capital of the World. Its lasting work is the Historic Barbecue Trail: a route of about two dozen restaurants, some 700 miles end to end, admitted only if the meat cooks on grates over pits with wood or charcoal, the owners make their own sauce, the pits have run fifteen consecutive years, and no town has more than two. Early wrote the guidebook, The Best Tar Heel Barbecue: Manteo to Murphy, and the society ran two-day cooking boot camps three times a year.

Jim Early had a law office in Winston-Salem and a self-published guide to every barbecue place from Manteo to Murphy when he founded the society in 2006; he closed the law office in September 2017 to run it full time. Searching the state's hundred counties for pits still cooking pork slowly over wood coals, he found fewer than thirty, and the Trail is that list under its rules — Wilber's in Goldsboro, the Skylight Inn in Ayden, B's in Greenville, Allen & Son near Chapel Hill, Stamey's in Greensboro, Short Sugar's in Reidsville, the Bar-B-Q Center in Lexington and Red Bridges in Shelby among them. Wikipedia's article counts twenty-five establishments in twenty-one locales; WRAL in 2021 counted twenty. The boot camps ran at Tanglewood Park in May, Sugar Mountain in July and Castle Hayne in September, teaching whole hog, butts, ribs, chicken, brisket and Early's pimento cheese; CNN put the school on a 2012 list of ten cooking schools worldwide, the only one in the United States. The society's motto, in its less formal version, was to cook and eat barbecue as often as possible, preferably among friends, and to promote the state as the Cradle of 'Cue. It took no side in the east-west argument but recorded it: the 2006 bills that would have made Lexington's festival official, and their failure. Early died on June 21, 2021, at 82, after a stroke. In March 2024 John Tanner's barbecue blog reported that the society 'appears to have withered considerably' since, with Ben Thompson keeping its Facebook page as a forum, and that a separate group of pitmasters, Chuck Hursey among them, had started a North Carolina Barbecue Hall of Fame. Neither ncbbqsociety.com nor ncbbqsociety.org resolved when this project checked on September 15, 2026.

Membership is by dues, and the sponsors are mostly barbecue restaurants. The Trail is followed by car with the map or Early's book; a stop earns its place by its pit, its sauce and its years, not its fame. The boot camps were two-day schools open to anyone who paid.

Status unknown as of September 2026: the founder is dead, both web addresses are down, and the Facebook page carries on as a forum. The Trail's list is reprinted by Our State and others.

title: South Carolina Barbeque Association
text:
A judging body and booster founded in 2004 by Lake E. High Jr., a wine judge, and Walter Rolandi, a psychologist, 'to train the best BBQ judges in the world and to preserve and promote the unique nature of South Carolina Barbecue'. It runs judging seminars in Columbia that turn eaters into certified judges — more than 800 by 2015 — sanctions cook-offs across the state, eight of them listed between September 12 and October 24, 2026, and keeps a points championship for the teams. Its account of the state's barbecue is Lake High's: South Carolina as the home of all four sauces — mustard, vinegar-pepper, light tomato and heavy tomato — mapped by region.

When High and Rolandi founded the association, South Carolina had two barbecue cook-offs a year; by 2015 it had thirty-seven, more per head than any other state, and the association's judge-training system was being copied elsewhere. High is its historian as well as its founder. His A History of South Carolina Barbeque (2013) and the association's history page hold that Europeans first learned barbecue from the Native Americans at Santa Elena, the sixteenth-century colony in what is now South Carolina; that vinegar-and-pepper is the original sauce, hundreds of years old; that mustard came with the German settlers of the 1730s to 1750s; that light tomato is vinegar-and-pepper with ketchup added, from around 1900; and that heavy tomato is the newest, of the last sixty years. Only South Carolina, the page says, is home to all four. Robert Moss, another South Carolinian, counts two — sweet mustard and spicy vinegar — and the state's Wikipedia article gives both counts, along with the four-or-five-region division first drawn by Charles Kovacik and John Winberry in South Carolina: A Geography (1987). High's line, to South Carolina Living in 2015: 'Barbeque is a noun, not a verb. It's something Southerners eat, not do.' In August 2018 the association named Jim Wellman of Lexington president and Don Adkins of Seneca vice president.

Judges train at an annual seminar in Columbia and advance through levels; a team enters a sanctioned cook-off, is scored by certified judges, and earns points toward the SCBA Championship. The cook-offs are run by towns, churches, scout troops and civic groups — Troop 61's competition at Pomaria and the Hopeful Hog Festival at Lancaster were on the 2026 list — with the association supplying the judging.

Active. The 2026 calendar lists cook-offs from Mauldin to Barnwell through October 24, the judge seminars are held in Columbia each year, and the association posts from PO Box 115, Blythewood.

title: Southern Foodways Alliance
text:
An institute of the Center for the Study of Southern Culture at the University of Mississippi, founded in 1999 and directed since then by John T. Edge, that documents the food of the South: oral histories, films, writing, awards and events, funded by about 800 members. For the Carolinas its work is the Southern BBQ Trail, an oral-history project begun in February 2011 across nine states, whose North Carolina set includes the Skylight Inn, Parker's, Grady's, B's, Bum's, Stamey's, Short Sugar's, Red Bridges, Cook's, Clyde Cooper's, the Barbecue Center and Ed Mitchell, and whose South Carolina set holds eight interviews: Sweatman's, Scott's, Midway, Jackie Hite's, Dukes, Cooper's Country Store, Brown's and Melvin's. Each interview is a transcript with audio, free online.

The SFA came out of a 1999 meeting called by the journalist John Egerton, with John Martin Taylor among the founders, and John T. Edge has directed it since. It gives the Ruth Fertel Keeper of the Flame award with the Fertel Foundation and the John Egerton Prize, and Corby Kummer in the Atlantic called it 'this country's most intellectually engaged (and probably most engaging) food society'. The Southern BBQ Trail went up on February 22, 2011, and the Carolina sets on April 25 of that year. The North Carolina introduction, by John Shelton Reed, opens on the point that barbecue was never home cooking — too much trouble — and until the early twentieth century was reserved for harvests, fundraisers and political rallies; the South Carolina introduction opens: 'Like everything in South Carolina, we cook barbeque cantankerously.' Rien Fertel interviewed Samuel Jones at the Skylight Inn for the project and went on to write The One True Barbecue (2016) about the whole-hog pitmasters; John and Dale Reed drew on the North Carolina interviews for Holy Smoke; in 2009 Edge himself profiled the Scott family of Hemingway. Rodney Scott's interview sits in the South Carolina set beside Bub Sweatman's and Jackie Hite's; Chip Stamey's, Sonny Conrad's of the Barbecue Center and Ed Mitchell's are in the North Carolina set.

Interviews are recorded by SFA oral historians, transcribed and posted with audio, a portrait and a short biography, under the project and the state; the site filters by state and by tag. Membership funds the work; the awards and events run alongside it.

Active at the University of Mississippi; the Carolina barbecue interviews remain online under the Southern BBQ Trail.

title: South Carolina Festival of Discovery
aliases: Greenwood BBQ and Blues Festival of Discovery
text:
A three-day barbecue-and-blues festival in Uptown Greenwood each July — Thursday to Saturday of the second weekend; July 9 to 11 in 2026 — hosted by the Uptown Greenwood Development Corporation. Its cook-off is sanctioned by the Kansas City Barbeque Society, the national competition body, and is billed as a South Carolina state championship with a Black Kettle hash competition beside it; the barbecue vendors fill the Main Street parking lot between Court and Seaboard avenues, and the Blues Cruise puts bands in restaurants and venues around the uptown into the night. The organizers billed 2026 as the twenty-fifth anniversary; press accounts date the first festival to 2000.

Greenwood is a county seat in the Old 96 District on the Piedmont side of the state, and the festival is its downtown corporation's summer event rather than a pit's or a church's. The competition is Kansas City's — KCBS judges, KCBS categories, and a date the society sets rather than the town — laid over a South Carolina crowd, with a hash kettle competition to keep the state's own dish in view and the public sampling and voting on Carolina hash, and a blues program, the Blues Cruise, run under the artistic direction of the bluesman Shrimp City Slim. *Inference —* it is the Upstate's festival in the way Lexington's is the Piedmont's, and the sanctioned cook-off, not a local pit, is its center.

Thursday evening through Saturday: teams cook overnight in the Main Street lot for KCBS judging; the public samples barbecue and hash and votes; the Blues Cruise runs at venues around the uptown from late morning to midnight.

Held July 9–11, 2026; the 2027 dates are July 8–10. Contact is the Uptown Greenwood office at 104 Main Street.

title: fundraiser barbecue
text:
The plate sale: a church, a volunteer fire department, a Ruritan club or a scout troop cooks pork — a whole hog or a stack of butts — and sells it by the plate on a Saturday to pay for a roof, a truck or a mission. In eastern North Carolina the plate is barbecue or barbecue chicken with slaw and bread; Back Swamp Volunteer Fire Department in Richlands sold pork or chicken plates for $10 on April 18, 2026, from 11 a.m. until the food ran out. In South Carolina the same money is often raised on hash: the Highway 34 Volunteer Fire Department outside Ninety Six cooks it in cast-iron pots and sells it by the quart to neighbors who read the notice in the paper and phone in an order.

The fundraiser is where the whole-hog barbecue of the colonial Carolinas went when the plantation left: barbecues for fundraisers, church gatherings and political rallies are on record in the Carolina colonies, and John Shelton Reed's line is that until the early twentieth century barbecue was reserved for harvests, fundraisers and rallies. Mallard Creek Presbyterian Church in Charlotte is the form at full scale: begun in 1929 to pay $89.50 of Sunday-school debt, it grew to 14,600 pounds of pork and 20,000 eaters by 2015 and ran ninety-three years on volunteers taking a week off work. Hillsborough's Hog Day began in 1983 as a chamber-of-commerce fundraiser and since 2014 has been the Orange County Optimist Club's, its proceeds to children's programs — Future Farmers of America, the Hillsborough 4-H and a church youth group in 2025. On the coast the volunteer fire departments own the Saturday calendar: Back Swamp's annual barbecue and raffle at the station on Catherine Lake Road is one of dozens. South Carolina's version is the hash sale: fire stations, churches and civic groups stew pork, liver and onions in iron kettles over a wood fire and sell hash by the quart; at Highway 34 VFD, Melvin Fouchee learned the recipe from Ike Berry and the department buys its equipment on the proceeds. The South Carolina Barbeque Association's cook-off calendar is much the same list under another name — Troop 61's competition at Pomaria, the Hopeful Hog Festival at Lancaster.

A Saturday, 11 a.m. until sold out. The pigs or butts cook overnight on a rented or department-owned cooker; volunteers make slaw and stew; plates are packed to go — barbecue, slaw, bread, sometimes potatoes or beans — and sold at a window or a drive-through for a set price, with a raffle beside the table. Hash is ordered by the quart in advance and picked up; Mallard Creek sold by the plate, sandwich, pound and quart.

Continuous. Back Swamp VFD's plate was $10 in April 2026; Mallard Creek's was $15 in October 2024 and is no more; the SCBA calendar listed eight cook-offs for the autumn of 2026.

title: Hillsborough Hog Day
text:
A two-day barbecue festival and cook-off at River Park in downtown Hillsborough, Orange County, held since 1983 — the oldest continuing barbecue festival in North Carolina, by the Daily Tar Heel's account — and run since 2014 by the Orange County Optimist Club as a fundraiser for children's programs. A Friday evening opens it; Saturday brings the cook-off, live music, a car show, a fun run and the Pigs on Parade. In 2019 the count was 27 cooking teams, more than 100 vendors and a collective three tons of barbecue; the 2025 festival, September 13 and 14, came two months after Tropical Storm Chantal flooded the Eno riverfront and lost its 5K to the water.

Hog Day was the Hillsborough/Orange County Chamber of Commerce's festival for thirty-one years, drawing up to 35,000 people as the county's largest festival, until the chamber's board voted in January 2014 that it was not 'an adequate use of resources' for the chamber's mission. Craig Lloyd, the chamber's former executive director and a Hog Day hand since he won a design contest more than thirty years ago, gathered the volunteers into a new Orange County Optimist Club and put the festival on that June 20 and 21 at the Efland Ruritan Club under the theme 'Bringing Home the Bacon', because it was '100% developed and produced by local volunteers'; after two years in Efland it came home to River Park in 2016, the thirty-fourth festival, now in September. Hurricane Florence pushed 2018 to a make-up weekend on November 2 and 3; the pandemic cancelled 2020 and 2021; 2022 was the return. The cook-off carries a North Carolina Pork Council contest alongside the festival's own — James Catlett and Brittany Thompson took the two first places in 2025 — and the proceeds go to youth: Future Farmers of America, the Hillsborough 4-H club and a Holy Family Catholic Church youth group in 2025. Lloyd, now the club's president, is the 'Godfather of Hog Day' on the festival's site; Al Hartkopf chairs it.

Friday night music at River Park; Saturday from 10 to 5, the cook-off teams sell plates and sandwiches, vendors line the park, and the car show, the fun run along the Eno and the Pigs on Parade fill the day. Proceeds go to the Optimist Club's charities.

Open. The 2025 festival ran September 13 and 14 at River Park; the organizer is the Orange County Optimist Club, at hogday.org.

title: Lexington Barbecue Festival
text:
A one-day street festival on Main Street in uptown Lexington, Davidson County, each October since 1984, built on the town's pork-shoulder barbecue: up to twenty area restaurants cook and sell, several blocks close to traffic, and hundreds of other vendors sell crafts and fudge around them. Wikipedia's article says it draws as many as 200,000 people; the first festival drew 30,000 and 3,000 pounds of barbecue, and by 1994 the count was over 100,000 and 11,000 pounds. Since 2007 it holds a title from the General Assembly — Official Food Festival of the Piedmont Triad Region of the State of North Carolina. The 2026 festival is planned for October 24.

The idea came from Joe Sink Jr., publisher of Lexington's daily, The Dispatch, in 1983; the bank BB&T hired Kay Saintsing to study whether a festival could work, the study found Lexington already a weekend destination for barbecue, and the first festival was held on October 27, 1984. In 1995 the North Carolina Championship Pork Cook-Off joined it, so that Piedmont crowds could watch eastern whole-hog cooks at work in the capital of the shoulder. NC By Train sets up a temporary stop a block away for the day, served by Amtrak's Carolinian and Piedmont. The 2020 festival went virtual. The politics is the story the festival tells about itself under the heading 'Pork-Barrel Politics'. In 2006 House Bill 21 and Senate Bill 47 would have made it the official barbecue festival of North Carolina; the east read that as making Lexington the official barbecue, nearly half the state prefers the other kind, and neither bill passed. In 2007 House Bill 433 gave it the Piedmont Triad title instead — a designation that names a region and so leaves the east out of the question. Jerry Bledsoe, the 'world's leading, foremost barbecue authority' by his own account, said that Dennis Rogers of the Raleigh News & Observer, the self-styled 'oracle of the holy grub', had ruined the state's chances of distinction in barbecue. Eastern vendors turn up on Main Street each year; the article calls the controversy mild, and sometimes not so mild.

One Saturday in October: Main Street closes, the restaurants set up on the street, and the plate is Lexington's — chopped or sliced shoulder with red slaw and hush puppies, the dip on the meat. Around it are four hundred or more vendors, live music on up to five stages, lumberjack games and street performers. Visitors come by car and, for the day, by train.

Held each October; the 2026 date is October 24. It is listed in 1,000 Places to See in the USA & Canada Before You Die, and in 2012 U.S. News & World Report ranked Lexington fourth among the country's barbecue cities.

title: Mallard Creek Barbecue
text:
The one-day church barbecue of Mallard Creek Presbyterian Church in northeast Charlotte, held on the fourth Thursday of October from 1929 to 2024 and retired in 2025 after ninety-three editions. It sold hickory-smoked chopped pork, Brunswick stew and the church's own slaw by the plate, sandwich, pound and quart — dine-in, drive-through and carry-out; a plate was $15 and a sandwich $7 in 2024 — and it was one of North Carolina's best-known political stops: a rope line in the parking field where candidates for every office from vice-president to dog catcher worked the crowd in the last weeks before an election.

In late 1928 or early 1929 the pastor, Dr. W. H. Frazer, and his brother Ben held a men's meeting with a barbecued pig; the church owed money on a Sunday-school building, and that October the deacons cooked three or four pigs and a goat to pay it. The first year cleared $89.50, enough to retire the debt with a little over. The fourth Thursday was chosen to keep clear of Halloween. The hogs cooked in ditches with hickory coals shoved underneath; by 1979, the fiftieth year, the church cooked 4,800 pounds of meat, 2,000 pounds of slaw and 250 gallons of Brunswick stew, and in the 1980s metal cookers replaced the dirt pits, with some meat still cooked on open pits inside a screened building. By 2015 Our State counted 20,000 people, 14,600 pounds of pork, 2,500 gallons of stew and two tons of slaw, and Tommy Oehler told the magazine the whole hogs were gone: 'Now we just use the butt', dressed with an eastern-style vinegar sauce. The politics grew with the plates. Dan Quayle came seeking the 2000 Republican nomination; Charlotte mayors Richard Vinroot, Pat McCrory and Jennifer Roberts worked the line; Deborah Ross came running for the Senate. No speeches: candidates set up booths, hand out fliers and court voters along a rope in the parking area. On October 1, 2025, the church announced with 'heavy hearts' that the barbecue was retired. The leaders of its four main components had stepped aside, co-chair Charles Kimrey said, and the church could not find volunteers able to take eight to ten days off work for the preparation; each prep day took about a hundred volunteers and the day itself about three hundred. 'Everything seems to have a life cycle and for the Mallard Creek BBQ, that life cycle is 93 years.'

For a week before, volunteers cooked pork butts — hickory-smoked, then chopped, cooled and seasoned — and stewed Brunswick stew in quantity; on the Thursday the church served from morning, dine-in, drive-through and walk-up, by plate (barbecue, stew, applesauce, slaw and bread), sandwich, pound or quart. Proceeds went to the church's missions and to the building debt the barbecue was founded to retire.

Retired. The last barbecue was held Thursday, October 24, 2024; the church announced the end on October 1, 2025, three weeks before the date it would have kept.

title: pig pickin'
text:
A party at which a whole hog is cooked for the crowd and the crowd eats it off the pig — picked by hand from the split carcass, or chopped on a block beside it. A barrow, a castrated male, or a gilt of about 80 to 120 pounds dressed weight is split and laid on a large charcoal or propane cooker for four to eight hours, under the direction of the host and whoever is helping; the meat is basted or dressed in the local sauce and served with slaw, hush puppies, baked beans, Brunswick stew or, in South Carolina, hash and rice. It is the eastern Carolinas' form of the wedding, the homecoming, the tailgate, the political rally and the fire-department fundraiser.

The whole-hog feast is older than the name. Communal barbecues of whole pigs spread from Virginia into the Carolinas in the mid-1700s and fed church gatherings, fundraisers and political rallies; George Washington wrote of attending a barbecue on August 4, 1769. The pig pickin' is that feast on a trailer cooker. Its year is the church's and the college's: 'dinner on the grounds', family reunions, Thanksgiving and Christmas, graduations and weddings, and the tailgate — East Carolina University in Greenville has run a pig pickin' contest, the Pigskin Pig-Out, since 1985. Politics keeps it: local parties and candidates still use a pig pickin' to draw a crowd, and in 1983 Rufus Edmisten, running for governor of North Carolina, was overheard saying he had eaten enough barbecue, would eat no more, and was taking his stand. Ed Mitchell's first hog was a family pickin' in Wilson: at fourteen or fifteen he tended the fire after the men, having passed the moonshine, fell asleep, and his grandfather woke to a cooked pig and poured him a glass. Kingstree, in the Pee Dee, holds a Pig Pickin' Festival each fall for the vinegar-based barbecue of Williamsburg County; seventy teams competed in 2010. The name is the one thing the article is sure of: the meat is picked off the hog by the guests, and the gathering is named for it.

The host borrows or rents a cooker, buys a dressed hog, and lights charcoal or gas the morning of, or the night before for a big pig. The hog goes on meat-side down and is flipped once when it stops dripping fat; some cooks wipe the ash from the skin with paper towels or a whisk broom before the flip so the cracklings come out clean. The baste is the region's: mustard in the South Carolina Midlands, vinegar and red pepper flakes in eastern North Carolina, a ketchup base in the west. When the meat falls from the bone the pig is carried to the table and the guests pick, or a cook chops it at the block; sweet tea, beer and soft drinks alongside.

Held year-round in a mild climate; cookers are rented by the weekend across the Coastal Plain, the tailgate pickin' is a college-football fixture, and Kingstree's festival and ECU's Pigskin Pig-Out put it on a calendar.

Root: pig + pickin' (picking): the guests pick the meat off the cooked hog with their hands, and the gathering takes its name from the act.

pig pickin' to pig cooker: the trailer cooker it is cooked on, charcoal or propane.

title: political barbecue
text:
The free feed a candidate or a party puts on to draw a crowd: a whole hog, or these days a pile of pork butts, cooked for whoever comes, with speeches or a rope line attached. It is as old as the republic in the Carolinas — the communal whole-hog barbecue fed political rallies in the colonial Carolinas and Virginia — and it has two living forms. In South Carolina the Galivants Ferry Stump Meeting in Horry County has gathered Democratic candidates on the Holliday family's land every second spring since 1880, descended from Wade Hampton's 1876 appearance there. In North Carolina the Mallard Creek church barbecue in Charlotte was the candidates' October stop from 1929 to 2024.

Robert Moss finds the political barbecue an institution of the early republic and the whole-hog rally established in the colonies by the 1700s. In North Carolina the tradition runs through the pig pickin' — local parties and politicians still use one to draw people to meetings and rallies — and its cost is recorded in one sentence from 1983, when Rufus Edmisten, running for governor, was overheard saying he had eaten enough barbecue and was not going to eat any more. In South Carolina the form is the stump meeting. Wade Hampton, the Confederate general running for governor, spoke at Galivants Ferry in 1876 and was elected that year; in 1880 Joseph William Holliday, merchant and tobacco farmer, invited the county's Democratic candidates to speak at his store, and the meeting has been held there in the spring of every second year since, carried on by the Hollidays and grown into a statewide event with national candidates — the longest-running Democratic campaign-speech site in the country, by the county's marker and the community's own account; by 2004 it counted 128 years. *Tradition holds —* chicken bog and barbecue are the food of the day. Mallard Creek's Presbyterians did not plan a political stop; they planned to pay off a Sunday-school building in 1929, and the candidates came to the crowd. By 2015 the crowd was 20,000 and the guests had included a former vice-president; the church retired the barbecue in 2025. The Lexington Barbecue Festival's politics — two bills in 2006 to make it the state's official festival, defeated by the east, and a regional title in 2007 — are the same appetite turned on the food itself.

A hog or a pile of butts is cooked by a church, a club or a hired pit; the candidate pays, or the host does; plates are free or cheap; the speaking is from a stump, a flatbed or a stage, or there is no speaking at all and the candidates walk a rope line with fliers. The date is the calendar's: spring of an election year at Galivants Ferry, the fourth Thursday of October at Mallard Creek.

Galivants Ferry continues on its two-year cycle; Mallard Creek ended in 2025; the pig pickin' rally goes on wherever a county party has a cooker.

political barbecue to pig pickin': the North Carolina rally's usual form: a pig, a cooker, a candidate.

political barbecue to fundraiser barbecue: the church that cooks the pig is usually raising money at the same time.

Not to be confused with fundraiser-barbecue: Who pays. A political barbecue is free to the eater and paid for by the candidate or the party; a fundraiser sells the plate.

Not to be confused with mallard-creek-barbecue: Mallard Creek was a church fundraiser the candidates attended; a political barbecue is the candidate's own.

title: barbecue
text:
The cooked meat itself — in the Carolinas, pork cooked slowly over coals or in a cooker and then chopped, pulled or sliced — and, by extension, the place that sells it and the gathering that eats it. Elsewhere in the country the same word means a grill, or a cookout of any meat; here the narrower sense is the ordinary one.

The word came north from the Caribbean with the Spanish and into English by way of the colonial Atlantic: a frame of sticks first, then the method, then the meat. Samuel Johnson's dictionary of 1755 already gives the Carolina sense — 'to barbecue: a term for dressing a whole hog', and the noun, 'a hog dressed whole'. *Tradition holds —* the whole-animal feast over wood coals was the shape of the colonial Southern gathering by the eighteenth century, and the political barbecue, a free feed put on by a candidate, was an institution of the early republic. *Inference —* the Carolina insistence that barbecue is a noun for pork is a memory of that feast: what was cooked at the rally was the pig, and the pig was what you came for.

Root: Taíno (Arawakan) barbacoa, a framework of sticks set on posts → Spanish barbacoa (1526, Oviedo) → English barbecue (1660s: the frame and the method; the cooked animal and the gathering by the 1700s).

barbecue to Eastern North Carolina barbecue: one of the two North Carolina answers to what the word means: the whole hog, chopped, with vinegar.

barbecue to Lexington-style barbecue: the other North Carolina answer: pork shoulder with a red dip.

barbecue to pig pickin': the gathering the word also names — a barbecue as an event, still a pig.

title: Carolina Gold
text:
Two South Carolina things with one name. The sauce: the yellow-mustard barbecue sauce of the Midlands — mustard, vinegar, sugar and spices — which Wikipedia says is sometimes called Carolina Gold and which Maurice Bessinger of Piggie Park sold in supermarkets under that brand. The rice: an heirloom variety of Oryza sativa named for the gold of its unhulled grain, grown in the Lowcountry by enslaved people from the 1780s, the staple of Lowcountry cooking, last harvested commercially in 1927 and revived from a seed bank in the 1980s.

The rice came first. Carolina Gold was popularized in South Carolina in the 1780s; at the outset of the Civil War 3.5 million of the 5 million bushels of rice grown in the United States were Carolina Gold, grown in the Lowcountry by enslaved people. The last commercial crop was harvested in 1927. In the 1980s Richard and Patricia Schulze, restoring rice ponds at Hardeeville, found a stock in a USDA seed bank in Texas, planted 14 pounds and harvested 64; by 1988 they had 10,000 pounds a year, and Anson Mills and Carolina Plantation Rice sold it to the public from 1998. The sauce's name is younger. Mustard sauce belongs to the German-settled Midlands. Maurice Bessinger, who opened Maurice's Piggie Park in West Columbia with his brother Joe in 1953, sold a sauce of mustard, brown sugar, soy sauce and vinegar under the Carolina Gold brand and by 1999 had the largest barbecue operation in the country; in 2000, when he raised Confederate flags over his restaurants, grocery chains dropped the sauce from their shelves. *Inference —* Carolina Gold for any yellow mustard sauce is the brand gone generic, wearing a name the rice made first.

Root: Carolina + gold. For the rice, the colour of the unhulled grain (Wikipedia); for the sauce, the colour of yellow mustard and the brand name under which Maurice Bessinger's Piggie Park sold it (Wikipedia). Two coinages, one name, no common root but the state.

Carolina Gold to Maurice Bessinger: who sold his mustard sauce under the Carolina Gold brand, and lost the shelves for it in 2000.

Carolina Gold to hash and rice: rice is the other half of the dish, and Carolina Gold is the Lowcountry's historic variety of it.

Not to be confused with mustard-sauce: The bottle says Carolina Gold; the sauce is mustard sauce. The rice is on a Charleston menu, not a barbecue one.

title: chopped
text:
The way most Carolina barbecue reaches the tray: cooked meat cut across on a block with cleavers — in the east fine enough to hold the thin vinegar sauce, in the Piedmont in larger pieces. At a Lexington counter it is an ordering word with a scale, chopped, coarse chopped, sliced, and each is a different plate from the same shoulder. 'Sliced' is the far end, the shoulder cut into slabs and not chopped at all. A whole hog is chopped all together, skin included, so that every tray gets every part.

Chop is a Middle English verb of uncertain parentage, and by the 1630s a chop was a slice of pork. The barbecue sense grows out of the whole hog: once the meat comes off the bones it goes to the block, and the food writers Jane and Michael Stern called the sound of cleavers on it among the most alluring things about Carolina whole hog. NCpedia gives the eastern meat as 'boned, chopped, or shredded' and the western as 'chopped or sliced pork shoulders or butts'; the Wikipedia article has the east chopping after the meat is pulled from the bone, for a finer texture that holds the thin sauce, and Lexington serving 'pulled' or very lightly chopped, leaving strands. Melton's in Rocky Mount chopped whole hog so fine that a 1988 magazine compared it to chopped peanut butter. At Lexington Barbecue the menu on 15 September 2026 reads Chopped BBQ, Coarse Chopped BBQ and Sliced BBQ, on plate, tray or sandwich, a chopped plate at $13.40 cash. *Tradition holds —* some eastern pits call their finest chop minced. *Inference —* the scale exists at Lexington because a shoulder can be sliced to order and a whole hog cannot.

Root: chop (v.), mid-14c., 'to cut with a quick blow', of uncertain origin, perhaps Old North French choper or Old French couper 'to cut'; the noun 'a slice of mutton, lamb or pork' from the 1630s. Coarse chopped: the same, in larger pieces. Minced: Old French mincier 'to chop in little pieces', in English cooking from the late 14c. Sliced: the far pole — not chopped at all.

chopped to Lexington-style barbecue: the style that made chopping an ordering scale: chopped, coarse chopped, sliced, all from the shoulder.

chopped to Eastern North Carolina barbecue: the style that chops everything — the whole hog, skin included — fine enough to hold vinegar.

chopped to chopping block: the block the chop happens on, with cleavers; the sound of it is the sound of an eastern pit.

chopped to whole hog: the cut that is chopped whole, crisp skin and all, so every tray gets every part of the hog.

chopped to pork shoulder: the cut that can also be sliced; Lexington's chopped and sliced come from the same shoulder.

chopped to pulled pork: the outsider's word for meat taken apart by hand instead of cut across with a blade.

chopped to outside brown: the other counter word: the crusted outer meat, which NCpedia notes some pits keep apart as 'outside meat' from 'inside meat'.

chopped to Lexington Barbecue: whose menu lists Chopped, Coarse Chopped and Sliced BBQ — the vocabulary in one line.

chopped to Melton's Barbecue: which chopped whole hog so fine a 1988 writer compared it to chopped peanut butter.

chopped to Skylight Inn BBQ: where the crisp skin is chopped through the meat on the block.

chopped to barbecue tray: the tray is chopped barbecue with slaw and no bread.

Not to be confused with pulled-pork: Chopped is cut across with a blade and comes in pieces; pulled comes in strands. Sliced is neither: slabs of shoulder, a Piedmont order.

title: dip
text:
The Lexington word for its sauce: vinegar, water, ketchup or tomato, salt, black and red pepper, sugar to taste — thin enough to pour, reddish rather than red. It goes on the chopped shoulder at the counter, sits on the table in a bottle, and is the dressing of the red slaw. Each pit's recipe is its own and, the town's own article says, closely guarded; the taste runs from tangy to slightly sweet or spicy. The eastern sauce is the same idea without the tomato, and is not called dip.

Dip is Old English dyppan, to plunge, kin to deep. The Online Etymology Dictionary dates the noun for a liquid you dip something into to 1825, and records a nineteenth-century kitchen sense: the juices and fat left in the pan after cooking meat. NCpedia explains the Lexington name by service — the thin tomato sauce is served at the table, because sauce on meat over an open fire is a hazard, so the meat is dipped after cooking. *Inference —* the pan-juice sense fits as well: the first Piedmont dips were drippings, vinegar and pepper, and the Wikipedia article on barbecue sauce has the early homemade sauces as vinegar, salt and pepper, with ketchup and sugar arriving in the 1920s. The Wikipedia article on Lexington says the shoulder is basted in a sauce 'called dip locally' of vinegar, ketchup, water, salt and pepper; the North Carolina Barbecue Society's page has red slaw made with the barbecue sauce 'locally called dip' in place of mayonnaise. *Tradition holds —* the recipe line runs from the tent pits on the Lexington courthouse square in the 1910s to Warner Stamey and the pits his cooks opened.

Root: dip (v.), Old English dyppan 'to plunge, immerse', from Proto-Germanic *daupejanan, a causative of *deup- 'deep'; the noun 'act of dipping' 1590s, 'liquid into which something is to be dipped' 1825; also in the 19th century 'a sweet sauce for pudding' and 'the juices and fat left after cooking meat'; the party dip of 1962 is, etymonline says, probably a re-coinage.

dip to Lexington dip: the sauce itself; this page is only its name.

dip to Lexington-style barbecue: the style whose sauce goes by this word; 'Piedmont' and 'Western' style mean the same dip.

dip to red slaw: the slaw is red because it is dressed with the dip instead of mayonnaise.

dip to pork shoulder: the cut the dip is made for, basted with it on the pit and dressed with it on the block.

dip to vinegar-and-pepper sauce: the eastern cousin: the same vinegar and pepper without the tomato that makes a dip red, and called sauce.

dip to heavy tomato sauce: the thick, sweet, molasses-and-brown-sugar sauce of the rest of the country and of western South Carolina — what a dip is not.

dip to Warner Stamey: the Lexington cook whose dip, *tradition holds*, is the ancestor of most of the others.

dip to Lexington Barbecue: a Lexington pit where the dip and the slaw come from the same kitchen, shoulders only, over oak and hickory coals.

Not to be confused with vinegar-pepper-sauce: Both are thin and vinegar-based. Dip has tomato or ketchup in it and is reddish; the eastern sauce has none and is clear or pepper-flecked. If the slaw beside it is red, the sauce is a dip.

Not to be confused with heavy-tomato-sauce: A dip pours and is tart; a heavy tomato sauce clings and is sweet. Dip is a Piedmont word; nobody calls the thick sauce a dip.

title: Down East
text:
In North Carolina, the coastal plain east of Raleigh — the barbecue east, where the hog is cooked whole and the sauce has no tomato; eastern North Carolina barbecue is also called Down East barbecue. The narrow sense is the string of fishing communities east of Beaufort in Carteret County — Bettie, Otway, Straits, Harkers Island, Gloucester, Marshallberg, out to Cedar Island — and Wikipedia says the phrase has broadened to mean eastern North Carolina generally, the central coastal plain of Greenville, Goldsboro, Kinston, New Bern, Rocky Mount, Tarboro, Washington and Wilson.

The phrase is New England's first: a ship from Boston bound for Maine ran before the south-west wind, so Maine was down east, and the term is on record from 1817. North Carolina has its own. To Carteret County, Down East is the villages east of Beaufort, where the accent is the coastal 'High Tider' brogue; to Raleigh and the Piedmont the same words cover the whole coastal plain, and the towns Wikipedia lists for that broader sense are the barbecue towns — Rocky Mount, where Bob Melton opened the state's first sit-down barbecue restaurant in 1924; Wilson, where Ed Mitchell grew up; Greenville, with Ayden and the Skylight Inn just south. In the 1980s newspaper war over what barbecue meant, Dennis Rogers of the Raleigh News & Observer spoke for the east and Jerry Bledsoe of Greensboro for Lexington. *Tradition holds —* in barbecue talk Down East means whole hog and vinegar, and where it begins is argued; the fall line east of Raleigh is the usual answer. *Inference —* down is the way the rivers run — Neuse, Tar, Roanoke — and east is where they go; the Carolina phrase needs no ship.

Root: down + east, a sailing direction. Along the New England coast the summer wind is south-westerly, so a ship bound east from Boston runs downwind, and Maine was Down East (Wiktionary; Wikipedia). In North Carolina the same phrase names the coastal communities east of Beaufort in Carteret County and, broadened, the eastern part of the state (Wikipedia).

Down East to Eastern North Carolina barbecue: the style, which is also called Down East barbecue.

Down East to whole hog: what Down East cooks.

Down East to vinegar-and-pepper sauce: the Down East sauce: no tomato.

Down East to white slaw: the Down East slaw: mayonnaise, pale, on the bun.

Down East to Piedmont: the other direction — west of the fall line, where the shoulder and the dip begin.

Down East to Pee Dee: South Carolina's name for the same whole-hog coastal plain, across the state line.

Down East to Skylight Inn BBQ: in Ayden, a Down East pit in the broad sense, cooking whole hogs over wood since 1947.

Down East to Melton's Barbecue: in Rocky Mount, in the broadened Down East: the first sit-down barbecue restaurant in the state, 1924.

Down East to Bob Melton: who cooked whole hog in an open pit by the Tar River before he sold it.

Down East to Ed Mitchell: of Wilson, a Down East town in the broad sense, who learned barbecue at family gatherings there.

Down East to Dennis Rogers: the Raleigh News & Observer columnist on the eastern side of the 1980s barbecue feud with Jerry Bledsoe.

Not to be confused with piedmont: Down East is east of the fall line — whole hog, clear sauce, white slaw. The Piedmont is west of it — shoulder, red dip, red slaw.

title: Dutch Fork
text:
The land between the Saluda and the Broad rivers above their meeting at Columbia, in Lexington, Newberry and Richland counties, settled by German-speaking Protestants in the middle of the eighteenth century and named for them, Dutch for deutsch. It is the upstream end of the mustard belt: the yellow mustard barbecue sauce of the Midlands is linked to the German families who settled between Orangeburg County and Newberry County, and the Fork is the Newberry end of that line. Lutheran churches, place names and family names are what remains of the German; the dialect is gone.

The British colony offered incentives to foreign Protestants to settle its backcountry, and between 1730 and 1766 German-speaking families took up the fork of the Saluda and the Broad; the South Carolina Encyclopedia dates the first European settlement to the 1740s and says German language and culture lasted in the Fork's isolation into the early twentieth century. The name is English for what the settlers called themselves. Their mark on the plate is mustard. Wikipedia says South Carolina's mustard sauce may have originated with the French and German immigrants of the eighteenth century and is linked to a 'Mustard Belt' from Orangeburg County to Newberry County where Germans settled; the Dukes family of Orangeburg County, of German origin, is the example historians give; and mustard goes into the hash of the German Midlands. Newberry is still the only South Carolina county more than a tenth Lutheran. *Inference —* the Fork is not the whole belt but its upstream end; Orangeburg, the other end, lies south of the Congaree and outside it. *Tradition holds —* the Dutch Fork is claimed as the birthplace of mustard sauce; no document in the sources consulted places the first pot.

Root: Dutch, in its older English sense 'German': from the late 14th century Dutch meant German and the non-Scandinavian continental Germanic peoples generally, from Middle Dutch duutsch, cognate with German deutsch, from Proto-Germanic *theudo 'of the people'; the sense narrowed to the Netherlands around 1600 in England, but in America the older sense lasted, as in Pennsylvania Dutch (etymonline) + fork, Old English forca from Latin furca, of rivers from 1753 (etymonline): the land between the Saluda and the Broad, which join to form the Congaree at Columbia.

Dutch Fork to South Carolina mustard barbecue: the style the Fork's Germans are credited with.

Dutch Fork to mustard-based barbecue sauce: the sauce the German families of the Midlands are credited with.

Dutch Fork to Carolina Gold: the brand name the mustard sauce goes by on bottles.

Dutch Fork to hash and rice: mustard goes into the hash in the German Midlands.

Dutch Fork to Dukes Bar-B-Que: an Orangeburg County family of German origin whose mustard sauce historians point to — the other end of the mustard belt.

Dutch Fork to Maurice's Piggie Park BBQ: the Midlands' best-known mustard-sauce pit, in West Columbia, a few miles from the Fork.

Dutch Fork to slaw: the other Dutch: koolsla came from the Netherlands, the Fork's Dutch from Germany.

Dutch Fork to Piedmont: the Fork's rivers join at Columbia on the fall line, where the Piedmont ends.

Not to be confused with slaw: Two Dutches. The Fork's Dutch is deutsch, German; slaw's Dutch is the Netherlands' koolsla. One brought mustard, the other cabbage.

title: fixins
text:
The sides and trimmings that come with the meat: slaw, hushpuppies or cornbread, boiled potatoes in the east, hash and rice in South Carolina, pickles, sweet tea. 'Fixings' is American English of 1839 for the garnishing of a meal; fixins is how it is said and, on Carolina signs and menus, how it is spelled. Beth Tartan wrote of a Raleigh hostess telephoning Melton's — 'Ride me a party' — and Melton's putting barbecue and fixings on the bus to her.

Fix is a verb that does a great deal of work in the South, and its noun did the same: fixings, first the apparatus of a thing, in 1820, then by 1839 the food that goes round the main thing. The barbecue plate is the word's natural home because the meat is one thing and the rest is a list. The Skylight Inn tray is barbecue, slaw and cornbread; Melton's plate in 1929 was barbecue with boiled potatoes for 45 cents, and in 1988 came with coleslaw, hushpuppies and Brunswick stew; a pig pickin' is eaten with hushpuppies, coleslaw, baked beans or Brunswick stew, and in South Carolina with hash over rice or pilaf; the Dukes buffets run to collard greens, macaroni and cheese, black-eyed peas, hushpuppies, corn nuggets, potato salad, coleslaw and white bread. The spelling is the speech: a menu that prints fixin's is telling you how the owner talks. *Inference —* the word keeps the order of the plate — barbecue is the noun, and everything else is fixins.

Root: fix (v.), late 14c., from Old French fixer, Latin fixus 'fastened' → fixing, verbal noun, 'act of putting in order', c. 1600 → fixings, American English, 'apparatus' 1820, 'food, garnishing' 1839 (etymonline); spelled fixin's or fixins for the g that Southern speech drops.

fixins to barbecue tray: the tray's fixins are slaw and cornbread, and nothing more.

fixins to slaw: the one fixin that is never missing.

fixins to hushpuppies: fried cornmeal, a fixin in both states.

fixins to cornbread: the Skylight's fixin, a dense pork-fat cake.

fixins to boiled potatoes: the eastern fixin — at Melton's a plate came with boiled potatoes for 45 cents in 1929.

fixins to hash and rice: the South Carolina fixin.

fixins to Brunswick stew: on the plate at Melton's and at pig pickin's.

fixins to sweet tea: the drink among the fixins.

fixins to light bread: the sandwich's bread; on a plate, one more fixin.

fixins to Melton's Barbecue: which put 'barbecue and fixings on the bus' for Raleigh parties.

fixins to Dukes Bar-B-Que: whose buffet is the fixins as a list.

fixins to Skylight Inn BBQ: whose tray is the fixins at their fewest: slaw and cornbread.

fixins to pig pickin': where the fixins are hushpuppies, slaw, baked beans or Brunswick stew, and in South Carolina hash and rice.

title: hog
text:
In Carolina barbecue speech the animal is a hog. Whole hog is the eastern North Carolina and Pee Dee style; a hog killing is the winter work of the farm; a hog's size is its dressed weight. American dictionaries make a hog a domesticated swine of 120 pounds or more raised for market and a pig the younger, smaller animal; the pit's small hogs of 80 to 120 pounds dressed sit at the bottom of that range. The pig pickin' hog is a barrow, a castrated male, or a gilt, a young female — boars and sows are too big.

Hog is older than pig for the grown animal. Old English hogg meant a swine of a certain age — a castrated male, or one reared for slaughter at about a year; pig, until the fourteenth century, meant a young one. Dressed weight is the pit's unit: the weight after the organs, head and inedible parts are removed, about 72 per cent of live weight for a pig by Wikipedia's example. A pig pickin' hog is 80 to 120 pounds dressed; elsewhere hogs run to 300 pounds, but in the Carolinas small hogs cooked hot so the skin crisps and can be chopped in. Hog killing was the farm's winter work: NCpedia describes it beginning on the first frigid day of autumn or winter, neighbours gathering before dawn, as many as 100 hogs penned and fattened on gleaned peas, potatoes and corn, and the weeks after full of spare ribs, liver and sausage, the hams a month or two later. *Tradition holds —* the barbecue was what a hog killing or a church homecoming did with fresh meat before curing. 'Go the whole hog', American English of 1828, is the same animal as a figure of speech.

Root: Old English hogg, implied in the late-12th-century hogaster and written hogge by the mid-14th century; origin uncertain — a Celtic source (Welsh hwch, Cornish hogh 'swine') is proposed, and the OED, quoted by etymonline, calls it improbable. The original sense was age, not species: a castrated male, or a swine reared for slaughter at about a year old; stockmen also said it of yearling sheep and horses.

hog to whole hog: the cut that is the whole animal; the phrase and the style share the word.

hog to hog killing: the winter farm work the word names: neighbours before dawn, scalding water, and the first frigid day.

hog to Eastern North Carolina barbecue: the style whose answer to what barbecue is, is the hog, entire.

hog to Pee Dee whole-hog barbecue: the South Carolina region where whole hog over hardwood coals is the common style.

hog to pig pickin': the gathering named for pulling meat off the hog by hand; its hog is a barrow or gilt of 80 to 120 pounds dressed.

hog to pork skins: the skin of the hog, fried; in the Pee Dee the hog is sometimes skinned before cooking and the skin fried.

hog to hash and rice: what the head and liver of the hog become in South Carolina.

hog to pork shoulder: the cut the Piedmont takes instead of the hog.

hog to barbecue: the word that in the east means the hog after cooking.

Not to be confused with whole-hog: 'Hog' is the animal; 'whole hog' is the cut and the style. The pig-or-hog tell is size: a hog is the market-weight animal, a pig the young one; the pit's hog is small, 80 to 120 pounds dressed.

title: light bread
text:
The Southern name for white yeast bread — a store loaf or a soft bun — as against cornbread, biscuits and pone, a dense cornmeal cake. On a Carolina barbecue tray it is what the sandwich is built on: chopped barbecue and slaw on a soft white bun. At the Skylight Inn the sandwich is on a white roll; Dukes buffets in South Carolina set out white bread beside the hash. Dictionary.com labels the term Midland and Southern U.S., and defines it as white bread or any bread leavened with yeast.

The word is old on the farm and young on the menu. Dictionary.com dates light bread to 1815–25; it is light in the baker's sense, risen with yeast, against the heavy cornmeal breads that fed the South because wheat would not keep in its heat. The barbecue sandwich is a twentieth-century form — Wikipedia says the tradition of whole hog as a sandwich filling began in the 1900s, and Melton's in Rocky Mount sold a barbecue sandwich for 15 cents in 1929 — and the bread it needed was the soft white bun that machine-sliced loaves made ordinary from the 1920s. The bun is never the point: Wikipedia's barbecue-sandwich article says the bread keeps the meat from drying and holds its heat, and in the east the slaw goes on the bun. *Tradition holds —* the tray, barbecue and slaw without bread, is the order for people who do not want the light bread at all; hushpuppies and cornsticks are the tray's bread and light bread the sandwich's. NCpedia's sides are baked corn sticks and fried hush puppies.

Root: light (adj.), Old English leoht 'not heavy', from Proto-Germanic *lingkhtaz — of bread, risen with yeast, against the dense pone and quick breads of cornmeal — + bread. Midland and Southern American English for white bread, or any bread leavened with yeast (dictionary.com); 'Southern US: white bread' (Wiktionary).

light bread to barbecue sandwich: the dish: barbecue and slaw on light bread.

light bread to barbecue tray: the order without it.

light bread to hushpuppies: the tray's bread instead — fried cornmeal, not wheat.

light bread to cornbread: the other bread, and the older; light bread is named against it.

light bread to white slaw: what goes on the light bread with the meat in the east.

light bread to Skylight Inn BBQ: where the sandwich is on a white roll.

light bread to Dukes Bar-B-Que: whose buffets set out white bread beside the hash and rice.

light bread to Melton's Barbecue: selling a barbecue sandwich for 15 cents in 1929.

light bread to fixins: on a plate, light bread is one more fixin.

Not to be confused with cornbread: Light bread is leavened with yeast and white; cornbread is cornmeal, quick or unleavened, yellow or white. The sandwich is on light bread; the tray comes with cornbread or hushpuppies.

title: Pee Dee
text:
The river and the region. The Pee Dee rises in the North Carolina mountains as the Yadkin, takes the name Pee Dee below the mouth of the Uwharrie, crosses into South Carolina and reaches the sea at Winyah Bay. The region is the state's north-east corner — Chesterfield, Darlington, Dillon, Florence, Marlboro and Marion counties always, Horry, Georgetown and Williamsburg usually. Its barbecue is whole hog over hardwood coals, sometimes skinned first with the skin fried, and a sauce of vinegar, salt and pepper that Wikipedia calls virtually identical to eastern North Carolina's.

The people gave the river its name and the river gave it to the land. The Pedee were a Southeastern Woodlands people of the South Carolina Piedmont and the river valley, part of the South Appalachian Mississippian culture — the mound-building culture of the Southeast, about 1000 to 1500 — and numbered about 600 in 1600; their language was never written down, and the name's meaning is a guess. Four state-recognized tribes claim their descent. Its barbecue is the whole hog. The South Carolina Encyclopedia gives the Pee Dee sauce as 'watery thin and fiery hot pepper and vinegar concoctions'; the Wikipedia article on South Carolina barbecue calls the vinegar sauce heavily based on Native American basting sauces, a claim it makes without a document behind it. Scott's Variety Store and Bar-B-Q opened in Hemingway in 1972 and became known for whole-hog platters; Rodney Scott grew up at its pit and took the Pee Dee hog to Charleston in 2017. Kingstree holds a Pig Pickin' festival every fall for Williamsburg County's vinegar barbecue. *Inference —* the Pee Dee and Down East are one barbecue country cut by a state line.

Root: from the Pee Dee (Pedee) people, an Indigenous nation of the South Carolina Piedmont and the river valley; the river took their name and the region took the river's. Their language was never recorded and the name's meaning is unknown.

Pee Dee to Pee Dee whole-hog barbecue: the style named for the region.

Pee Dee to Eastern North Carolina barbecue: the same cooking north of the line: whole hog, vinegar and pepper.

Pee Dee to Down East: North Carolina's name for the same coastal-plain whole-hog country.

Pee Dee to whole hog: the Pee Dee's cut.

Pee Dee to vinegar-and-pepper sauce: the Pee Dee sauce: 'watery thin and fiery hot'.

Pee Dee to pork skins: in the Pee Dee the hog is sometimes skinned before cooking and the skin fried.

Pee Dee to hash and rice: the Pee Dee's hash is liver hash.

Pee Dee to chicken bog: the Pee Dee's rice dish, most common there and in the Lowcountry.

Pee Dee to Scott's Bar-B-Que: Hemingway, 1972: the Pee Dee's best-known whole-hog pit.

Pee Dee to Rodney Scott: who cooked at Scott's from about age eleven and took the Pee Dee hog to Charleston.

Pee Dee to Rodney Scott's Whole Hog BBQ: the Charleston restaurant, opened 2017, that carried the Pee Dee hog to the coast.

Pee Dee to pig pickin': Kingstree's fall festival is a Pig Pickin', for the county's vinegar barbecue.

Pee Dee to Piedmont: where the Pee Dee people lived before the name moved downriver.

Not to be confused with sc-mustard: Pee Dee sauce is thin, clear and hot; Midlands sauce is yellow with mustard. If the sauce is yellow you have left the Pee Dee.

title: Piedmont
text:
The plateau between the coastal plain and the Blue Ridge, from New York to Alabama and nearly 300 miles wide in North Carolina; its eastern edge is the fall line, where rivers drop off hard rock onto the soft plain and towns grew at the head of navigation. In North Carolina barbecue, Piedmont style is Lexington style — pork shoulder, a red vinegar-and-ketchup dip, red slaw — and 'Western' means the same. In South Carolina the Piedmont is the Upstate, Greenville, Spartanburg and Anderson, where the sauce is a thin ketchup and vinegar and the hash is pork and beef.

Piemonte is the foot of the Alps, named in Latin documents by 1200; English took it through French and in 1755 applied piemont to the country at the foot of the Appalachians, adding the d by 1855. The fall line is where the name earns itself: the Piedmont's rivers leave the hard rock in a line of rapids, and the Congaree forms at Columbia on it. Wikipedia calls Lexington style 'Piedmont- or Western-style', most common in the Piedmont and west, pork shoulder only, with a red dip and red slaw; the South Carolina Encyclopedia has shoulders, hams and Boston butts in the Piedmont against the whole hog of the coastal plain. Lexington, 20 miles south of Winston-Salem in the Piedmont Triad, calls itself the Barbecue Capital of the World, and in 2007 the legislature made its festival the Official Food Festival of the Piedmont Triad Region. South Carolina's Upstate takes a light tomato sauce that Wikipedia attributes to North Carolina's influence, and its hash is beef and pork with onions. *Inference —* the Piedmont cooks the shoulder because a shoulder is what a town butcher sells; the whole hog stayed with the farm.

Root: Italian Piemonte, from medieval Latin Pedemontium, ad pedem montium, 'at the foot of the mountains' — Latin pes, pedis 'foot' + mons, montis 'mountain' — the region below the Alps, in documents from the end of the twelfth century (Wikipedia); through French Piémont; applied to the American plateau at the foot of the Appalachians as piemont in 1755, with the d by 1855, and extended to the foot of other ranges by 1860 (etymonline).

Piedmont to Lexington-style barbecue: the style the word means in North Carolina barbecue: 'Piedmont- or Western-style'.

Piedmont to dip: the Piedmont's word for its sauce.

Piedmont to Lexington dip: the Piedmont's sauce.

Piedmont to red slaw: the Piedmont's slaw, dressed with the dip.

Piedmont to pork shoulder: the Piedmont's cut; the coastal plain cooks the whole hog.

Piedmont to Light tomato barbecue: the South Carolina Piedmont's sauce, a thin ketchup and vinegar credited to North Carolina's influence.

Piedmont to Heavy tomato barbecue: western South Carolina's sweeter, thicker sauce, also Piedmont country.

Piedmont to hash and rice: in the Upstate the hash is beef and pork with onions.

Piedmont to Lexington Barbecue Festival: the Official Food Festival of the Piedmont Triad Region, by act of the legislature, 2007.

Piedmont to Down East: the other side of the fall line.

Piedmont to Dutch Fork: the Fork lies where the Piedmont's rivers join at the fall line.

Piedmont to Pee Dee: the people the river is named for lived in the South Carolina Piedmont.

Not to be confused with down-east: Piedmont means west of the fall line: shoulder, red dip, red slaw. If the tray has white slaw and chopped skin through the meat, you are east of it.

title: pit
text:
The place the cooking happens. First a trench in the ground filled with hardwood coals, the split hog on a rack above; then a wide, shallow container of cinder block, brick or steel above ground, still a pit; then, at many places, a gas cooker, still the pit. The word also names the room, the building — a pit house — and the restaurant, as in Backyard BBQ Pit or Dickey's Barbecue Pit. A smokehouse is a different building: a windowless outbuilding where hams and bacon are cured in cold smoke for weeks, not a place a meal is cooked.

Pit is a Germanic borrowing of Latin puteus, a well; in Old English a hole, a well, a grave and hell. The barbecue pit was that hole: Wikipedia's article on pit barbecue describes meat cooked buried below ground, an earth-oven practice of Indigenous peoples. The whole-hog article has the pit dug into the earth or built above it as a wide, shallow container, usually of cinder blocks, filled with charcoal burned down from wood in a fireplace or a burn barrel; the South Carolina Encyclopedia gives the traditional pit as an open pit fuelled by hardwood coals in a rectangular cement-block structure, the meat suspended above. NCpedia says few commercial pits today are dug in the ground; the whole-hog article says new restaurants mostly use gas-fired pits and many older ones have switched. At the Skylight Inn the pit crew makes its charcoal from oak and hickory logs in fireplaces beside the pits. Ed Mitchell co-founded a Raleigh restaurant called The Pit. *Inference —* a word that survived the loss of the hole survived the loss of the fire: the pit is wherever the barbecue is made, and the name on the sign says so.

Root: Old English pytt 'a hole in the ground, water hole, well, grave', a Germanic borrowing of Latin puteus 'well, pit, shaft'; the barbecue sense keeps the hole's name after the hole has become a box of brick or cinder block above ground, and then a gas cooker inside a building.

pit to brick pit: the masonry pit, the first form above ground.

pit to block pit: the cinder-block pit, the common whole-hog form: a rectangular cement-block structure with the meat above the coals.

pit to burn barrel: the drum beside the pit where logs become the coals shovelled in.

pit to hickory and oak: what burns beside the pit to make its coals.

pit to direct heat: the pit's way of cooking: coals under the meat, the meat on a rack above.

pit to gas and electric cookers: the cooker that replaced the coals at many pits and kept the name.

pit to pig cooker: the pig pickin's charcoal or propane cooker, homemade or custom-built: a pit on wheels.

pit to pitmaster: the person; the word is built on this one.

pit to Backyard BBQ Pit: a Durham restaurant named for the thing.

pit to Skylight Inn BBQ: where the coals for the pits are burned down from oak and hickory in fireplaces beside them.

pit to Henry's Smokehouse: a Greenville, South Carolina pit that calls itself a smokehouse — the two words meet on the sign.

pit to Ed Mitchell: who co-founded The Pit in Raleigh and left it in 2011.

Not to be confused with gas-and-electric-cookers: A cooker is an appliance; a pit is a place. When a pit switches to gas the appliance sits inside the place and the sign does not change.

Not to be confused with pig-cooker: A pig cooker is towed to the party; a pit stays where it was built.
