title: pitmaster
text:
The person who runs the pit — the fire, the coals, the turning of the hog, the call that it is done. A recent word for an old job. Wiktionary defines it as one who operates a barbecue pit and adds that it is used as a term of respect; dictionary.com dates it 1980–85; Wikipedia titles its articles 'Ed Mitchell (pitmaster)' and 'Rodney Scott (pitmaster)', and BBQ Pitmasters has been on cable since 2009. In the Carolinas the older words are the cook and the pit man, and a place is known by a family's name before any title.

Pit is the hole and master is Latin magister, the chief; the compound follows quartermaster. Texas Monthly traced 'pit master' through unrelated trades and found the earliest barbecue use it could in a 1939 North Carolina newspaper item: 'Jeter Crutchfield, pit master, will supervise the beginning of roasting pork for the barbecue tonight at midnight.' Destination BBQ gives the paper as the Burlington Daily Times-News of 22 September 1939 and points at the verb: Crutchfield supervised, and the men at the pit that night were Black. Adrian Miller's Black Smoke traces the history of those cooks — Black barbecuers, pitmasters and restaurateurs — and their place in the tradition. Dictionary.com dates the one-word pitmaster to 1980–85; the television series BBQ Pitmasters premiered on TLC on 3 December 2009. Rodney Scott of Hemingway, named Best Chef Southeast by the James Beard Foundation in 2018, was only the second pitmaster to win a Beard chef award. *Inference —* the word arrived with the audience: once barbecue was written about, the cook needed a title a writer could print. *Tradition holds —* in the Carolinas he still answers to his name.

Root: pit (Old English pytt, the cooking pit) + master (Old English, from Latin magister 'chief, teacher'; 'a workman qualified to carry on a trade on his own account' from c. 1300), on the pattern of quartermaster and the other -master compounds for the person in charge of a thing.

pitmaster to pit: the word it is built on.

pitmaster to Ed Mitchell: the Wilson pitmaster the press calls North Carolina's most famous.

pitmaster to Rodney Scott: the Hemingway pitmaster who won a James Beard chef award in 2018, the second pitmaster to do so.

pitmaster to Pete Jones: who ran the Skylight Inn's pits from 1947 until 2006, most of it before the word was common.

pitmaster to Wayne Monk: owner of Lexington Barbecue, 'serving pork barbecue since 1962' — two decades before dictionaries record the word.

pitmaster to Adrian Miller: whose Black Smoke tells the history of the Black pitmasters the word was late to name.

pitmaster to whole hog: the cut whose cooking most needs one: several people to flip and tend, and a cook who becomes prominent in the community.

pitmaster to Southern Foodways Alliance: whose oral histories record pitmasters in their own words.

title: pulled pork
text:
Pork cooked slowly over coals or in a cooker until it comes off the bone in strands, then taken apart by hand or with forks rather than cut. Outside the Carolinas it is the name of the dish, and the dish is a shoulder — the Boston butt, the upper shoulder, is the cut it almost always means. Inside the Carolinas the meat is called barbecue, and 'pulled' is one answer, with 'chopped' and 'sliced', to how you want it: Memphis pulls by hand; the North Carolina east chops fine; Lexington serves it pulled or lightly chopped, leaving strands.

Pull is Old English pullian, to pluck off or draw out, and pork came in from Old French porc after 1300. Together they name a texture: meat cooked until its connective tissue gives way, which the Wikipedia article puts at an internal temperature of 195 to 205 °F, and taken apart along the grain. The cut the phrase assumes is the shoulder, and the shoulder's upper half is the Boston butt, named for the New England barrels, called butts, that pork was packed in; the name is in print by 1915. The Carolinas had the thing before the phrase. The east chopped its whole hog with cleavers; Lexington chopped or sliced its shoulders; Memphis built its sandwich on shoulder pulled by hand, not chopped with a blade. Ed Mitchell of Wilson builds a pulled pork sandwich from a whole hog, shoulder, ham and belly together; the Dukes restaurants of Orangeburg list pulled pork on the buffet; the South Carolina mustard sandwich is described as pulled pork. *Inference —* a Carolina menu that says pulled pork is speaking to the road; one that says barbecue is speaking to the county. No source consulted dates the compound.

Root: pull (v.), Old English pullian 'to pluck off (wool), to draw out', of uncertain origin + pork (n.), c. 1300, Old French porc 'pig', Latin porcus; the participle names how the cooked meat leaves the bone — pulled apart, not cut.

pulled pork to barbecue: the Carolina word for the same meat; pulled pork is what it is called when the menu speaks to the rest of the country.

pulled pork to chopped: the other answer at the counter — cut with a cleaver rather than taken apart by hand; the east chops fine, Lexington coarse.

pulled pork to pork shoulder: the cut the phrase assumes: almost always a shoulder, and the upper half of it is the Boston butt.

pulled pork to whole hog: the cut the east pulls instead; Ed Mitchell's pulled pork sandwich is shoulder, ham and belly from one hog.

pulled pork to Lexington-style barbecue: the North Carolina style most often served 'pulled' or very lightly chopped, leaving larger strands of muscle.

pulled pork to Eastern North Carolina barbecue: the style that chops after pulling from the bone, so its meat is never called pulled.

pulled pork to barbecue sandwich: the sandwich the phrase usually sells; in South Carolina the mustard-sauce version is described as pulled pork.

pulled pork to South Carolina mustard barbecue: the style whose sandwich Wikipedia describes as pulled pork under a yellow sauce.

pulled pork to Ed Mitchell: the Wilson pitmaster who builds a pulled pork sandwich from a whole hog rather than a shoulder.

pulled pork to Dukes Bar-B-Que: the Orangeburg family of restaurants whose buffets list pulled pork beside hash and rice.

Not to be confused with chopped: Pulled meat comes in strands the length of the muscle; chopped meat has been cut across with a blade into pieces. On a Carolina tray, strands mean the Piedmont or a hand-pulled kitchen; a fine, even chop means the east.

title: slaw
text:
Shredded raw cabbage, dressed and served cold, on every Carolina barbecue tray and most sandwiches. East of Raleigh the dressing is mayonnaise or whipped salad dressing and the slaw is white or yellow; in Lexington it is vinegar, ketchup and pepper — the dip — and the slaw is red, also called barbecue slaw. South Carolina buffets list coleslaw among the sides. The word is the back half of coleslaw, and the front half is not said; coleslaw came to the colonies with the Dutch settlers of New York.

Dutch koolsla, cabbage salad, was written down in American English in 1794 as 'cold slaw', the Dutch kool heard as the English cold; the folk spelling lasted until the 1860s, when cole came back, and by then the back half had come loose and slaw stood alone. Dutch colonists brought coleslaw to the Thirteen Colonies. Jerry Bledsoe, the Greensboro columnist of the 1980s barbecue war, wrote in 1996 that barbecue is always served with slaw in North Carolina and always has been. The split is by region. The Wikipedia article on coleslaw calls North Carolina slaw fine and vinegary and says that around Lexington red slaw is made with ketchup and vinegar rather than mayonnaise and is the prevailing kind, unlike the rest of the state; NCpedia has white or yellow coleslaw in the east and red coleslaw, 'barbecue slaw', coloured with ketchup or dip, in the Piedmont. The Lexington sandwich's distinguishing feature, the town's article says, is its red slaw, and in the late 1990s Wendy's put red slaw on a 'Carolina Classic' burger. *Inference —* red slaw is the dip's second job, and a pit that makes one makes the other from the same pot.

Root: Dutch koolsla 'cabbage salad' — kool 'cabbage' (from Latin caulis) + sla, clipped from salade (from French) — → American English cole slaw, 1794, heard and written as 'cold slaw' → slaw, the back half alone, by the 1860s.

slaw to red slaw: the Lexington slaw: cabbage, vinegar, ketchup, pepper, no mayonnaise — also called barbecue slaw.

slaw to white slaw: the eastern slaw, dressed with mayonnaise or whipped salad dressing, and put on the bun of an eastern sandwich.

slaw to Lexington dip: the dressing of the red slaw; the dip's second use.

slaw to barbecue sandwich: in both halves of North Carolina the sandwich comes with slaw on it.

slaw to barbecue tray: on the tray, slaw is the one side that is always there — Bledsoe: always served with slaw, and always has been.

slaw to Eastern North Carolina barbecue: white slaw there.

slaw to Lexington-style barbecue: red slaw there, and no question asked.

slaw to Jerry Bledsoe: who wrote 'Slaw Crazy' (1996): barbecue is always served with slaw in North Carolina.

slaw to Dutch Fork: the other Dutch: the Fork's Dutch is deutsch, German; slaw's Dutch is the Netherlands' koolsla.

slaw to fixins: the first fixin on every plate.

Not to be confused with red-slaw: Red means dip-dressed and Piedmont; white means mayonnaise and east. Ask for slaw in Lexington and it comes red without a question; ask in Ayden and it comes white.

title: barbecue postcards
text:
Between about 1930 and 1945 an American restaurant could order its own postcards by the thousand. A printer took a photograph, had an artist colour it by hand, and ran it on paper with a woven texture — the linen card, whose surface takes bright ink and softens a plain building into something worth mailing. Roadside businesses on the highways through both Carolinas bought them and set them by the register. The caption on the back names the route number, because that is how a customer found the place again.

Why a barbecue stand printed postcards. A linen card was cheap advertising that the customer paid to deliver. It carried the name, the highway, the distance from town and a picture of a building that was otherwise unremarkable, and somebody mailed it to Ohio.

The captions are the useful part. Barbecue Lodge, published by the Carolina News Company of Fayetteville and printed in the 1930s or 1940s, is the Carolina example in the Boston Public Library's Tichnor collection: a low red-brick building with a flat roof and a squat brick chimney, and along the parapet in illuminated letters BARBECUE LODGE, with a red strip beneath it reading AIR CONDITIONED · Charcoal STEAKS · PRIVATE DINING ROOMS. The neighbouring cards in the same file — Warren's Motel & Restaurant on U.S. 301 at Pleasant Hill, the White House Restaurant on U.S. 1 at Henderson, Clark's Restaurant at Santee on U.S. 301, 15 and 15A at the junction with S.C. 6 — show the pattern: the route number is doing the work a street address does now. These are highway businesses and the card is a map.

Tichnor Brothers, and the Boston connection. Most of these were printed a long way from the Carolinas. Tichnor Brothers of Boston turned out linen postcards for the whole country, and the Boston Public Library holds around 25,000 of them, arranged by state and digitised. The library put the scans on Flickr under a licence that allows reuse with credit, which is why a project like this one can print a 1940 North Carolina motor-court card without asking anyone.

*Inference —* the distance shows. A Boston artist colouring a Fayetteville barbecue lodge from a black-and-white photograph is guessing at the paint, and the skies in these cards are all the same blue. What is reliable in them is the architecture, the signage and the caption; the colour is decoration.

What the Carolina cards do not show. Pits, mostly. The card is a picture of a front elevation with cars parked at it, because that is what the owner wanted photographed: a clean building on a numbered highway, not a cinder-block cookhouse out the back with smoke coming out of it.

A reader looking for barbecue in this file finds it in the lettering. Barbecue Lodge says so on its face. Elsewhere the word turns up on a panel over a door, or on a board by the road at the edge of the frame, in a card that is nominally about a motel. *Tradition holds —* barbecue and lodging shared premises all along U.S. 301 and U.S. 1 through the eastern Carolinas in these years, because both were selling to the same car.

barbecue postcards to roadside barbecue signs: the same buildings and the same highways, photographed forty years later in colour.

barbecue postcards to the pig mascot: the house pig, which turns up on the card as often as on the sign.

barbecue postcards to barbecue: the word as a card caption, which is how a business told a stranger what it sold.

barbecue postcards to The FSA photographs of Carolina eating: the same decade, photographed by a government rather than a printer, and with nothing to sell.

barbecue postcards to Melton's Barbecue: a Rocky Mount pit of exactly this period, when a Carolina barbecue house would order cards.

title: the pig that serves itself
text:
A barbecue sign on which the pig is not the meat but the staff: a pig in a chef's toque carrying a covered tray, a pig in an apron at a pit, a pig in sunglasses eating a pork sandwich, a pig holding the restaurant's own name over its head. The animal about to be served is drawn recommending the meal, and the joke is never explained on the sign because it does not need to be. The form runs from nineteenth-century trade cards to lit plastic on a bypass, and both Carolinas are full of it.

What the pig is doing. Three arrangements cover most of them, and a reader can sort a sign from a moving car.

The pig is the cook. A toque — the tall white pleated chef's hat — an apron, sometimes a fork. Red Pig Drive-In at Nahunta, Georgia, photographed by John Margolies in 1979, is the neon version: a white pig in a toque, upright on two trotters, carrying a domed serving tray at shoulder height, the words RED PIG running down a red pylon beside it and DRIVE IN in neon along the base.

The pig is the customer. Carol Highsmith's photograph of the Pig on Beale sign in Memphis catches a neon pig in wraparound sunglasses with both trotters round a pork sandwich, mid-bite, under the line PORK WITH AN ATTITUDE!

The pig is the employee. Three Little Pigs Bar-B-Q in Memphis has a pig in blue dungarees holding the whole signboard over its head, and three more along the roofline each carrying one letter of BAR-B-Q. The pig here is not eating and not cooking. It is working for the business that sells it.

The blog that named it. For five years a Seattle blogger collected these. Suicide Food ran from 20 December 2006 to 27 December 2011 and posted 929 times, most posts carrying several images. Its author signs himself Ben; the surname Grossblatt comes from a profile Lindy West wrote in The Stranger in November 2007, and appears nowhere in the blog itself.

The blog's own definition, from its header, is a depiction of animals that "act as though they wish to be consumed". Every entry got a rating on a five-point scale headed Psych Evaluations and counted in nooses, from one noose, mildly troubling, to five. The pig tag holds 539 posts and the bbq tag 399, which is the largest strand in the file by a wide margin; chef hat runs to 114 and sunglasses to 107. An eleven-part series across four years gave the recycled stock-clipart pig its own name: Repetitious Porcine Emblemology.

The blog is vegan advocacy and says so; the last post calls the project a pause rather than an ending. It is still online. This project uses it as what it is — the only systematic catalogue of the genre anyone has made — without taking up its argument.

Older than the neon. The pig was doing this before electricity. Richard Sheaff, writing for the Ephemera Society of America, notes that American chromolithograph trade-card makers had a particular fondness for pigs on two legs, and singles out cards from J. S. & M. Peckham of Utica, New York — a firm that made agricultural furnaces and pig scalders — as apparently cannibalistic. The cards are not dated on that page, and Peckham was a nineteenth-century firm, so the genre is older than 1900 by an unfixed margin.

*Inference —* what the form solves is a drawing problem. A barbecue restaurant has to put an animal on its sign, because that is what it sells, and a dead pig does not sell lunch. Standing the pig up, dressing it and handing it a tray moves it out of the category of carcass and into the category of host. The sign painter is not making a point about slaughter. He is avoiding one.

In the Carolinas. The Carolina examples that are free to show are the ones a government camera happened to catch. Margolies photographed Maurice Bessinger's sign at West Columbia, South Carolina, in 1988: a pig called Little Joe in a red shirt, hands behind its back, standing on the crown of a BAR-B-Q sign over the words Flying Pig, Coast to Coast. The pit offices burned in October 2024 and the sign survived.

*Tradition holds —* the form is everywhere in both states, on plastic pylons, on painted plywood at a firehouse fundraiser, on a smoker trailer's door, and most of those pigs are the same few pieces of clip art bought by a sign shop and reused across a county. What is scarce is not the pigs but free photographs of them: most Carolina signs standing today are photographed under copyright, so this record leans on Georgia, Tennessee and one South Carolina survivor to show a form the Carolinas are thick with.

the pig that serves itself to the pig mascot: the same animal without a job: a smiling pig that stands for the business but is not cooking, eating or serving.

the pig that serves itself to Pigs in the City: Lexington's painted sculptures, which take the upright pig and give it every job except this one.

the pig that serves itself to Maurice's Piggie Park BBQ: whose West Columbia sign carries Little Joe, the best-documented Carolina example.

the pig that serves itself to Bessinger's Bar-B-Q: the Charleston side of the same family, and the same pig on its packaging.

the pig that serves itself to Maurice Bessinger: who put the pig on the sign and kept it there for half a century.

the pig that serves itself to hog: the animal, drawn as a person, which is the whole trick.

the pig that serves itself to barbecue: the word most of these signs spell Bar-B-Q, because the hyphens fit a pylon better.

the pig that serves itself to Going the whole hog — the 1830s barbecue lithographs: the 1830s habit of drawing a pig with a part to play, which the sign painters inherited.

the pig that serves itself to pig pickin': the occasion a hand-painted plywood pig usually announces.

title: The FSA photographs of Carolina eating
aliases: Marion Post Wolcott in the Carolinas
text:
The Farm Security Administration — a New Deal agency for rural poverty — kept photographers on the road from 1935, and their negatives went to the Library of Congress as federal work, free of copyright. Marion Post Wolcott worked North and South Carolina in 1939. What survives of Carolina eating is the occasion rather than the pit: a corn shucking at Tally Ho, near Stem in Granville County, North Carolina, with the tables that followed it; ministers and deacons at an outdoor picnic near Yanceyville; and a Fourth of July on St. Helena Island, South Carolina, shot on Kodachrome, which was new.

Tally Ho, Granville County, November 1939. A corn shucking was a work party: neighbours came, shucked a farmer's crop, and were fed. Wolcott photographed one at Uncle Henry Garrett's place near Stem. The men sit on kitchen chairs in a chest-high drift of shucks with the crib behind them, hats on, working through the pile.

The agency's own caption sheet says who ate when, and the project reproduces its wording because the arrangement is the fact: 'White women don't go to Negro shucking to help with the cooking but white men are fed by Negro women just the same as at other shucking week previous at Mr. Fred Wilkins' home.' A second frame is captioned 'The Negro tenants and neighbors eating dinner after the white men have finished.' It shows a long white-clothed table, ten or twelve men at it, glasses and plates and a big enamel basin at the near end. Two sittings, in that order, at a meal the second sitting had cooked.

St. Helena Island, July 1939. The FSA shot most of its work in black and white and a small part on Kodachrome, a colour film then a few years old. Wolcott's St. Helena Island Fourth of July is in that colour set, which is why these frames look nothing like the rest of the period.

Under pines hung with Spanish moss, a crowd stands around a cloth-covered table and a scatter of washtubs, pots and crates; one frame takes in a Texaco filling station behind the flag. The catalogue calls it a Fourth of July celebration and a Fourth of July picnic. It does not call it a barbecue.

What is not in the file. No photograph in the Carolina part of this collection that reached Wikimedia Commons is captioned as a barbecue, and none shows a hog on a pit. The agency's photographers caught Carolina barbecue only in its surroundings: the work party, the church meeting, the holiday crowd, the table afterwards. Two frames from near Yanceyville in Caswell County are captioned as an outdoor picnic held during the noon intermission of an all-day meeting of ministers and deacons — the church dinner, mid-century, in a field.

*Inference —* that is a fact about the photographers' brief rather than about the food. The FSA sent people to document rural poverty and federal relief, so a camera went where a committee met or a crop came in. An all-night pit in a shed behind a store was nobody's assignment. The pictures that do exist of a Carolina hog on a pit come later, from restaurants and from towns, and are mostly still in copyright.

A caution on the captions: the descriptions carried with these files are the agency's, written in 1939, and they use the racial vocabulary of that year. They are quoted rather than rewritten so that what the file says and what the file shows can be read against each other.

The FSA photographs of Carolina eating to hog killing: the other November work party a Carolina farm held, and the one Wolcott did not photograph here.

The FSA photographs of Carolina eating to fundraiser barbecue: the church dinner the Yanceyville picnic is an early frame of.

The FSA photographs of Carolina eating to pig pickin': the gathering these photographs stand next to: a crowd, a yard, food set out on boards.

The FSA photographs of Carolina eating to Adrian Miller: whose Black Smoke follows the cooks the FSA caption sheet records as feeding two sittings.

The FSA photographs of Carolina eating to Pee Dee whole-hog barbecue: the style whose region reaches down to St. Helena Island; the Fourth of July frames are the Lowcountry's oldest colour pictures here.

The FSA photographs of Carolina eating to Eastern North Carolina barbecue: Granville County lies at its western edge, where the whole hog and the Piedmont shoulder meet.

The FSA photographs of Carolina eating to roadside barbecue signs: the other government-owned picture collection this project draws on, from fifty years later.

title: the pig mascot
text:
One pig, drawn once, used everywhere a barbecue business puts its name: the sign, the menu, the sauce label, the takeout box, the trailer door, the roofline, the weather vane. It is standing, smiling and usually dressed. It has no job in the picture — it is neither cooking nor eating — and that is what separates it from the pig that serves itself. A mascot is an identity: a customer who sees a pig on a bottle in a grocery aisle is meant to think of a particular pit in a particular town.

Little Joe, and what a mascot is for. Maurice Bessinger's pig is the clearest Carolina case because it was photographed under a public-domain licence. John Margolies shot the West Columbia sign in 1988: at the top of a tall pylon, above illuminated block letters reading BAR-B-Q, a pink pig stands on two trotters in a red shirt with LITTLE JOE across the chest, a small cap on its head, hands tucked behind its back. The panel beneath reads Maurice Bessinger's Flying Pig, Coast to Coast, and under that a changeable letterboard was advertising for waitresses on the day of the photograph.

Coast to Coast is the point. The same pig went on the Carolina Gold sauce bottles that by 1999 made this the largest barbecue operation in the country, which is how a pig painted for one drive-in in West Columbia ended up on shelves in states with no barbecue of their own. When grocery chains pulled the sauce in 2000 over the Confederate flags Bessinger raised at his restaurants, what came off the shelf was the pig.

On a roof, and on a rod. The mascot does not stay on the sign. Wilber's Barbecue in Goldsboro put a pig on a weather vane, cut flat from sheet metal, turning above the roof of a restaurant that opened in 1962 — a running pig in silhouette, nose into the wind, with the four cardinal letters under it.

*Inference —* a weather vane is a particular choice. A sign faces the road and can be read only from one direction; a vane is visible from every direction and points nowhere in particular, so it says a building is here rather than pointing at a door. Putting the pig up there treats it less as advertising than as the thing on top of a church.

The form recurs: a fibreglass pig on a porch, a pig on a trailer, a pig outline in neon over an entrance. The animal ends up in the place a weathercock, a cross or a name would otherwise go.

Where these pigs come from. *Tradition holds —* most house pigs are not commissioned. A sign shop keeps a book of pig artwork, a new pit buys one, the letters change and the pig does not, so a county can carry the same six or eight pigs across twenty businesses that have never met. The blog Suicide Food gave that recycling its own name across an eleven-part series: Repetitious Porcine Emblemology, the stock pig turning up again and again under different names.

A few are drawn once and stay drawn. Those are the ones that end up on a bottle, a T-shirt and a tattoo, and the ones people can describe from memory years after the restaurant closed.

the pig mascot to the pig that serves itself: the same pig given something to do — a tray, a fork, a sandwich — which changes the joke.

the pig mascot to roadside barbecue signs: the pylon, the neon and the bottler's panel the mascot rides on.

the pig mascot to Pigs in the City: Lexington's sculptures, which are the house pig taken off the roof and set on the pavement.

the pig mascot to Maurice's Piggie Park BBQ: Little Joe's home pit at West Columbia, and the sign that survived the 2024 fire.

the pig mascot to Maurice Bessinger: who took one drive-in's pig onto grocery shelves across the country.

the pig mascot to Wilber's Barbecue: whose pig turns on a weather vane over Goldsboro rather than standing on a sign.

the pig mascot to Carolina Gold: the sauce brand the pig went onto, and came off when the chains dropped it.

the pig mascot to mustard-based barbecue sauce: what is in the bottle the pig is standing on.

the pig mascot to hog: the animal, and the word a customer reads off the picture without being told.

title: Pigs in the City
text:
Life-sized pig sculptures, painted by artists and set out on the sidewalks of Lexington, Davidson County. Uptown Lexington, Inc. — the non-profit set up to bring business back to the town centre — ran the first exhibition in 2003 with twenty pigs, each sponsored by a business for $1,000, which paid for the whole thing. More than 40,000 people came that first year. The pigs are fibreglass blanks, identical until the artist gets them, and they come back painted as anything: a fire engine, a bulldozer, a jigsaw puzzle, a winged horse. Retired ones stay out around town.

Where the pigs came from. The form is borrowed. *Tradition holds —* the painted-animal street exhibition spread from the cow parades of the late 1990s, and each town that took it up picked an animal of its own. Lexington's animal chose itself: the town calls itself the Barbecue Capital of the World and has held a barbecue festival on Main Street every October since 1984.

The exhibitions ran 2003 to 2005, and again in 2008 and 2009. In 2019 Uptown Lexington announced the pigs would return in 2020. A sponsor paid $1,000 in the first round and got a pig with the sponsor's commission on it; the money covered the programme. What the town got was a reason to walk from one block to the next, which is what a downtown revitalisation programme is usually trying to buy.

The names. The pigs are named, and the names are the point. Caterpiggar is a Caterpillar bulldozer: yellow, with an exhaust stack, a radiator grille, a dozer blade across the front, a model number P8 on the flank, and CATERPIGGAR lettered in the machine-maker's own typeface with its red underline. Fire Hog is a fire engine, red, with ladders down the side, the city fire department's crest on the shoulder and a black helmet over the snout. Pork Knox is money — banknotes and coins painted all over it, gold trotters, a bar chart along the back. Pigsaw is covered in jigsaw pieces. Pigasus is deep blue with gold wings, planets and stars. Newbee is banded teal and gold with gold antennae and a gauzy wing laid over its back. Deck the Halls is three small pigs in Santa hats and striped scarves around a signboard.

*Inference —* the naming is doing the same work as a barbecue restaurant's sign: it takes an animal that is about to be eaten and makes it a character with a job. The difference is that a Pigs in the City pig has no meat to sell, so the pun can be about anything at all, and usually is. None of these pigs is eating.

What happens to them afterwards. They do not go away. Dennis Brown photographed a set in 2008 and captioned them as previous entries now on display in various places in Lexington — a pig outside the business that sponsored it, a pig on a corner, a pig by a door. A visitor walking uptown meets pigs from several different years at once and cannot tell which round each came from without asking.

*Tradition holds —* the Barbecue Festival is when most people see them, because that is the Saturday the street is closed and everyone is walking. The festival brings its own inflatable and costumed pigs on top of the permanent ones.

title: Going the whole hog — the 1830s barbecue lithographs
text:
A small group of American political prints from the 1830s in which the barbecue is the joke and the pig is the politician. A lithograph — a print pulled from a drawing made on stone, the cheap illustrated medium of the period — could be sold loose from a shop window within days of the news. H. R. Robinson of New York issued The Political Barbecue in 1834, laying Andrew Jackson on a grid iron over a brick pit lettered PUBLIC OPINION, with one bystander remarking that in South Carolina it is called barbecue. Others draw out the campaign phrase going the whole hog. They are the oldest barbecue pictures this project can show.

What going the whole hog meant. The phrase was already a political term of art before the prints. To go the whole hog was to back a man or a measure entirely, without the hedging and half-support a faction could otherwise offer, and in the Jackson years it attached itself to the Democrats — a Whig could use it as an accusation of blind loyalty and a Democrat could use it as a boast, which is what makes it usable in a picture.

Both sides did use it. One of these sheets is not a cartoon at all but a ballot: a Democratic ticket for Martin Van Buren for President and Richard M. Johnson for Vice President, with the Ohio electors listed under them, and at the head a woodcut of a man in a tall hat carrying a hog across his shoulders. Two banners come off the hog. One reads Going the whole Hog. The other reads Pork 10 cts. p lb.

The pun sits on a real thing. A whole hog was what a barbecue actually cooked: the animal split and laid over coals, fed to a crowd assembled to hear a candidate. A print that draws a whole hog in an election year is making a joke and reporting a fact at once, and the audience had to be told neither half.

Robinson's Jackson on the grid iron. The Political Barbecue, a lithograph on wove paper about 25.5 by 36.6 centimetres, was published by H. R. Robinson at 52 Courtlandt Street, New York, in 1834, and is held by the Library of Congress. Andrew Jackson lies stripped on a grid iron over a brick pit with two arched fireboxes, and the word lettered along the brickwork between them is PUBLIC OPINION. Justice stands at the left with her scales and a knife. Five men in tall hats lean over the body; two more crouch at the fireboxes working the coals.

The speech balloons are a survey of what the country called the thing. One man says that in Massachusetts they call it roasting; another that in Kentucky it is their High Game to their Low Jack. A third says: 'In South Carolina it is called Barbecue only he wants a little more Basting.' The sheet is a national joke that stops to name South Carolina as the place where the word lives.

A second treatment of the subject, undated but placed around 1832 to 1833, survives in the Digital Commonwealth from an unknown artist, captioned The political barbecue, Going the whole hog. Robinson's other sheet drops the fire altogether: Going the Whole Hog shows an enormous sow lying in a yard, a band across her shoulders reading THE EMPIRE STATE, and a litter of small pigs at her, each labelled with an office or a favour. A signpost points To Kinderhook, Van Buren's home village. Van Buren leans over the fence and says the sow and her litter have made him the greatest man in the Union; a farmer opposite, drawn with a Dutch accent, says the pigs will suck the life's blood out of that old sow.

Why they sit in a Carolina catalogue. None of these prints is Carolinian. They are New York and Boston commercial lithographs about national politics. They belong here because the thing they are joking about is the Carolina and Virginia political barbecue: the free feed a candidate laid on to gather a crowd, which Robert Moss finds established in the colonies by the 1700s and running through the early republic.

*Inference —* a cartoonist only reaches for an image his readers already hold. That a northern print shop could draw a candidate on a barbecue grid iron in 1834 and expect the country to get it says the southern political barbecue was national furniture by then. South Carolina's Galivants Ferry stump meeting, which began in 1880 and is still held, is the same institution two generations later, with the pig still on the fire.

Going the whole hog — the 1830s barbecue lithographs to political barbecue: the institution the prints are drawing: the candidate's free pig and the crowd it gathers.

Going the whole hog — the 1830s barbecue lithographs to whole hog: the cooking the phrase is a pun on, and the meat of the colonial rally.

Going the whole hog — the 1830s barbecue lithographs to hog: the word doing the work in every one of these prints.

Going the whole hog — the 1830s barbecue lithographs to Robert F. Moss: the historian who puts the whole-hog political rally in the colonies by the 1700s.

Going the whole hog — the 1830s barbecue lithographs to barbecue: the word a bystander in the 1834 print says South Carolina uses, while Massachusetts says roasting.

Going the whole hog — the 1830s barbecue lithographs to the pig that serves itself: the later American habit of putting a pig on a sign and giving it a part to play.

Going the whole hog — the 1830s barbecue lithographs to fundraiser barbecue: the surviving form of the free feed that gathers a crowd for a purpose.

title: roadside barbecue signs
text:
The sign a barbecue place puts at the road: a steel pylon with a lit box on top, neon or bulbs picking out a name, a bottler's disc above it, and a changeable letterboard underneath for the day's news. Most spell the word Bar-B-Q, hyphenated, because three short units fit a tall narrow cabinet better than nine letters do. What survives in photographs that anyone may reuse comes almost entirely from one man's slides: John Margolies drove American highways from the late 1960s to 2008 photographing exactly this, and the Library of Congress bought the archive and the rights with it.

Who paid for the sign. Often not the restaurant. Steve's Bar-B-Q in Spencer, North Carolina, photographed by Margolies in 1982, is a blue steel cabinet with STEVE'S and BAR-B-Q in white neon script on two lines — and above it, larger than either, a Pepsi-Cola bottle cap in red, white and blue neon, chipped and weathered. The soft-drink bottler supplied and maintained signs like this in return for the top panel and the exclusive pour.

*Inference —* that arrangement explains a good deal about how these signs look. The restaurant's name sits under a national brand's disc, in the bottler's palette rather than its own, and the proportions are the bottler's too. A place that later bought its own sign generally got a bigger pig and a smaller cola.

The pig on top. Where the pit paid for its own, the pig went above the letters. Margolies photographed Maurice Bessinger's West Columbia sign in 1988 from two angles: a pylon in white and pale-blue stripes, a red panel of BAR-B-Q in bulb-lit block capitals with a chase of yellow lamps round the border, the pig Little Joe standing on the crown, and below the box a white panel reading Maurice Bessinger's Flying Pig, Coast to Coast. Under all of it the letterboard, on the day, said NOW HIRING WAITRESSES.

The layout is the standard one: brand on top, product word in the largest type, the human business — hours, hiring, specials — on a board somebody changes with a suction cup on a pole. Bessinger's offices and pits burned in October 2024; the sign was still standing afterwards.

The Margolies archive, and why this record leans on it. John Margolies photographed roadside commercial architecture for about forty years and left 11,710 colour slides. The Library of Congress digitised them and bought the intellectual property, so the whole archive carries no known restrictions on publication — which makes it the largest freely reusable picture file of American signs in existence, and the reason a page about Carolina barbecue signs can be illustrated at all.

He shot only a handful in the Carolinas that touch this subject: Bessinger's twice, Steve's at Spencer once. Elsewhere in the same file are the Red Pig at Nahunta, Georgia, and a plain BAR-B-Q at Brownsville, Tennessee, bulbs round a rectangle on a pole in 1979. *Inference —* he was driving routes, not surveying a cuisine, so what he caught in any state is a function of which highway he was on that week.

The practical consequence for this project: the Carolina signs standing today — Lexington's, Ayden's, Hemingway's — are photographed constantly, and very few of those photographs are free to reuse.

The board and the plaque. Not every barbecue sign is lit. At the Lone Star BBQ and Mercantile at Santee, South Carolina, the signs are wooden boards hung from the porch roofs of old frame buildings moved to the site and set on brick piers: Shuler's DINING HALL on one, Dantzler's SOCIAL HALL on the next, painted in a serif face with the family name above the room's function. This is the older Carolina form — the building carries the sign rather than a pole beside it — and it reads at walking pace rather than at fifty miles an hour.

The third kind is cast. A bronze tablet set into a stucco wall in Lexington commemorates the site of the first known business selling Lexington-style barbecue, prepared under tents on open pits, and records that the North Carolina House of Representatives designated the city the Hickory-Cooked Barbecue Capitol of Piedmont North Carolina. The Lexington City Council commissioned it on March 11, 1985. *Inference —* a town that has a plaque made has stopped advertising and started claiming.

title: Where all of this came from
text:
Everything on this site is built from things anyone can open: public-domain cookbooks, openly licensed encyclopaedias and photographs, open map data, oral histories published by the people who recorded them, and the directories that businesses list themselves in. This page is the list, so a reader can check the work or go further than we did.

Recipes you may cook from and republish. Cookbooks published in the United States before 1930 are in the public domain, and the Southern ones are digitised. Michigan State University's *Feeding America* project holds scanned and transcribed historic American cookbooks; the Internet Archive holds the rest. The books this site draws on include *Dixie Cookery* (Maria Massey Barringer, Concord, North Carolina, 1867), *The Carolina Housewife* (Sarah Rutledge, Charleston, 1847), *Housekeeping in Old Virginia* (1879), *Mrs. Hill's New Cook Book* (1867), *What Mrs. Fisher Knows About Old Southern Cooking* (Abby Fisher, 1881) and *The Carolina Rice Cook Book* (1901).

Wikibooks' Cookbook is CC BY-SA: its recipes may be copied anywhere, with the page named and the licence carried along.

A recipe still in copyright is different. The list of ingredients is a fact and may be repeated; the instructions are the author's writing. Where this site gives a modern recipe it gives the ingredients and links to the rest.

Pictures. Wikimedia Commons is the vein: every file states its licence, and this site accepts only CC0, public domain, CC BY, CC BY-SA and the Free Art License. The Library of Congress holds three collections worth the trip — Carol M. Highsmith's photographs, the John Margolies roadside archive of 11,710 slides of American signs, and the Farm Security Administration negatives from the 1930s and 1940s — all with no known restrictions, and much of it mirrored on Commons, which is how this site reached them.

The State Archives of North Carolina keeps 117,159 photographs on Flickr Commons, and it is the one place with postcards and pit photographs of named Carolina barbecue houses — Wilbur's, Parker's, Clyde Cooper's on East Davie Street in Raleigh in 1963. They are marked no known copyright restrictions, which is a weaker statement than public domain: it means nobody has found a rights-holder, not that there is none. The marking also runs photograph by photograph rather than collection by collection, and some images sit in that archive twice, once reserved and once released. Nothing from it is used here yet.

The New York Public Library's digitised *Green Book* collection is the record of where Black travellers could eat in these two states between 1936 and 1966. Twenty-two of its twenty-three volumes are public domain; the 1966-67 International Edition is not, and carries an orphan-works statement instead — the copyright may exist and no holder has been found. The scans carry no searchable text, so a Carolina listing has to be found by eye.

Maps and places. OpenStreetMap supplies every place point here, under the Open Database Licence, which is share-alike: the derived table at api/places.json carries the same licence. Natural Earth supplies the state outlines and is public domain. Nominatim, OpenStreetMap's own geocoder, filled in the towns and counties.

Directories that make a tag possible. A tag on a place here means somebody published something, and this is where we look.

Black-owned: EatOkra's directory, Black Restaurant Week's listings, and the Southern Foodways Alliance's oral histories, in which owners speak for themselves.

Woman-owned: WBENC's certified directory and the federal Women-Owned Small Business search, plus press profiles that name the owner.

LGBTQ+ welcoming: the Charlotte LGBT Chamber of Commerce, Blue Ridge Pride in Asheville, the Alliance For Full Acceptance in the Lowcountry, SC Pride, and OpenStreetMap's own lgbtq=* tag, which businesses and mappers set deliberately.

Cooks over wood: True 'Cue's certified list, the North Carolina Barbecue Society's Historic Barbecue Trail, and the South Carolina Barbeque Association.

None of these is inferred. If a page does not say it, this site does not tag it — and a place without a tag has only not been read yet.

Oral history. The Southern Foodways Alliance has recorded pitmasters in both states and publishes the transcripts and the audio. Where a place or a person here has an interview, the page links to it. It is the best single source on this subject that costs nothing to read.

Where all of this came from to Southern Foodways Alliance: the archive most of the first-person material on this site comes from.

Where all of this came from to Campaign for Real Barbecue: publishes the list of certified wood-cooking pits this site reads the wood tag from.

Where all of this came from to North Carolina Barbecue Society: publishes the Historic Barbecue Trail, the other wood list.

Where all of this came from to South Carolina Barbeque Association: publishes South Carolina's trail and the four-sauce map.

Where all of this came from to Adrian Miller: whose Black Smoke is the history behind half the directories on this page.

title: How to order
aliases: what to say at the counter
text:
At a Carolina barbecue counter the words are short and they mean particular things. Barbecue is the meat, not the event. A tray has no bread; a plate does. Chopped, coarse chopped and sliced are three different textures off the same shoulder. Outside brown is the crust and you have to ask for it. This is the vocabulary, west and east, with what it gets you.

Say the meat first. "Barbecue" on its own means chopped pork here, and ordering "pulled pork" marks you as from somewhere else — which is fine, and will be understood, and may be remarked upon.

In the Piedmont the shoulder comes three ways. **Chopped** is worked small on the block with cleavers. **Coarse chopped** is left in bigger pieces, which holds the smoke better and is what half the regulars order. **Sliced** is what it sounds like, and is the oldest form; Lexington Barbecue will do all three.

In the east it is chopped, and the crisp skin is chopped through it. That is the texture; there is no other option and no one wants one.

Outside brown. The outside of a shoulder that has been over coals for ten hours goes dark and firm and tastes more of smoke and dip than anything else on the tray. In Lexington you ask for **outside brown**, or **brownies**, or just **brown**, and you get it chopped through the rest or on its own. Some pits charge the same; some charge more; a few will tell you they ran out at eleven.

The eastern equivalent is not a cut but a texture: ask for **more skin** and the block will oblige.

Tray, plate, sandwich. A **tray** is barbecue and slaw in a paper boat, no bread. A **plate** adds hushpuppies or cornbread and usually a second side. A **sandwich** is chopped pork on a soft white bun with slaw on the meat, not beside it — if you do not want slaw, say so when you order, because it goes on by default.

By the **pound** is how a family eats. A pound feeds three people who are not very hungry. Sauce comes in a jar if you ask.

South Carolina adds one word. **Hash.** It is a thick meat gravy cooked from the hog, ladled over white rice, and in the Midlands it is not a side but half the reason to be there. Order **hash and rice** and you will be taken seriously. Many South Carolina pits run a **buffet** on Friday and Saturday only, which is the other thing to know before driving out.

What not to say. Do not ask for brisket in a whole-hog house; they will point at the pig on the sign. Do not ask which sauce is correct — you will get an answer, at length, and it will be the house's. Do not arrive at two in the afternoon on a Saturday expecting a whole-hog pit to still be open: several of them close when the hogs are gone, which is the point of cooking only as many as they cook.

And whatever you order, they have heard it. The counter is not a test.

How to order to chopped: the word for how the meat comes off the block, and the three textures it names.

How to order to outside brown: the crust you have to ask for by name.

How to order to barbecue tray: what you get when you say tray: meat and slaw, no bread.

How to order to barbecue sandwich: slaw goes on the meat unless you say otherwise.

How to order to hash and rice: the South Carolina order that changes the conversation.

How to order to barbecue: the word itself, which here is a noun for pork.

How to order to dip: the Piedmont's word for the sauce on the table.

How to order to Lexington Barbecue: the Lexington counter where all three textures are on the board.

How to order to Skylight Inn BBQ: the eastern counter where the menu is short and the answer is a tray.

title: The Great Divide
text:
North Carolina cooks barbecue two ways and has never agreed to disagree about it. East of Raleigh the whole hog goes on the pit and the sauce is vinegar, salt and pepper with no tomato in it. In the Piedmont only the shoulder goes on, the sauce gets ketchup and a little sugar, and the slaw turns red because it is dressed with that sauce. The argument between them has run in newspapers, been put to a vote in the General Assembly, and is conducted daily at lunch counters in both places.

Two columnists and a state legislature. The modern quarrel has named combatants. Jerry Bledsoe of the Greensboro Daily News, who styled himself the world's leading, foremost barbecue authority, wrote for Lexington. Dennis Rogers of the Raleigh News & Observer, the oracle of the holy grub, wrote for the east. Bledsoe's verdict on his opponent went into print: Rogers, he wrote, 'has ruined any chances of this state being distinguished in its barbecue.'

It got as far as the statute book. Bills in 2006 would have made the Lexington Barbecue Festival the official barbecue festival of North Carolina, and were defeated — naming one style's festival meant choosing a side. The 2007 compromise, House Bill 433, made it the Official Food Festival of the Piedmont Triad Region instead: a regional title, carefully bounded, so that no barbecue could be called the state's.

What is actually different. Four things, and a Carolinian can check all four from the doorway.

The animal. East: the whole hog, everything but the squeal, chopped together so that ham, shoulder, belly and crisp skin end up in the same forkful. Piedmont: the shoulder only, which is fattier and darker, cooked longer, and comes off the block in bigger strands.

The sauce. East: vinegar, salt, black pepper, crushed red pepper. Piedmont: the same, plus ketchup or tomato, water and sugar — thin enough to pour, reddish rather than red, and called dip.

The slaw. East: white, mayonnaise. Piedmont: red, because it is dressed with the dip. This is the fastest tell on a plate.

The bread. East: cornbread, or corn sticks. Piedmont: hushpuppies.

The part both sides skip. The two styles are closer to each other than either is to anywhere else in the country: both are pork, both are vinegar at the root, both are served with slaw and a soft white roll, and neither sweetens the way Kansas City or the South Carolina Upstate does. The tomato in a Lexington dip is a tablespoon of ketchup, not a sauce.

*Inference —* the loudness of the argument is a function of how small the difference is. Nobody in Ayden argues with Texas.

The other thing both sides skip: for most of two centuries the people at the pit through the night were Black cooks, enslaved and then paid, in the east and the Piedmont alike, and their names came off the signs as the restaurants incorporated. Adrian Miller's *Black Smoke* is the book that follows that labour and its disappearance, and it is the one history neither camp can claim against the other.

South Carolina, which has four of these arguments. Across the line the map is busier. South Carolina's tourism office prints four sauce regions: mustard through the Midlands where German families settled, vinegar and pepper in the Pee Dee and along the coast, a light tomato sauce through the middle, and heavy tomato in the Upstate. The Pee Dee cooks the whole hog with vinegar and pepper, which makes it eastern North Carolina's first cousin and a long way from Columbia in every sense.

South Carolinians will tell you the four-way map is the more interesting problem. North Carolinians will tell you that a state which puts mustard on a pig has forfeited the right to an opinion.

The Great Divide to Eastern North Carolina barbecue: one of the two combatants: whole hog, clear vinegar, white slaw, cornbread.

The Great Divide to Lexington-style barbecue: the other: shoulders, red dip, red slaw, hushpuppies.

The Great Divide to Lexington Barbecue Festival: the festival the 2006 bills tried to make the state's own, and the 2007 act made the Piedmont Triad's instead.

The Great Divide to Jerry Bledsoe: the Piedmont's columnist, who called himself the world's foremost barbecue authority and meant it about half seriously.

The Great Divide to Dennis Rogers: the east's columnist, the oracle of the holy grub, who took the whole hog's side for decades.

The Great Divide to red slaw: the fastest way to tell which side of the line a plate came from.

The Great Divide to vinegar-and-pepper sauce: the sauce the east will not add tomato to.

The Great Divide to Lexington dip: the tablespoon of ketchup that started a war.

The Great Divide to Pee Dee whole-hog barbecue: eastern North Carolina's cousin across the state line, cooking the same hog with the same sauce.

The Great Divide to South Carolina mustard barbecue: the answer South Carolina's Midlands gives, which neither North Carolina camp accepts.

The Great Divide to Adrian Miller: whose Black Smoke follows the cooks both camps forgot to argue about.

title: The Sunday question
text:
Sunday is the day a Carolina barbecue house is most likely to be shut, and the day some people will tell you not to order barbecue anyway. Neither is about the meat being worse on a Sunday. Both are about when the fire was lit. This page lays out what can be counted, what the pits themselves say, and what is belief — and this directory does not take a side.

What the days actually show. Of the places here whose days we could read, Saturday is kept by nearly all of them and Sunday is the one they drop. Monday is the next thinnest. The rest of the map has not published its days at all, and that is a hole in this directory rather than a finding about the Carolinas.

*Inference —* the shape is the cooking week, not the calendar. A pit that cooks whole hogs overnight needs the crew rested and the pits cleaned before it starts again, so the quiet end of the week lands where the trade is thinnest.

Why the pit is cold on Sunday. Our State, writing about Wilber's in Goldsboro, put it as plainly as anyone: the only day the pit isn't fired up is Sunday, when the restaurant is closed. The fire and the opening hours are the same fact stated twice.

That sentence has since been overtaken, and the way it was overtaken is the point. Wilber's closed in 2019, reopened in 2020, and now posts Sunday hours itself. A pit's week is a business decision that gets revisited, not a law — which is why this directory dates what it knows and says who said it.

Church is the other half, and the two have never been in competition: a Sunday closing suits a staff at service in the morning and a town that eats at home after it. *Tradition holds —* a pit that has cooked through Friday night and sold out Saturday has nothing left to sell on Sunday even if it wanted to, which is why 'closed Sunday' and 'closes when it runs out' so often sit on the same door.

The belief about Sunday meat. *Tradition holds —* that barbecue eaten late in the week, Sunday included, is not the same as barbecue eaten the day it came off the pit; that what you are served on a slow day is the tail of a cook that started days earlier; and that a pit which is busy is a pit that is cooking fresh. Some people will not order barbecue on a Sunday for that reason, and some will not order it on a Monday for the same one.

This directory records the belief and does not test it. Nobody here has tasted anything, and a pit that reheats well is not a lesser pit. What the belief is useful for is reading a door: a place that cooks to sell out and closes is telling you its schedule, and a place open seven days is telling you a different one. Both are ways of running a barbecue house, and the Carolinas are full of both.

How to use the filter. The finder has an Open Sunday chip and an Open today chip. They show only the pits a source actually says are open, so a pit whose days nobody has published is left out of the answer rather than guessed at — which keeps the list short and keeps a guess off the map. If you know a pit's days, that is exactly the kind of thing this directory is missing.

The Sunday question to Wilber's Barbecue: the pit Our State used to describe as dark on Sunday, and which now posts Sunday hours — the example and its own correction.

The Sunday question to whole hog: the cut that sets the schedule — an overnight cook is why the week has a shape at all.

The Sunday question to Eastern North Carolina barbecue: the style most likely to cook to a number and stop when it is gone.

The Sunday question to pitmaster: whose week this is, and who needs the day off.
